content:
Ich war hier im Rahmen einer Tour die von meinem Hotel angeboten wurde. Die Sandbank selbst ist fast schon unwirklich schön und hat sicher mehr als einen Stern verdient. Drum herum gibt es viele Korallen und kleine Riffe mit Seeigeln oder Fischen. Und da fängt das Drama eigentlich auch schon an.
Täglich werden zur Lunch und vermutlich auch dinnerzeit Touristen mit Booten angekarrt. Es werden Tische, Stühle und Grills aufgebaut ( was ein Aufwand), um Seafood anzubieten. Der Müll wurde eingesammelt, zumindest grob.
Was mir gar nicht gut abging war der Umgang mit der Natur. Touristen griffen an Korallen rum, überall lagen Plastikflaschen und es wurde krach ohne Ende gemacht. Die Boote krachten gegen bestehende Korallenkolonien und Tiere wurden aktiv gefangen um sie den Touristen zu zeigen.
Es gab natürlich keinen Schatten, bis auf mitgebrachte Segel, die Temperatur stiegen auf ca. 45 Grad, es wundert mich, dass niemand kollabiert ist. Durch den weißen Sand und die Spiegelung, war die Sonne einfach unerträglich. JEDER auf der Tour hatte trotz Sonnenschutz einen heftigen Sonnenbrand.
Als alle Boote da waren, (ca. 50) sah es etwa so aus wie am Ballermann. Alkohol wurde allerdings nicht konsumiert, ich vermute mal dass die Leute Angst hatten umzukippen. Dafür war es Laut und voll,was dieser einzigartigen Landschaft keineswegs gerecht wurde.
Ich fand es schrecklich und habe einfach nur das Ende dieses Ausflugs beigesehnt.
Bad tourism.
translated_content:
I was here as part of a tour offered by my hotel. The sandbank itself is almost unrealistically beautiful and certainly deserves more than one star. Surrounding it are many corals and small reefs teeming with sea urchins and fish. And that's where the trouble really begins.
Every day, tourists are ferried in by boat for lunch and presumably dinner as well. Tables, chairs, and grills are set up (what an effort!) to offer seafood. The trash was collected, at least roughly.
What I found particularly disturbing was the way nature was treated. Tourists were touching corals, plastic bottles were lying everywhere, and there was constant noise. The boats were crashing into existing coral colonies, and animals were being actively caught to show the tourists.
Of course, there was no shade, except for the sails people brought with them. The temperature climbed to around 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), and I'm surprised no one collapsed. The white sand and its reflection made the sun simply unbearable. Everyone on the tour got a terrible sunburn, despite using sunscreen.
Once all the boats had arrived (around 50), it looked like a scene from a beach resort. No one was drinking alcohol, though; I suspect people were afraid of passing out. Instead, it was loud and crowded, which didn't do justice to this unique landscape at all.
I thought it was awful and just longed for the trip to end.
Bad tourism.

content:
I visited Zakir Wildlife in Zanzibar and unfortunately left very upset and concerned about the treatment of the animals.
There was a monkey there with a large, clearly visible wound on her tail. What concerned me even more was her reaction to the handler. She appeared very scared of him, while at the same time she was extremely gentle and friendly with us. She willingly came to us, lay down, and allowed us to cuddle and interact with her. The contrast between how comfortable she was with visitors and how frightened she appeared around the handler was very disturbing to witness.
We asked the staff directly why the monkey was injured and why she was not receiving treatment. We did not receive a clear or convincing answer.
Afterwards, we contacted Zakir Wildlife through Instagram because we were genuinely concerned about her welfare. They told us that the monkey was at the vet.
It has now been about a month, and  this monkey is no longer there, but theres no clear information what happened to her or whether she actually received proper treatment.
I sincerely hope she is alive, safe, and receiving veterinary care. However, the lack of transparency and the original condition of the animal are extremely concerning.
I am leaving this review because wildlife tourism should be about protecting and caring for animals, not simply allowing tourists to interact with them. If an animal has a serious visible wound, visitors deserve a clear explanation that appropriate veterinary care is being provided.
I strongly encourage anyone considering visiting to ask questions about the animals’ welfare and veterinary care before supporting this place

content:
Wir haben am 18.06.2026 eine Schnorcheltour zur Insel Mnemba  gebucht. Der Ablauf war bestens organisiert und wir wurden sehr pünktlich am Strand abgeholt. Unterwegs gab es ausreichend Früchte und Wasser.
Leider war unser Guide der englischen Sprache nicht ganz so mächtig und die Verständigung war daher eher schwierig und es gab nicht so viele Erklärungen.
Ein weiterer Punkt ist, dass uns die Tour zu Plätzen führte, die von weiteren Ausflugsbooten nur so überlaufen waren. Am Schnorchelplatz war es so voll, dass man Angst haben musste mit einem Boot zusammenzustoßen.
Beim Besuch der Sandbank konnten wir etwas abseits des Trubels ankern, was wirklich sehr, sehr schön war.
Als es dann um eine evtl. Delphinsichtung ging, waren wir schockiert. Es tauchten zwei Tiere auf, die regelrecht von den ganzen Booten (ca. 20) gejagt wurden, Leute sprangen ins Wasser um mit den Tieren zu schwimmen. Gott sei Dank haben die beiden Delphine das Weite gesucht. Wir hatten daraufhin keine Lust mehr weiter Ausschau zu halten.
Der Besuch eines weiteren Strandes oben im Norden war zwar ganz nett, aber letztendlich haben wir nicht ganz verstanden, was wir da sollten. Da das Englisch des Guides nicht ausreichte, konnte er es auch nicht wirklich erklären. Alle Boote fuhren dorthin, hinterm Strand lag ein Markt, wo lauter Touri-Nippes verkauft wurde, das sollte man sich sparen. Es war dort völlig überlaufen.
Alles in allem würden wir die Tour so nicht nochmal buchen.
Der schöne Besuch der Sandbank und die auch recht schöne Fahrt an der Küste entlang kann leider die anderen negativen Erfahrungen nicht aufwiegen.
translated_content:
We booked a snorkeling tour to Mnemba Island on June 18, 2026. The tour was very well organized, and we were picked up from the beach right on time. Plenty of fruit and water were provided along the way.
Unfortunately, our guide's English wasn't very good, making communication rather difficult, and there weren't many explanations.
Another issue was that the tour took us to places that were absolutely overrun with other tour boats. The snorkeling spot was so crowded that we were afraid of colliding with another boat.
When we visited the sandbar, we were able to anchor a little away from the hustle and bustle, which was truly wonderful.
When the topic of a possible dolphin sighting came up, we were shocked. Two dolphins appeared and were practically chased by all the boats (around 20 of them). People were jumping into the water to swim with them. Thankfully, the two dolphins took flight. After that, we didn't feel like looking for any more. Visiting another beach further north was nice enough, but ultimately we didn't quite understand what we were supposed to be doing there. Since the guide's English wasn't good enough, he couldn't really explain it. All the boats went there, and behind the beach was a market selling nothing but tourist trinkets – definitely not worth the trip. It was completely overcrowded.
All in all, we wouldn't book this tour again. The lovely visit to the sandbank and the rather scenic boat trip along the coast unfortunately couldn't compensate for the other negative experiences.

content:
Great company great owner. We stayed near this beach and from our beach We were quoted 100usd for two people for the dolphin tour. We decided to drive around and ask around. This owner gave us the best offer directly without bargaining back n forth which saved us time. We also drive to nungwi and it was cheaper like 50 usd for two but it''s shared trip with maybe 8 other people And We didn''t want to drive 50mins for that. So We made the arrangement with the owner the night before. He prepared lots of fruits for us way more than enough for two. His customer service was great He asked for our feedback And made sure that we were not pushed by the skippers to come back. We saw dolphins And were able to swim with them 3 out if 4 attempts. We then snorkeled at one or two spots before we went for the break at the sandbank. The sandbank was so nice one of the best beaches i have ever been to. We had the option to snorkel here again but it was getting a bit cold for us so we skipped it. Some people found starfishes here.
The service was quite professional We had a local guy called cappuccino And the skipper was Mobi. Cappuccino was guiding us in the water the also took a swim ring with him for safety the whole time we snorkled.
The trip from this beach to the dolphin spot was taking longer than expected. Due to the low tides And shallow water the boat was going at a very slow speed the whole time. So it took almost 1hr each way. Plan that into your Overall time. We chose to leave at 7.30am (actually left around 7.40) And got back just after 12.10pm.
To Avoid the crowd i suggest departing at6.30am as suggested by the owner but it was too early so we asked for 7.30am ourselves. There were a lot of boats already. If you want to take photos of the dolphins make sure you do that before leaving for snorkeling as you won''t be able to turn back and see the dolphins again Once left.

content:
Anglikański kościół – Katedra Kościoła Chrystusowego, zbudowana w miejscu dawnego targu niewolników w Stone Town (w starej części miasta Zanzibar, stolicy Zanzibaru – obszar Stone Town został w roku 2000 wpisany na listę światowego dziedzictwa UNESCO). To co najbardziej mnie zszokowało, to fakt, że handel niewolnikami został zniesiony na rozkaz sułtana dopiero pod koniec XIX wieku, w roku 1873!
Zanzibar był we władaniu Portugalczyków od końca XV wieku aż do 1698 roku, kiedy wyspę przejęli sułtani Omanu. Miejsce stało się wtedy centrum handlu, w tym handlu niewolnikami – ze względu na strategicznie korzystne położenie geograficzne na Oceanie Indyjskim, Europejczycy chętne zaopatrywali się tutaj w siłę roboczą do pracy w koloniach. Według szacunków historyków, w latach 1830-1873 sprzedano tutaj jako towar około 600.000 osób, a wielu innych niewolników było tu przetrzymywanych w drodze do miejsc docelowych. Było to największy rynek niewolników w Afryce Wschodniej.
W roku 1861 Zanzibar stał się kolonią brytyjską. Już wtedy wielu aktywistów prowadziło kampanię na rzecz zniesienia niewolnictwa. Szczególnie aktywni byli brytyjski (szkocki) odkrywca i medyk David Livingstone, a także anglikański biskup Edward Steere. Po ostatecznym zniesieniu niewolnictwa w 1873 roku biskup Steere położył kamień węgielny pod budowę kościoła, który miał być symbolem uwolnienia od tyranii. Katedra została ukończona w 1879 roku, jest zbudowana z kamieni z rafy koralowej, łącząc różne style architektoniczne, z wyraźnymi akcentami lokalnymi i arabskimi.
Zanzibar odłączył się od Imperium Brytyjskiego w 1963 roku. W  styczniu 1964 roku doszło do rewolucji, w wyniku której kraj stał się niezależną Republiką Zanzibaru i Pemba, a trzy miesiące później, w kwietniu tego roku, utworzył z Republiką Tanganiki nowe państwo – Tanzanię, zachowując znaczną autonomię (m.in. oddzielny rząd i prezydent).
Obok katedry znajduje się pomnik Pamięci Niewolników, wykonany przez szwedzką rzeźbiarkę Clarę Sörnäs w 1998 roku. Od 2006 roku otwarta jest wystawa Wschodnioafrykańskiego Rynku Niewolników – zwiedzanie zmusza do zadumy nad człowieczeństwem. Można zobaczyć m.in. dwa pomieszczenia w wilgotnych i zimnych piwnicach, w których w nieludzkich warunkach przetrzymywano nieprawdopodobnie stłoczonych niewolników, a także ekspozycję materiałów i zdjęć dotyczących tego haniebnego procederu (transport niewolników, handel, cele podróży, zniesienie niewolnictwa, ale też nowe formy niewolnictwa, które występują w XXI wieku).
translated_content:
The Anglican church, Christ Church Cathedral, was built on the site of a former slave market in Stone Town (in the old part of Zanzibar City, the capital of Zanzibar – the Stone Town area was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000). What shocked me most was the fact that the slave trade was abolished by order of the Sultan only at the end of the 19th century, in 1873!
Zanzibar was under Portuguese rule from the late 15th century until 1698, when the island was taken over by the Sultans of Oman. It then became a center of trade, including the slave trade – due to its strategically advantageous geographical location in the Indian Ocean, Europeans eagerly sourced labor for their colonies. According to historians' estimates, between 1830 and 1873, approximately 600,000 people were sold here as merchandise, and many more slaves were held here en route to their destinations. It was the largest slave market in East Africa.
In 1861, Zanzibar became a British colony. By then, many activists were campaigning for the abolition of slavery. British (Scottish) explorer and physician David Livingstone, as well as Anglican Bishop Edward Steere, were particularly active. After the final abolition of slavery in 1873, Bishop Steere laid the foundation stone for a church intended to symbolize freedom from tyranny. The cathedral, completed in 1879, is built of coral reef stones, combining various architectural styles with distinct local and Arabic accents.
Zanzibar seceded from the British Empire in 1963. In January 1964, a revolution took place, resulting in the country becoming the independent Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba. Three months later, in April of that year, it formed a new state – Tanzania – with the Republic of Tanganyika, while retaining significant autonomy (including a separate government and president).
Next to the cathedral stands the Slave Memorial, created by Swedish sculptor Clara Sörnäs in 1998. Since 2006, the East African Slave Market exhibition has been open – a visit forces one to reflect on humanity. Visitors can see, among other things, two rooms in the damp and cold basements where slaves were held in incredibly cramped conditions, as well as an exhibition of materials and photographs relating to this shameful practice (the transport of slaves, the trade, their destinations, the abolition of slavery, and the new forms of slavery occurring in the 21st century).

What made the experience even more special was the artisan shop located nearby. The shop features incredible artwork and pictures, many of which are inspired by Zanzibar’s history, culture, and natural beauty. The artists’ craftsmanship is remarkable, and it’s a fantastic opportunity to support local talent while taking home a meaningful souvenir.
Overall, the combination of history, spirituality, and art makes this cathedral a place that touches your heart and leaves a lasting impression. Whether you’re exploring the historical landmarks of Stone Town or simply looking for a moment of quiet reflection, this cathedral should definitely be on your itinerary.

response_content: Unfortunately, this place is steeped in history, but like almost everywhere on the island, you're treated like a walking ATM. The island doesn't have much history, strictly speaking, and what little they do have, they make you sick of it. Let me explain: after touring the island and its monuments, I'm disappointed that it's not being used properly and that you're seen as just a cash cow. We paid 25,000 shillings to enter a church (well-maintained, admittedly), but it wasn't anything special, especially considering I'm Catholic and know about church history, and that in France, church visits are free. In short, if that were all, I'd come to see the infamous Slave Market Square, where the only evidence of this is five stone statues buried in the ground with a sign saying "with the participation of..." Nothing explains the history or purpose of the site, etc. Before leaving, we stumbled upon (because yes, otherwise it would have been over in 10 minutes, and I'm being generous) a room with explanations about slavery in Zanzibar (in English, of course), which delayed our exit. So, to conclude, it's steeped in history, all of which is great, but unfortunately, you're just a walking ticket. I have no other words. Perhaps others will be more objective than me, but it's true that I based my visit to most of the monuments in Stone Town on previous comments; perhaps mine will help. A word to the wise.

content:
To wade through the history of Zanzibar move a little north towards Bububu and reach Mtoni Palace Ruins. It islocated just north of Maruhubi, built between 1828 and 1834 for Sultan Said. The land believed to be belonged to Saleh bin Haramil, the Arab trader who imported the first cloves to Zanzibar. Mtoni means ‘place by the river’. This is the oldest Palace in Zanzibar.
Read the history before you are there.
One of Sultan Said’s daughters, Princess Salme later took the name Emily Ruete in her book, describes Mtoni Palace in the 1850s and her life.
Salama bint Said was born on 30 August 1844 and she spent her initial years in huge  Mtoni Palace, 8km north of Stone Town. After parents death she moved to Kisimbani, one of her estates. Finally moving to Stone Town. Here she became close to her neighbor, a German merchant, Rudolph Heinrich Ruete (born 10 March 1839; died 6 August 1870) and became pregnant by him. She fled to Germany. Her memoirs give insight into the history of Zanzibar.
Feel the history of beautiful Zanzibar with reading it and visiting the place. Good luck.

content:
If disappointment were a water sport, Coconuts Kite Zanzibar would be world champions.
From the moment I arrived, it felt less like a kite school and more like an experiment in how little effort can be stretched over an entire day. Organization was apparently optional, communication was a fun guessing game, and time moved at its own mysterious pace—mostly backward.
The vibe? Imagine enthusiasm being actively discouraged. Any questions were met with the kind of silence usually reserved for awkward elevators. Equipment looked like it had lived several previous lives and was now just tired of existing.
The beach itself is beautiful—though that’s entirely Zanzibar’s fault and in no way thanks to Coconuts. In fact, the highlight of the experience was realizing that simply standing still and staring at the ocean was infinitely more rewarding than engaging with anything offered here.
If you enjoy confusion, waiting around for no clear reason, and wondering how a place managed to get such a good location while doing absolutely nothing with it, then congratulations—you’ve found your spot.
Everyone else: do yourself a favor and keep walking. The wind deserves better.

content:
Our experience in Jambiani was unfortunately overshadowed by constant harassment from some beach vendors. Saying “no” was often not respected. We were repeatedly approached, whistled at to get our attention, and sometimes followed or pressured to continue the conversation after refusing. Instead of feeling able to relax, we felt we had to stay on guard whenever we walked along the beach.
We were also uncomfortable seeing children approach tourists asking for money or trying to attract attention. Whether encouraged by adults or not, it created an uneasy atmosphere and raised concerns about the involvement of children in tourist interactions.
We found that several beachfront restaurants offered disappointing value for money, with prices that felt high compared with the portion sizes served. In contrast, local restaurants away from the beachfront, e.g. Banana restaurant, provided better meals and better value during our stay. We also found that the Blue Oyster - beachfront - is really receptive to feedback and the food is delicious
The beach itself is beautiful, and many local residents going about their daily work, such as fishermen and seaweed harvesters, were respectful and did not disturb visitors. However, travellers looking for a peaceful and uninterrupted beach experience should be aware that this was not our experience in parts of Jambiani, and because of the above we don’t recommend Zanzibar.
full_address: MGJW+XQJ Jambiani Beach, Jambiani, Tanzania

content:
Zanzibar/Jambiani has real beauty — I’ve visited three times in five years because I wanted to believe in it. I won’t be returning.
The beach experience has deteriorated significantly. Declining vendors is now met with hostility, passive-aggressive comments, and verbal abuse. Not occasionally — consistently. “La asante” and walking away no longer works.
The food situation is equally frustrating. Restaurants are charging European prices for portions that wouldn’t satisfy a child. You’re paying Lisbon prices for a quarter of the plate.
If you’re coming to genuinely rest and recover, manage your expectations carefully. The paradise you see in photos requires a lot of work to access — and increasingly, it’s not worth the effort.

content: Szeroka plaża, która nadaje się do spokojnego kameralnego wypoczynku z dala od większych kurortów i dużych grup turystów. Znajduje się w południowo-wschodniej części wyspy, jest oddalona od dużych ośrodków. Nawet w szczycie sezonu jest tutaj dosyć cicho i każdy znajdzie dla siebie ustronne miejsce z dala od innych plażowiczów. Mniej Masajów niż w innych miejscach. Jambiani ciągnie się na długości ponad 2 km. Jest w całości pokryta drobnym, śnieżnobiałym piaskiem, który przypomina puder. Woda w oceanie jest krystalicznie czysta i ciepła, jednak dno nie jest wyłącznie piaszczyste, mogą pojawiać się tutaj zarówno drobne kamienie, jak i większe głazy. Na brzegu często można natomiast spotkać rozgwiazdy, kraby czy jeżowce. Dlatego też zaleca się noszenie specjalnych, gumowych butów do wody. Plaża jest również często pokryta glonami, które nanoszą silne pływy pojawiające się w tej okolicy. Co więcej, warto wiedzieć, że w tym miejscu odpływy są dosyć spore. W tym czasie możliwe jest jedynie plażowanie, natomiast nie ma możliwości korzystania z kąpieli w oceanie. Jeśli kochasz piękne plaże, ekscytujące atrakcje, dobre restauracje z pysznym jedzeniem i autentyczność, to miejsce przypadnie Ci do gustu.
translated_content: This wide beach is perfect for a quiet, intimate getaway away from the larger resorts and large tourist groups. Located in the southeastern part of the island, it's far from the major resorts. Even in peak season, it's relatively quiet, and everyone can find a secluded spot away from other beachgoers. There are fewer Maasai than in other locations. Jambiani stretches for over 2 km. It's entirely covered in fine, snow-white sand that resembles powder. The ocean water is crystal clear and warm, but the bottom isn't exclusively sandy; both small stones and larger boulders can appear. Starfish, crabs, and sea urchins are often found on the shore. Therefore, wearing special rubber water shoes is recommended. The beach is also often covered with algae, brought in by the strong tides that occur in this area. Furthermore, it's worth knowing that the tides here are quite high. During this time, only sunbathing is possible, not swimming in the ocean. If you love beautiful beaches, exciting attractions, good restaurants with delicious food and authenticity, you will love this place.

content:
We chose Jambiani over Kendwa or Nungwe in the north because it’s said it’s less touristy. There are plenty of hotels and resorts so there is still lot of tourism going on but the beach is so vast and there’s so much space for everyone.
In the evening the locals are coming to play soccer on the white sands which is fun to watch.
There are many kite surf shops for hiring equipment and one can take classes. The wind was pretty good when we were there in July and many people came to kite.
There’s an abundance of nice restaurants and bars along the beach and one holiday is not enough to try them all.
Almost endless walks along the beach are possible but at high tide sometimes there’s no space left to walk.
At low tide the water leaves big puddles behind and the local women are wading through them to collect crabs and shells.
Snorkelling is offered by tour operators but the reef is unfortunately not healthy and there’s not that much to see.

At first glance, Jambiani Beach is a dream beach, just like the ones you see in travel brochures. The water shimmers in a beautiful turquoise, the fine white sand is lined with palm trees – a true paradise.
However, there is one major drawback that can spoil the experience and could even harm tourism in the long run: the many beach vendors. Of course, it's understandable that locals try to earn a living selling coconuts, tours, or massages. But unfortunately, this is often done in a very pushy way. As soon as you respond to a friendly "Jambo, how are you?" or a similar greeting, you'll have a hard time getting rid of them.
For many tourists, a day at the beach means relaxation and peace – and this is precisely what is often disrupted here. The constant approach and the feeling of having to justify yourself if you don't want to buy anything can quickly become unpleasant. It would be desirable if there were a better solution so that both locals and tourists could have a more pleasant experience.
Nevertheless, Jambiani Beach remains a beautiful place in terms of scenery – those who can get used to the situation with the vendors or have appropriate strategies to avoid them will certainly have a great time here.

content:
Une destination kite et voile sur les bateaux de pêche. Difficile de s''y baigner, la marée basse permettant difficilement de nager, surtout s''il y a des kites dans le lagoon. Il faudra donc attendre la marée haute (attention aux bulles-méduses urticantes). Les hôtels sont quasiment à prix français sur le front de mer. Difficile de trouver quelque chose de propre sobre et sympa à moins de 70$ en pleine saison. La population vit dans la misère et les détritus juste derrière les hôtels du front de mer.
Si vous voulez réaliser des excursions en voiture, négociez plutôt tous les déplacements avec un chauffeur plutôt que de prendre un pack cher, qui ne vous permettra de voir qu''un seul lieu. (Programmez plutôt une journée complète Grotte-Épices-Joziani)
N''hesitez pas aller snorkler depuis la plage à marée haute, via un bateau de pêcheur. Les coraux sont au loin et nécessitent un bateau pour être vus.
translated_content: A kiteboarding and sailing destination on fishing boats. Swimming is difficult, as the low tide makes it hard to swim, especially if there are kiteboarders in the lagoon. You'll have to wait for high tide (beware of stinging jellyfish). Hotels on the waterfront are practically at French prices. It's hard to find anything clean, simple, and pleasant for less than $70 in peak season. The local population lives in poverty and amidst the trash right behind the waterfront hotels. If you want to take excursions by car, negotiate all the trips with a driver rather than buying an expensive package that will only allow you to see one place. (Plan a full day trip to Grotte-Épices-Joziani instead.) Don't hesitate to go snorkeling from the beach at high tide, using a fishing boat. The corals are far out and require a boat to see them.

content:
Plaża jest bardzo ładna. Długa i szeroka. Piasek idealnie biały. Na piasku leżą jednak często wodorosty i algi. Dodatkowo jeśli ktoś liczy na obserwacje życia morskiego to nie ma tu za wiele do obserwowania. Z racji odpływów i przypływów linia przegowa zmienia swoje położenia o jakieś 200 metrów. Ciężko wypłynąć tak daleko w ocean (bez łódki), żeby móc zobaczyć cokolwiek. Także w trakcie odpływu ocean jest bardzo daleko, a dodatkowo ciężko do niego dojść. W bardzo płytkich kałużach jest masa jeżowców.
Podsumowując na samo opalanie się super. Ewentualnie na kąpiele dla dzieci. Jeśli ktoś chce popływać o dowolnej porze dnia, albo pooglądać coś pod wodą, to raczej inna plaża.
translated_content:
The beach is very beautiful. Long and wide. The sand is perfectly white. However, the sand is often covered in seaweed and algae. Furthermore, if you're hoping to observe marine life, there's not much to see here. Due to the ebb and flow of the tide, the seabed changes position by about 200 meters. It's difficult to sail out far enough into the ocean (without a boat) to see anything. At low tide, the ocean is also very far away, and it's difficult to reach it. There are tons of sea urchins in the very shallow pools.
In short, it's great for sunbathing alone. It's also great for swimming with kids. If you want to swim at any time of day or just watch something underwater, this is a different beach.

content:
Мы стартовали из Нунгви на тук-тук- транспорте за 20.000 шиллингов в обе стороны,  и доехали до пещеры за 20 минут. Далее водитель нас ждал.
Здесь можно не только посетить две большие пещеры , но и небольшую ферму с хамелеонами. Когда-то остров Занзибар находился под водой и был морским дном, миллионы лет назад смещение плит вытолкнуло остров и эти пещеры – явное свидетельство морского прошлого этих мест. Морская вода миллионы лет назад своими течениями создала эти лабиринты. А оказавшись на поверхности Земли , и покрываясь постепенно слоем органики, эти пещеры заполнились наземными обитателями – летучими мышами, насекомыми. Со слов гида здесь были найдены и следы обитания древнего человека, а именно посуда для приготовления пищи из глины. Постепенно грунтовые воды протекали в щели камней , сформировали под сводами пещер сталактиты, некоторым из которых более 1000 лет. Вода тихонько капает и сейчас, так что вы может видеть процесс создания этих причудливых форм. Нужно сказать , что во вторую пещеру я бы не рекомендовала ходить пожилым людям и детям. Так как она не сквозная, ощущается нехватка воздуха, резкий спуск вниз, многие проходы очень узкие либо низкие. Для людей боящихся замкнутых пространств вторая пещера точно не подходит. Первая же пещера достаточно комфортна  для посещения. Гид сопровождает всю вашу экскурсию и очень интересно и подробно обо всём рассказывает. Также вам предоставляются фонарики. На видео видно,  что фонарики дают возможность подсветить красивые участки стен и свод пещеры и полюбоваться кружевами белых кристаллов полностью покрывающих стены и свод.. В них можно различить очертания виртуальных различных животных, таких как черепаха ,улитка, акула или гигантский баобаб. Стоимость посещения пещеры 10 $, однако добавьте ещё пять и вы сможете посетить отличную маленькую фирму хамелеонов. Общий тайминг не менее часа.
translated_content:
We departed from Nungwi by tuk-tuk for 20,000 shillings roundtrip and reached the cave in 20 minutes. The driver was waiting for us.
Here, you can not only visit two large caves but also a small chameleon farm. Zanzibar Island was once underwater, a seabed; millions of years ago, shifting plate formations pushed the island up, and these caves are clear evidence of this area's marine past. Millions of years ago, seawater currents created these labyrinths. Once on the surface, and gradually covered with a layer of organic matter, these caves became filled with land dwellers—bats and insects. According to the guide, traces of ancient human habitation were also found here, namely clay cooking utensils. Gradually, groundwater flowed into the crevices of the rocks, forming stalactites under the cave roofs, some of which are over 1,000 years old. Water is still gently dripping, so you can see the process of creating these bizarre shapes. I should note that I wouldn't recommend the second cave for older people or children. Since it's not a walk-through cave, there's a feeling of air shortage, a steep descent, and many of the passages are very narrow or low. The second cave is definitely not suitable for those with a fear of confined spaces. The first cave is quite comfortable to visit. A guide accompanies you throughout the tour and explains everything in great detail and interest. Flashlights are also provided. The video shows how the flashlights illuminate beautiful sections of the cave walls and ceiling, allowing you to admire the lacework of white crystals that completely cover the walls and ceiling. You can discern the outlines of various virtual animals, such as a turtle, a snail, a shark, or a giant baobab tree. A visit to the cave costs $10, but add another $5 for a visit to a wonderful small chameleon farm. The total time is at least an hour.

We asked the guide for two flashlights, which they readily provided. The cave's size and interior are impressive. A 300-year-old baobab tree grows nearby; you can climb it and take photos. Chameleons live in a fenced area—it's fun not only to hold them but also to feed them insects. The guides are friendly and welcoming. You can get here from Nungwi on bus 116 for 1,000 shillings and take 10 minutes.

content:
Se avete qualche giorno da passare a Kendwa questa esperienza è molto consigliata. Le due grotte scoperte dal papà della guida che vi accompagnerà sono belle da visitare, con cristalli, minerali, stalattiti, stalagmiti (e pipistrelli e ragni giganti). content: This cave system is located next to Mbuyuni Village, in just about 10-15min drive form Nungwi and Kendwa. It is really easy to find it, lots of shields and signs will show you the way from the main road. Some local guys will greet you at the entrance, where you can discuss the about the entrance fee. If you visit the Chameleon farm, which is right next to the Cave, you can get an even cheaper price for both attractions. There is no electricity inside the cave. Bring your own flashlight if you have one because those, they provide are rather creepy. You should wear proper shoes and light clothes, it can be hot inside. Since this is a natural cave with many narrow and low passes, it is not recommended for disabled people. Inside of the cave you can see different sized stalactites and stalagmites and dozens of dripstone formations. Make sure you don’t touch them to keep them as beautiful as they are. The cave is the habitat of bats, lizards, cave scorpions and other creatures, so watch your steps and try not to disturb them. The guide will show you in about 1h around and tell some information about the cave’s history but you shouldn’t expect a geology or archeology lesson. In our opinion it is worth to visit the cave and we would recommend it for thoughtful tourists.
full_address: Tazari Caves, Nungwi Rd, Tanzania

content:
Généralement je donne peu d''avis sur les attractions mais là je pense qu''il est nécessaire de parler de la plage de Nungwi (Nungwi public beach sur Google maps et non pas Nungwi Beach) .
Cette plage n''a rien à voir avec celles de la côte est. Le sable n''y est pas plus fin et y est moins blanc. En ce mois de septembre, la plage est envahie d''algues, aussi bien sur le sable que dans l''eau, d''ailleurs personne ne s''y baignait. J''ai aussi remarqué qu''il y a plus de Massai ou d''équipes d''acrobates locaux que de touristes. Comme la plage est étroite et encastrée entre des rochers et une terrasse sur puloties d''un hotel, il est impossible de rejoindre une autre plage avoisinante par marrée haute. À noter aussi qu''en plus d''être alpagué par les Beach Boys, les vendeurs de shit et de cocaïne y sont nombreux.
Il existe d''autres plages comme celles des hôtels où bien celle de Nungwi Beach. Pour cette dernière, là aussi, si la marrée est haute, l''accès par le village n''est pas évident. Il faut demander son chemin ou bien passer par les hôtels.
Vraiment, le seul intérêt de Nungwi est peut être le choix entre les nombreuses boutiques de souvenirs.
translated_content:
I don't usually give many reviews of attractions, but I think it's necessary to talk about Nungwi Beach (Nungwi Public Beach on Google Maps, not Nungwi Beach).
This beach is nothing like the ones on the east coast. The sand isn't any finer or whiter. In September, the beach was covered in seaweed, both on the sand and in the water; in fact, nobody was swimming there. I also noticed that there were more Maasai or local acrobatic troupes than tourists. Because the beach is narrow and hemmed in by rocks and a hotel's thatched terrace, it's impossible to reach another nearby beach at high tide. It's also worth noting that, in addition to being accosted by the Beach Boys, there are many drug dealers and cocaine sellers.
There are other beaches, like the hotel beaches or Nungwi Beach itself. For the latter, too, if the tide is high, access through the village isn't straightforward. You have to ask for directions or go through the hotels.
Really, the only real draw of Nungwi is perhaps the sheer number of souvenir shops.

content: In Nungwi, where the northernmost shores of Zanzibar meet the vast Indian Ocean, the beach hums with a rhythm that feels eternal. The sands, cool and fine underfoot, stretch endlessly, kissed by water so clear it mirrors the sky. Fishermen anchor their dhows after the day’s work, their wooden boats carrying whispers of centuries-old traditions. Nearby, a local artisan threads beads onto bracelets, her fingers moving deftly as laughter ripples from children chasing the tide. The air is warm, scented faintly of salt and the smoke of seafood grills along the shore. By twilight, the world seems to pause—only the sound of waves and murmured conversations remain. Nungwi is not merely a beach; it is an experience of connection: to the land, to its people, and to the stories carried in every grain of sand.

content:
Las playas son increíbles. Para empezar, no hay mucha gente y es posible caminar por la fina arena hasta hallar un lugar más o menos apartado. Los sube y baja de la marea son hasta cierto punto interesantes: hasta el medio día la marea está creciendo de manera que hay zonas en las que hay que mojarse para pasar, una pequeña aventura. A partir de entonces y ya durante el resto del día, la marea va bajando y la costa arenosa se ensancha. Recomiendo sobretodo la mañana para permanecer en la playa, el ambiente está mucho más tranquilo, también provocado por la marea alta. Por la tarde, cosa que también vale la pena ver, los autóctonos salen a practicar deportes varios en la misma orilla del mar.
Hay cansinos que te intentan vender el tándem mango-coconut, productos decorativos como pulseras, o salidas en barca para realizar las actividades típicas en el mar... aunque esto es algo inevitable. Se acercan y se marchan con una sonrisa, que es lo importante.
translated_content:
The beaches are incredible. For starters, there aren't many people, and you can walk along the fine sand until you find a secluded spot. The ebb and flow of the tides are quite interesting: until midday, the tide is rising, so there are areas where you have to wade through the water to get across—a little adventure. From then on, and for the rest of the day, the tide goes out, and the sandy shore widens. I especially recommend spending the morning on the beach; the atmosphere is much more peaceful, partly due to the high tide. In the afternoon, which is also worth seeing, the locals come out to practice various sports right on the water's edge.
There are a few pushy people trying to sell you mango-coconut snacks, decorative items like bracelets, or boat trips for typical water activities... although this is somewhat unavoidable. They approach and leave with a smile, which is what matters.

content:
My visit to Maasai World was an incredible and eye-opening experience. It offers a deep dive into the Maasai culture, which is so unique yet sadly disappearing. Learning about their traditions, lifestyle, and history was both interesting and enriching, and it made me realize how important it is to preserve and support this culture.
Maasai World isn’t like the professional museums you might find in Europe—it has a more authentic and grassroots feel, but that’s part of its charm. While it’s not polished in a commercial sense, the experience is real, personal, and full of potential. You can tell they’re passionate about what they’re doing, and I truly believe Maasai World is going to be a great success in the future.
If you’re interested in cultural experiences and want to understand more about the Maasai people, I highly recommend visiting. It’s a beautiful way to connect with a way of life that deserves to be remembered and celebrated.

content:
Masai World - это открытие!
Экскурсия, которая привнесений насчитана на полтора часа у нас продлилась два с половиной. Нам дали ответы на все интересующие вопросы, показали быт, рассказали историю с момента рабства до современности, напоили вкусным чаем, провели мастеркласс по разведению огня и ритуальных танцев. Только положительные эмоции, главное условие - понимайте английский! По завершению экскурсии каждый может приобрести сувениры ручной работы сделанные с душой.
Если кто-то едем не экскурсией, а самостоятельно на автомобиле - обратите внимание на дорогу. После поворота на с асфальта на грунтовую дорогу лучше оставить автомобиль и пройти 700 метров пешком, дорога каменистая и не любая машина может проехать!
Masai World is a discovery!
The excursion, which instead an hour and a half, lasted two and a half.  We were
given answers to all our questions, showed us the way of life, told the story from the time of slavery to the present, gave us delicious tea, held a master class on making fire and ritual dances.  Only positive emotions, the main condition is to understand English!  At the end of the tour, everyone can buy handmade souvenirs made with soul.
If someone is not going on a tour, but on their own by car, pay attention to the road.  After turning from asphalt to a dirt road, it is better to leave the car and walk 700 meters on foot, the road is rocky and not every car can pass!

content:
Старый форт в Стоун-Тауне — одно из тех мест, где история буквально под ногами.
Толстые стены из кораллового камня, потемневшие от времени, запах моря, старого известняка и чего-то пряного — всё это вместе сразу возвращает в эпоху, когда Занзибар был центром торговли специями и рабами.
Форт построили в конце XVII века арабы из султаната Омана. Тогда они только что отбили остров у португальцев и укрепляли свои позиции. Здесь держали гарнизон, защищали гавань, потом здание служило тюрьмой, а позже — даже складом и железнодорожным вокзалом, когда британцы пришли со своими порядками.
История у этого места насыщенная, с переменами, как у самого Занзибара.
Сейчас форт выглядит сурово, но живо.
Внутри — амфитеатр, где проходят концерты и фестивали, вокруг лавки с сувенирами и специями, женщины продают ткани, дети гоняют мяч.
Сидишь на камне, смотришь на башни, слушаешь, как кто-то поёт на суахили, и понимаешь, что история здесь не замерла — она просто перешла на другой ритм.
Я поднялся на стену, посмотрел вниз на старый город — белые фасады, крыши из жестяных листов, море вдалеке. И подумал: Занзибар — это не просто остров, это место, где всё смешалось — арабы, африканцы, индийцы, европейцы — и каждый оставил свой след. Старый форт стоит как напоминание об этом — грубый, красивый и честный.
translated_content:
The Old Fort in Stone Town is one of those places where history is literally beneath your feet.
Thick coral stone walls, darkened by time, the scent of the sea, old limestone, and something spicy—all of this instantly transports you back to the era when Zanzibar was a center of the spice and slave trade.
The fort was built in the late 17th century by Arabs from the Sultanate of Oman. They had just recaptured the island from the Portuguese and were strengthening their position. They maintained a garrison here, defended the harbor, then served as a prison, and later even as a warehouse and train station when the British arrived with their own rules.
This place has a rich history, full of changes, like Zanzibar itself.
Today, the fort looks stern, but vibrant.
Inside is an amphitheater where concerts and festivals are held, surrounded by souvenir and spice stalls, women selling fabrics, and children kicking a ball around.
You sit on a rock, looking at the towers, listening to someone singing in Swahili, and you realize that history hasn't stopped here—it's just shifted to a different rhythm.
I climbed the wall and looked down at the old town—white facades, tin roofs, the sea in the distance. And I thought: Zanzibar isn't just an island, it's a place where everything has mixed—Arabs, Africans, Indians, Europeans—and each has left their mark. The old fort stands as a reminder of this—rough, beautiful, and honest.

content:
As the name suggests, Old Fort truly lives up to its heritage  a city built from stone, rich in history and timeless beauty. Dating back to around the 18th century, this was once the royal palace area, and walking through it feels like stepping into another era.
You’ll come across old cannons, gun storage areas, and elevated platforms once used for defense  fascinating reminders of the town’s strategic past. There’s also a theater space where performances and cultural plays are held, adding a touch of artistry to the historical setting.
One thing that stood out to me and something every cat lover will appreciate is how many beautiful cats freely roam around the gardens. They’re calm, friendly, and almost part of the town’s charm. You can easily spend time just taking photos of the cats, the stone buildings, and the lush gardens around.
The view from Stone Town is spectacular, especially facing the ocean. From here, you can spot large ships, ferries, and container vessels gracefully moving across the turquoise water  a perfect blend of history meeting modern trade.
As the sun sets, Stone Town transforms into a lively scene with its night market. The air fills with the aroma of freshly prepared street food seafood, grilled meat, and local treats. One drink I particularly enjoyed was a refreshing sugarcane juice mixed with ice, made fresh by local vendors.
Stone Town is more than just a historic site; it’s a place that combines culture, ocean views, architecture, and authentic street life. Whether you’re exploring during the day or enjoying the lively evenings, it’s a spot that captures the true essence of Zanzibar historic, vibrant, and full of character.

content:
Fuerte Viejo (En suajili: Ngome Kongwe), también conocido como el Fuerte Árabe y con otros nombres, es una fortificación ubicada en Stone Town, Zanzíbar, Tanzania.
Es el edificio más antiguo​ y una de las principales atracciones turísticas de Stone Town.
Se encuentra en el paseo marítimo principal, adyacente a otro edificio emblemático de la ciudad, la Casa de las Maravillas.
Fue construido por árabes omaníes después de expulsar a los portugueses en 1699. Con el paso de los años ha tenido varios usos, como prisión y club de tenis.
​ En el patio hay algunos restos de edificios anteriores, incluidos los de una iglesia portuguesa.
El Fuerte Viejo es una de las principales atracciones para los visitantes en Stone Town, y su patio ha sido adaptado para servir como un centro cultural con tiendas de curiosidades que venden mercadería orientada al turismo. También cuenta con un anfiteatro al aire libre donde se realizan espectáculos de música y danza en vivo la mayoría de las noches, un restaurante y un mostrador de información turística.
También es el lugar principal utilizado para grandes eventos como el Festival Internacional de Cine de Zanzíbar y el Sauti za Busara (un festival de música africana que se realiza en febrero de cada año).
translated_content:
Old Fort (Swahili: Ngome Kongwe), also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, Zanzibar, Tanzania.
It is the oldest building and one of the main tourist attractions in Stone Town.
It is located on the main waterfront, adjacent to another iconic building in the town, the House of Wonders.
It was built by Omani Arabs after they expelled the Portuguese in 1699. Over the years, it has served various purposes, including as a prison and a tennis club.
In the courtyard, there are some remains of earlier buildings, including those of a Portuguese church.
Old Fort is one of the main attractions for visitors to Stone Town, and its courtyard has been adapted to serve as a cultural center with souvenir shops selling tourist-oriented merchandise. It also features an open-air amphitheater where live music and dance performances are held most evenings, a restaurant, and a tourist information desk. It is also the main venue used for major events such as the Zanzibar International Film Festival and Sauti za Busara (an African music festival held in February each year).

content: In Stone Town, the Old Fort, or Ngome Kongwe, rises with quiet strength, a relic of Zanzibar’s past that has transformed into a vibrant cultural hub. Built in the late 17th century by the Omanis to fend off Portuguese attacks, its sturdy, weathered walls now embrace a more peaceful rhythm. By day, its courtyard hums with the chatter of artisans selling hand-carved wood and intricate jewelry, while the amphitheater comes alive with the rhythmic beat of taarab music, weaving Swahili traditions into the air. As the sun sinks into the Indian Ocean, the fort becomes a gathering place for dreamers and storytellers, each sharing tales that echo through the arches of its ancient corridors. The Old Fort is no longer a site of defense but a living bridge between the Zanzibar of history and the island’s boundless future—a space where every visitor, local or traveler, feels the pulse of a heritage that refuses to fade.

الحصن القديم في زنجبار، المعروف أيضًا باسم الحصن العربي القديم (Old Fort)، هو أحد أبرز المعالم التاريخية في جزيرة زنجبار، ويقع في منطقة فرضاني قرب الساحل.
تاريخ الحصن:
•	التأسيس: تم بناؤه في أواخر القرن الـ17 على يد العمانيين بعد تحرير الجزيرة من البرتغاليين، لحمايتها من أي محاولات غزو مستقبلي.
•	الهيكل المعماري: يتميز بتصميمه الدفاعي، حيث تحيط به أسوار حجرية سميكة، وأبراج مراقبة دائرية.
•	الاستخدامات:
•	في البداية كان يستخدم كحصن دفاعي ومركز إداري.
•	في العصور اللاحقة تم استخدامه كسجن ومركز تجاري.
•	لاحقًا أصبح مقرًا للأنشطة الثقافية والفنية.
أهميته:
•	ثقافيًا: يُعد رمزًا لتراث زنجبار العماني والعربي.
•	سياحيًا: يجذب آلاف الزوار الذين يستكشفون تاريخه العريق وموقعه المميز المطل على المحيط.
•	حاليًا: يُستخدم كمركز ثقافي، ويحتضن مهرجانات فنية ومعارض تراثية، مثل مهرجان زنجبار السينمائي الدولي.
يقع الحصن بالقرب من مناطق جذب أخرى مثل حدائق فوروداني، مما يجعله جزءًا لا يتجزأ من استكشاف ثقافة وتاريخ زنجبار.
translated_content:
The Old Fort of Zanzibar, also known as the Old Arab Fort, is one of the most prominent historical landmarks on the island of Zanzibar, located in the Fardhani district near the coast.
History of the Fort:
• Establishment: It was built in the late 17th century by the Omanis after liberating the island from the Portuguese, to protect it from any future invasion attempts.
• Architectural Structure: It is characterized by its defensive design, surrounded by thick stone walls and circular watchtowers.
• Uses:
• Initially, it served as a defensive fortress and administrative center.
• In later periods, it was used as a prison and trading center.
• Later, it became a venue for cultural and artistic activities.
Importance:
• Culturally: It is a symbol of Zanzibar's Omani and Arab heritage.
• Touristically: It attracts thousands of visitors who explore its rich history and its unique location overlooking the ocean.
• Currently: It is used as a cultural center, hosting art festivals and heritage exhibitions, such as the Zanzibar International Film Festival.
The fort is located near other attractions such as the Forodhani Gardens, making it an integral part of exploring Zanzibar's culture and history.

content: Built around 1700 by SeyyidSeif bin Sultan of Ya’aruba Dynasty who ruled Oman from 1692 to 1711 D. This site was once occupied by Portuguese chapel and small fortified houses before their total expulsion from East Africa in 1698. The Oman Arabs replaced the Portuguese remnants by construction of western side of the fort. Some of chapel remnants can be seen on north western corner wall of the fort until today. In 1836, Seyyid Said himself added eastern half of the fort for the purpose of keeping his garrison. The Omanis partially demolished the Portuguese chapel and a Portuguese merchant house and incorporated them in the construction of what was described in 1710 as a ridiculous little Fort. In the later years it was used as a prison. In 1905, the fort was used as a railway station and a deport. The front passage was constructed in 1946 to house ladies club. From 1964, it is used for cultural performances. Currently, it is a home for several festivals such as ZIFF, Sauti za Busara (Sound of Wisdom) etc.

content:
The old Fort in Zanzibar, also known as the Arab Fort or Ngome Kongwe, is a historical and architectural landmark located in Stone Town, Zanzibar City, Tanzania. Here are some key points about it:
1. **Historical Background**:
- The fort was built by the Omanis in the late 17th century (1698) after they had driven out the Portuguese. Its primary purpose was to defend against the Portuguese and any other potential invaders.
- The fort was constructed on the site of a Portuguese chapel and garrison.
2. **Architecture**:
- The fort is characterized by its large, sturdy stone walls and defensive towers. Its design reflects traditional Omani military architecture.
- Inside, there is a large, open courtyard, which originally served as a prison and later was used for military barracks and other administrative purposes.
3. **Cultural Significance**:
- The Old Fort is one of Stone Town''s most important cultural sites and is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
- It hosts a variety of cultural events, including the Zanzibar International Film Festival (ZIFF), music performances, and other community events.
4. **Modern Use**:
- Today, the fort is a popular tourist attraction. Visitors can explore its historical architecture, shop at a number of small shops and stalls selling local crafts and souvenirs, and enjoy performances at the amphitheater within its walls.
- The site has been adapted to serve contemporary cultural purposes while preserving its historical integrity.
5. **Restoration and Preservation**:
- Efforts have been made to preserve and restore the Old Fort to maintain its historical and cultural significance. These efforts are part of broader initiatives to preserve the heritage of Stone Town.
The Old Fort remains a testament to Zanzibar''s rich history, blending African, Arab, Indian, and European influences over the centuries.

content:
The Old Fort in Zanzibar is a historical landmark that offers visitors a unique experience. The fort was built in the 17th century by the Omani Arabs and was used as a defensive structure to protect the island from invaders. Today, it has been transformed into a cultural center that showcases the history and culture of Zanzibar.
Visitors to the Old Fort can explore the various exhibits and displays that highlight the island''s rich history and cultural heritage. There are also regular performances of traditional music and dance, as well as art exhibitions featuring local artists.
One of the main attractions of the Old Fort is the nightly food market, which offers a wide variety of local cuisine and street food. Visitors can sample dishes such as Zanzibari biryani, grilled seafood, and samosas while enjoying live music and entertainment.
Another popular activity at the Old Fort is shopping for souvenirs and handicrafts. The fort is home to a number of shops and stalls selling traditional Zanzibari items such as spices, textiles, and jewelry.

content:
Fort strategic pe drumul către Mizingani, această cladire datează din epoca Omană din 1700. A fost folosit ca garnizoană pentru sultan si mai apoi gara de tren.
Vechiul Fort din Stone Town este o cladire istorică impresionantă, acum e un centru comercial și cultural. De îndată ce ce treci prin poarta, vezi măreția și amploarea fortului, cu zidurile lui falnice și poarta impunătoare.
Fortul găzduiește o varietate de magazine unde se vinde de toate, de la meșteșuguri și bijuterii realizate manual până la îmbrăcăminte și suveniruri. Am fost impresionat de frumusetea articolelor oferite, care reprezinta bogatul patrimoniu cultural al Zanzibarului.
O caracteristică a Fortului Vechi a fost curtea mare și frumoasă, care e plina de iarbă verde unde am stat liniștit și departe de agitația din Stone Town. Mi-a plăcut să stau la umbra copacilor și să privesc cum trece lumea în timp ce beau un suc de fructe răcoritor de la unul dintre vânzătorii locali din apropiere.
translated_content:
A strategic fort on the road to Mizingani, this building dates back to the Omani era in the 1700s. It was used as a garrison for the Sultan and later a train station.
The Old Fort in Stone Town is an impressive historical building, now a commercial and cultural center. As soon as you walk through the gate, you see the grandeur and scale of the fort, with its towering walls and imposing gate.
The fort is home to a variety of shops selling everything from handicrafts and handmade jewelry to clothing and souvenirs. I was impressed by the beauty of the items on offer, which represent the rich cultural heritage of Zanzibar.
A feature of the Old Fort was the large and beautiful courtyard, which is full of green grass where I sat quietly and away from the hustle and bustle of Stone Town. I enjoyed sitting under the shade of the trees and watching the world go by while drinking a refreshing fruit juice from one of the local vendors nearby.

content:
Idegen vezetővel voltunk, nagyon sok információt elmondott a városról.
Egy rövid leírásban nagyon nehéz öszefoglalni. A régi épületek nagyon érdekesek, koralból és mészkőböl épültek, ezért szürkék (nem a gomba miatt). A furcsa ajtók elárulják, hogy milyen család lakik mögöttük. A városrész Sone Town nem túl nagy de sok látnivalót rejt. A sok sikátor közül van elhagyatott és elég zsúfolt is. Sétáló utca, bazársor, piac, Freddie Mecury szülőháza. A piac másabb mint az európai. Az asztalra felrakott portékák között mászkál az eladó, ez jópofa volt.
A hal piac zsúfolt és nem büdös, pedig jeget nem láttam semelyik asztalon.
A városrészt egyszer érdemes megnézni annak aki arra jár.
translated_content:
We had a foreign guide, he told us a lot of information about the city.
It is very difficult to summarize in a short description. The old buildings are very interesting, they are built of coral and limestone, so they are gray (not because of the fungus). The strange doors reveal what kind of family lives behind them. The Sone Town district is not very big but it hides a lot of attractions. Among the many alleys, there are deserted and quite crowded ones. A walking street, a bazaar, a market, Freddie Mercury's birthplace. The market is different from the European one. The seller walks among the goods placed on the tables, which was a good thing.
The fish market is crowded and not smelly, although I did not see ice on any of the tables.
The district is worth seeing once for anyone who goes there.

content:
Restes de l''antic fort construït pels àrabs omanís després d''expulsar als portuguesos l''any 1699.
En el segle XIX esdevingué una presó. També fou emprat com estació de ferrocarril entre els anys 1905 i 1928. Al voltant dels anys 50 esdevingué un club de senyores, i finalment s''hi afegí un anfiteatre en els anys 90 i actualment és la seu del Festival Internacional de Cinema de Zanzibar. També s''hi fan altres activitats culturals.
Entre els seus murs també hi ha alguna petita galeria d''art i botigues de souvenirs.
translated_content:
Remains of the old fort built by the Omani Arabs after expelling the Portuguese in 1699.
In the 19th century it became a prison. It was also used as a railway station between 1905 and 1928. Around the 1950s it became a ladies' club, and finally an amphitheatre was added in the 1990s and it is currently the venue for the Zanzibar International Film Festival. Other cultural activities are also held there.
There are also a few small art galleries and souvenir shops within its walls.

Admission is free but it is very small.
The Old Fort (Swahili: Boma la Kale la Zanzibar), also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar. It is the oldest building and a major visitor attraction in Stone Town. It is located on the main promenade, next to another landmark of the city, the House of Wonders (the former palace of the Sultan of Zanzibar), and opposite the Forodhani Gardens.
History
Edit
"It was built by the Omani Arabs after they expelled the Portuguese in 1699. It was used as a garrison and prison in the 19th century, and as a terminus for the Zanzibar Railways from 1905–28. A new guardhouse was built in 1947 and used as a women's club, and an amphitheatre was added in the 1990s. It is now the home of the Zanzibar International Film Festival."
It was later used as a prison and barracks. In the early 20th century it was also used as a depot during the construction of the railway connecting Stone Town to the village of Bububu.
The fort is essentially a square of high, brown walls with merlons, protecting an inner courtyard. In the courtyard are some remains of earlier buildings, including a Portuguese church and another Omani fortification.

content: Old Fort znany również jako Fort Arabski został zbudowany przez Arabów w 1699 roku na głównym nabrzeżu naprzeciwko Ogrodów Forodhani. W  XIX wieku służył jako garnizon i więzienie a w latach 1905-28 był zajezdnią kolei Zanzibar. W 1947 roku zbudowano nową wartownię która służyła jako klub tenisowy dla pań. W latach 90 -tych dobudowano amfiteatr który obecnie jest siedzibą Międzynarodowego Festiwalu Filmowego Zanzibar.
translated_content: The Old Fort, also known as the Arab Fort, was built by the Arabs in 1699 on the main quay opposite the Forodhani Gardens. In the 19th century, it served as a garrison and prison, and from 1905 to 1928, it served as a depot for the Zanzibar Railway. In 1947, a new guardhouse was built, which served as a ladies' tennis club. In the 1990s, an amphitheater was added, which currently houses the Zanzibar International Film Festival.

reviewed_at:
We visited in January 2021.
Entrance to the grounds is free, and we found the best deals on souvenirs there. We picked out a whole bag, including some paintings, which we didn't expect or plan at all.
There are some very good prices on souvenirs made from a special type of wood, but be careful—some shops are scamming you by painting ordinary wood. One item was already discovered at home. I packed it in a dress for travel to protect the small parts, and when I got home, I discovered that the dress was stained ((( and couldn't be washed off. That figurine was bought at a shop on the narrow streets of the city. I think you can tell even by rubbing the item with a regular damp cloth... !! But all the other souvenirs turned out to be good, and we are very happy!
Prices in the photo are in Tanzania's national currency (shilings). Don't be shy about bargaining, as they make up prices and can easily inflate them. A 50% discount is normal for both the seller and the buyer. Ask for a "super chip price" 👍, which means a very good price, a discount.
Ebony wood, or Eben, is the black (or black with stripes) wood of certain tropical trees of the genus Persimmon (Diospyros), growing in the tropical rainforests of Western, Central, and East Africa, South and Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean islands, and the monsoon forests of India and Ceylon.
The heartwood, without discernible annual rings, is very hard and heavy and is considered one of the most valuable timber species. The yellow-gray sapwood, which is removed from the tree immediately after felling, can occupy up to 70% of the trunk and is never sold commercially, as it is considered unsightly.
Ebony wood is very difficult to dry. In countries where this wood is harvested, preliminary (two years before harvesting) pruning of trees is still practiced. This involves cutting back the cambium (sapwood) layers in a circle at the base of the trunk to stop the tree's growth.
After harvesting and sawing, the boards are stacked, the ends are sealed with lime or another material, and carefully protected from the sun and strong drafts to avoid excessive heat. Rapid wood drying. Natural drying takes at least 6 months. If drying conditions are not met, boards will warp and crack rapidly. Ebony wood shrinks little.

content: Старый Форт, также известный как арабский форт, это оборонительное сооружение находится в каменном городе , столице Занзибара . Это самое старое здание  и главная достопримечательность Каменного города. Он расположен на главной набережной, рядом с другим знаковым зданием города, Домом чудес (бывший дворец султана Занзибара ), и выходит окнами на сады Фородхани. Здесь можно купить сувениры. Вход бесплатный.
translated_content: The Old Fort, also known as the Arab Fort, is a defensive structure located in Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar. It is the oldest building and the main attraction of Stone Town. It is located on the main promenade, next to another iconic building of the city, the House of Wonders (the former palace of the Sultan of Zanzibar), and overlooks the Forodhani Gardens. You can buy souvenirs here. Entrance is free.

content:
الحصن القديم والمعروف أيضا باسم حصن العرب وغيرها من الأسماء، هو حصن يقع في المدينة الحجرية وهو أقدم مبنى في زنجبار وموقع سياحي رئيسي لجذب السياح في المدينة الحجرية. ويقع على الواجهة البحرية الرئيسية ، القريبة من معلم آخر وهو بيت العجائب.
كان يستخدم كحامية للجنود وسجن في القرن ومحطة لسكك الحديد الزنجبارية من 1928-1945.
ويستخدم كمستودع خلال بناء سكك زنجبار الحديدية الذي كان يربط المدينة الحجرية إلى قرية بوبوبو.
الحصن عبارة عن مربع عالي الجدران ومقامات تحمي الفناء الداخلي. في الفناء هناك بعض بقايا مباني سابقة بما في ذلك  كنيسة برتغالية وتحصينات عمانية أخرى قديمة.
وهو من أبرز مناطق الجذب السياحي في المدينة الحجرية والفناء  تم تكييفها كمركز ثقافي مع محلات بيع التحف السياحية ومكتب للمعلومات السياحية.
translated_content:
The Old Fort, also known as Arab Fort and other names, is a fort located in Stone Town. It is the oldest building in Zanzibar and a major tourist attraction in the city. Situated on the main waterfront, it is close to another landmark, the House of Wonders.
It served as a garrison for soldiers, a prison in the 19th century, and a station for the Zanzibar Railway from 1928 to 1945.
It was also used as a warehouse during the construction of the Zanzibar Railway, which connected Stone Town to the village of Popopopo.
The fort is a high-walled square with shrines protecting the inner courtyard. Within the courtyard are the remains of several earlier structures, including a Portuguese church and other ancient Omani fortifications.
It is one of the most prominent tourist attractions in Stone Town, and the courtyard has been adapted into a cultural center with souvenir shops and a tourist information office.

content:
The Old Fort (Swahili: Ngome Kongwe), also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar. It is the oldest building[1] and a major visitor attraction of Stone Town. It is located on the main seafront, adjacent to another landmark building of the city, the House of Wonders (former palace of the Sultan of Zanzibar), and facing the Forodhani Gardens.
'It was built by Omani Arabs after expelling the Portuguese in 1699. It was used as a garrison and prison in the 19th century

content:
Our visit to Freddie Mercury Museum was a special and slightly nostalgic experience, especially if you’re a fan of music or someone who appreciates cultural history.
Located right in the heart of Stone Town, the museum sits in the very house where Freddie Mercury (born Farrokh Bulsara) spent his early years before moving abroad. That itself makes the visit quite meaningful — you’re literally stepping into a place connected to one of the greatest musical legends of all time.
The museum is relatively small, but thoughtfully curated. It showcases photographs, personal stories, handwritten lyrics, and memorabilia that trace Freddie Mercury’s journey — from his childhood in Zanzibar and schooling in India to his rise as the iconic frontman of Queen.  ￼
It doesn’t take very long to explore (roughly 20–40 minutes), but if you take your time reading through everything, it becomes a much richer experience.
Opening hours: 10:00 AM – 6:00 PM daily  ￼

Nicht als Ausstellung.
Nicht als Objekt.
Sondern als Bewegung im Inneren.
Die Wände verschwinden, die Zeit verliert ihre Schärfe, und irgendwo zwischen dem ersten Ton und dem zweiten Herzschlag beginnt etwas, das größer ist als Erinnerung. Eine Stimme hebt sich, nicht laut, sondern notwendig. Sie trägt keinen Namen mehr, sie trägt Menschen. Millionen. Sie hebt sie an, lässt sie stampfen, lachen, weinen, sich erkennen. We will rock you – nicht als Titel, sondern als Versprechen. Ein Rhythmus, der durch die Beine steigt, durch den Brustkorb geht, bis man merkt, dass man längst mitmacht, ohne gefragt worden zu sein.
Hier, in diesen schmalen Räumen, ist nichts wichtig außer dem einen Punkt:
Ein Mensch hat beschlossen, sein Leben nicht klein zu halten.
Farrokh wird zu Freddie.
Nicht durch Zufall, sondern durch Mut.
Durch das tägliche Wiederaufstehen gegen Angst, gegen Zweifel, gegen Einsamkeit.
Durch den Willen, aus Herkunft kein Gefängnis zu machen, sondern ein Sprungbrett.
Durch die leise Entscheidung, der eigenen Stimme zu vertrauen, bis sie stark genug wird, andere zu tragen.
Man sieht Fotografien, Briefe, Noten – und plötzlich versteht man:
Es geht nicht um Originale.
Es geht um Wahrheit.
Die Musik hat nicht deshalb die Welt bewegt, weil sie perfekt war,
sondern weil sie ehrlich war.
Weil sie aus einem Inneren kam, das bereit war, alles zu riskieren, um echt zu sein.
Und in diesem Moment, wenn man still steht und hört, wie die Lieder im eigenen Körper weiterklingen, begreift man:
Das Wunder war nie das Museum.
Das Wunder war der Mensch.
Ein einziger Funke, der gereicht hat, um Millionen in Bewegung zu setzen.
Nicht durch Lautstärke.
Sondern durch Wahrhaftigkeit.
Und etwas in uns erkennt sich darin wieder.
Nicht als Fan.
Nicht als Tourist.
Sondern als Mensch, der spürt:
Auch mein Leben ist größer, als ich es mir bisher erlaubt habe.
Man geht hinaus, nicht mit einem Souvenir,
sondern mit einer Entscheidung im Herzen:
Das Eigene nicht mehr klein zu halten.
Und genau deshalb wirkt es.
Weil man nicht reagieren möchte –
sondern muss.

Not as an exhibition.
Not as an object.
But as movement within.
The walls disappear, time loses its sharpness, and somewhere between the first note and the second heartbeat, something begins that is greater than memory. A voice rises, not loudly, but necessarily. It no longer bears a name; it carries people. Millions. It lifts them up, makes them stomp, laugh, cry, recognize each other. We will rock you—not as a title, but as a promise. A rhythm that rises through your legs, through your chest, until you realize that you've been participating all along, without being asked.
Here, in these narrow rooms, nothing matters except one thing:
A person has decided not to let their life be small.
Farrokh becomes Freddie.
Not by chance, but through courage.
Through getting up every day against fear, against doubt, against loneliness.
Through the will to make one's origins not a prison, but a springboard.
Through the quiet decision to trust one's own voice until it grows strong enough to carry others.
You see photographs, letters, sheet music—and suddenly you understand:
It's not about originals.
It's about truth.
The music didn't move the world because it was perfect,
but because it was honest.
Because it came from within, willing to risk everything to be real.
And in that moment, when you stand still and listen to the songs resonate within your own body, you realize:
The miracle was never the museum.
The miracle was humanity.
A single spark that was enough to set millions in motion.
Not through volume.
But through authenticity.
And something within us recognizes itself in this.
Not as a fan.
Not as a tourist.
But as a person who senses:
My life, too, is bigger than I've allowed myself to believe.
You leave not with a souvenir,
but with a decision in your heart:
To no longer keep your own life small.
And that's precisely why it works.
Because you don't want to react—
but have to.

content:
Freddie Mercury Museum, una decepción agridulce.
Como fan de Freddie Mercury, mi visita al museo me dejó con sentimientos encontrados, tirando a la decepción. Si bien es emocionante tener un espacio dedicado a una leyenda como él, la experiencia se ve empañada por dos grandes problemas.
El primero, y el más hiriente, es la hipocresía de que un museo que celebra la vida de un ícono gay como Freddie exista y se lucre en un país donde la homosexualidad está prohibida y criminalizada. Es una contradicción inaceptable que roza la explotación, y como fan y homosexual, me genera una profunda indignación. ¿Cómo es posible que se beneficien de su legado mientras se persigue y se oprime a personas por ser quienes son en este pais? Esta situación ensombrece por completo cualquier aspecto positivo de la visita.
Además, el museo es caro para lo que ofrece. La colección es bastante limitada y no justifica el precio de la entrada. Quizás me esperaba algo más profundo de la vida y obra de Freddie, pero lo que te encuentras es una exhibición modesta que deja con ganas de más. La relación calidad-precio es deficiente, lo que agrava la sensación de que se están aprovechando del nombre de Freddie sin ofrecer algo a su altura.
En resumen para mi ha sifo una experiencia agridulce y algo frustrante. La contradicción moral y el precio elevado hacen que no pueda recomendarlo con entusiasmo a otros fans. Lo siento.
translated_content:
The Freddie Mercury Museum: A Bittersweet Disappointment
As a Freddie Mercury fan, my visit to the museum left me with mixed feelings, leaning towards disappointment. While it's exciting to have a space dedicated to a legend like him, the experience is marred by two major problems.
The first, and most hurtful, is the hypocrisy of a museum celebrating the life of a gay icon like Freddie existing and profiting in a country where homosexuality is prohibited and criminalized. It's an unacceptable contradiction that borders on exploitation, and as a fan and a gay man, it fills me with deep indignation. How is it possible that they profit from his legacy while people are persecuted and oppressed for being who they are in this country? This situation completely overshadows any positive aspects of the visit.
Furthermore, the museum is expensive for what it offers. The collection is quite limited and doesn't justify the entrance fee. Perhaps I was expecting something more profound about Freddie's life and work, but what you find is a modest exhibition that leaves you wanting more. The value for money is poor, which only intensifies the feeling that they're exploiting Freddie's name without offering anything worthy of him.
In short, for me it was a bittersweet and somewhat frustrating experience. The moral dilemma and the high price mean I can't enthusiastically recommend it to other fans. I'm sorry.

content:
The first ever Museum dedicated to the world legend Freddie Mercury, located in Shangani, in the heart of Zanzibar Stone Town, officially inaugurated on Sunday the 24th of November 2019, in order to commemorate the 28th anniversary of the beloved passing of the rock legend.
The Freddie Mercury Museum is officially partnered with Queen Productions Ltd. in the United Kingdom, who have loaned us exclusive pictures of Freddie Mercury throughout different stages in his life. Poco si sa dei primi anni di Freddie, che nacque proprio all’ospedale pubblico di Stone Town il 5 settembre 1946, quasi nulla sulla sua infanzia tra Zanzibar e l’India e men che meno della religione zoroastriana seguita dalla comunità parsi di cui la sua famiglia faceva parte… ecco qui in questo museo potete trovare la risposta a tante vostre curiosità, trovare molte foto inedite e approfondimenti sulla società di Zanzibar a quei tempi, sulla religione zoroastriana e sulla comunità parsi oltre che ovviamente un sacco di cimeli, disegni realizzati da Freddie, i testi delle  canzoni scritte direttamente da lui, gli abiti di scena e molto altro! translated_content: Finally, a museum dedicated to Freddie Mercury in his homeland. Little is known about Freddie's early years, as he was born in Stone Town's public hospital on September 5, 1946. Almost nothing is known about his childhood in Zanzibar and India, and even less about the Zoroastrian religion followed by the Parsi community to which his family belonged. In this museum, you can find answers to many of your questions, discover many unpublished photos, and insights into Zanzibar society at the time, the Zoroastrian religion, and the Parsi community. There's also, of course, tons of memorabilia, drawings by Freddie, lyrics from songs he wrote himself, stage costumes, and much more! If you go to Zanzibar, you absolutely must stop by.

Были в январе 2021 года.

Фаррух Балсара жил на Занзибаре до восьми лет, после чего семья отправила его учиться в Индию недалеко от Бомбея.
Уже в школе Фаррух стал называть себя Фредди и помимо спорта и живописи проявлял большой интерес к музыке. В 12 лет он с четырьмя своими друзьями создал группу 'The Hectics'" ('"Чахоточные'")

We visited in January 2021.
The house is a museum; admission is $8-10, but there's no point in visiting. Inside are a few photos and a few papers, nothing more. The outside is more interesting and mysterious than the inside.
Freddie Mercury was born on September 5, 1946, in Zanzibar, in the oldest district of the island's capital, Stone Town. His real name was Farrukh Bulsara. He and his family were Parsis (a rare ethnic group in Southeast Asia—India and Pakistan—of Iranian descent). Farrukh Bulsara lived in Zanzibar until he was eight, after which his family sent him to study in India near Bombay.
Already in school, Farrukh began calling himself Freddie and, in addition to sports and painting, showed a keen interest in music. At age 12, he and four of his friends formed a band, "The Hectics," which played primarily rock 'n' roll at school parties. Having failed his final exam, Farrukh returned to Tanzania, Zanzibar, at the age of 16.
