- 15-19 per i più pesanti del gruppo
In ogni caso mare e spot consigliatissimo.
Preferiscono pagamento cash in quanto altrimenti applicano una commissione aggiuntiva del 3%.
translated_content:
Fantastic kite school, like all the Duotone ones.
The owners are really helpful and always gave us good advice!
Excellent sails, decent boards, harnesses and impact kites that could use some updating, friendly and helpful beach boys.
I rented, while my girlfriend took lessons with Tom.
She made great progress.
Overall, the spot is highly recommended for those just learning, as low tide really helps with board recovery.
You can kite at both high and low tide.
Strangely, we had bad weather at the beginning of January and didn't always get out.
We always used sails:
-13-15 for the lightest ones
-15-19 for the heaviest in the group
In any case, the sea and spot are highly recommended.
They prefer cash payment, as otherwise they charge an additional 3% commission.

content:
I recently spent 14 days kiteboarding at this incredible spot in Paje, Zanzibar, and I have to say it exceeded all my expectations. The beach is stunning with a vast lagoon that offers plenty of space for kiteboarders. I was fortunate to stay at a hotel on the same premises, so accessibility was a breeze.
One of the best things about this spot is how uncrowded it is, offering a serene environment for both beginners and experienced kiteboarders. I rented my gear here, and the equipment was either new or nearly new, with excellent performance and safety features.
The water conditions were generally calm, with little to no chop, and only small waves during high tide. Wind conditions varied, but that actually helped me learn to kite in different settings, under the guidance of their extraordinarily helpful and friendly instructors.
Safety is a high priority here. The team is vigilant and always available to help, ensuring everyone has a good time while prioritizing safety.
Overall, I give this kiteboarding spot a full 5 out of 5. My highlight was gaining the confidence to kite independently under different wind conditions. I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend this place to family and friends; it’s a kiteboarding paradise!

content: I went to Zanzibar for a week to learn kite surfing. I had my eyes already on this school but hadn''t pre-booked anything. When I arrived in Paje, I just walked in and was welcomed very warmly. The staff is very friendly, relaxed and flexible. They ran me through my options and I ended up taking 2-hours sessions every day for 5 days. It was my first-time kite surfing and I didn''t know what to expect really. My instructor put a lot of emphasis on making me feel comfortable and safe and adjusted the sessions to my learning speed. Once I managed the water start, they installed a walkie talkie on my helmet so that I could stay in touch with my instructor which gave me a lot of reassurance. I had lots of fun in the water and it''s a nice feeling if someone guides you while slowly becoming more independent and cheers for you through a mic for each of your small successes. In terms of bookings and payment - you can book your sessions for the next day after your session. They will recommend you the times depending on your level, the tides and the expected weather conditions - so the more flexibility you have the better. Payment can be done via card (5% surcharge like all of Zanzibar apart from Stonetown) and cash. The school is Dutch hence you might want to find out if you can do bank transfer to a Euro account. If you are new to water sport, they also run a small shop where you get the right water wear for your experience.

content:
Matemwe Beach is probably one of the most beautiful beaches on all of Zanzibar, comparable to the northern beaches and the area around Mnemba Island. The turquoise water and white sand are truly stunning.
Unfortunately, there is a significant problem with plastic waste. Large amounts of trash can be found on the beach, and the locals do not seem to care much about it. We tried to clean up some of it ourselves but eventually stopped when we noticed that holes are dug in the sand at night to bury the garbage. Additionally, during high tide, a river further north appears to be used to flush the village’s waste directly into the ocean.
Another downside is the constant presence of sellers. While they are generally friendly, they are extremely persistent and quickly become exhausting.
You should urgently pay attention to low and high tide. Otherwise, it is sometimes not possible — or even dangerous — to enter the water. In addition, you should expect sea urchins.
Zanzibar has incredible natural beauty, but the local population still has a lot to learn when it comes to environmental protection and respectful interaction with tourists.

content:
La grande arnaque des guides... Vous pouvez lire une grande et belle plage de 10km, quelques photos bien cadrées et le rêve est là...
Quelle déception a l''arrivée... Oui elle est longue de 10 km...
Mais il n''y a rien sur la plage, pas un transat ni touriste... La raison est simple. Il y a du vent en permanence, et la plupart du temps c''est marée basse... Et donc totalement impossible de se baigner... Un cauchemar !
Bref ne faites pas comme moi, ne prenez en aucun cas un hôtel a cet endroit. Il n''y a rien a faire, pas un restaurant, personne, et on ne peut pas se baigner en étant prisonnier de son hôtel...
Qui plus est la plage n''est pas du tout entretenue !
Bref cela ne vaut pas le détour, même pour quelques heures ! A fuir !
translated_content:
The ultimate rip-off with guidebooks... You read about a long, beautiful 10km beach, see a few well-framed photos, and the dream seems complete... But what a disappointment when you arrive! Yes, it's 10km long... But there's nothing on the beach, not a single sun lounger or tourist... The reason is simple. It's constantly windy, and most of the time it's low tide... So swimming is completely impossible... A nightmare!
In short, don't make the same mistake I did, and under no circumstances should you stay in a hotel there. There's nothing to do, not a single restaurant, nobody around, and you can't even swim while you're stuck inside your hotel... What's more, the beach isn't maintained at all!
In short, it's not worth the trip, not even for a few hours! Avoid it!
full_address: 3996+H9 MATEMWE BEACH, Zanzibar, Pwani Mchangani, Tanzania

content:
Best spice farm tour in Zanzibar! Ask for Ibrahim to be your tour guide, he is fanatastic! If you do the Tangawizi Bistro cooking class with Shara (highly recommended!) she can request Ibrahim for you.
I did this tour in conjunction with Shara’s Tangawizi Bistro cooking class. Shara (the cook) met me at the market in Stonetown to create the menu and shop for the food and while she set up I did this spice tour. One of the highlights of my trip! All the people here are artisans from the handmade flower baskets to collect your spices and herbs in to the sellers of the soaps and oils and spices straight from the village. Ibrahim is so knowledgeable, funny, excellent English and an overall great tour guide. I loved the end where a guy climbed a coconut tree singing a traditional song and brought down coconuts for us to eat and drink. Bring cash to tip them, they deserve it and it’s all so worth it! Also cash to buy spices, perfumed oils and handmade lotions and other great items. Much of my souvineers came from here and everyone loved the authentic gift I brought back. I did 3 spice farm tours and this one blew me away and it was all because my amazing guide, the talented artesians you meet along the way and Shara’s cooking class where I got to cook with my collected herbs 🌿 💖😊 it’s an amazing experience and one not to miss!

content:
We had a great overall experience on the Mnemba Island and dolphin tour in Zanzibar.
The excursion was well organized and we really enjoyed most of the activities.
Swimming with the dolphins was definitely one of the highlights of the day.
However, there was one uncomfortable moment at the end of the excursion.
The guide became upset because we did not have exact change for the tip.
We believe it is important to remember that tips are not mandatory, but voluntary.
A tip should be given freely, depending on the customer''s satisfaction with the service.
One thing we missed was a stop at the famous sandbank.
We were expecting to visit it as part of the excursion, but unfortunately this did not happen.We dont know why.
response_content:
Hello Jose,
Thank you so much for taking the time to share your experience, and we''re happy to hear you enjoyed the Mnemba Island Tour and its organization.
At the same time, we sincerely apologize for the uncomfortable situation at the end of your excursion. You are absolutely right: tips are never mandatory, and they should only ever be given freely, as a personal gesture of appreciation. It is not acceptable for a guide to pressure guests over a tip or the exact amount, and we are truly sorry this happened to you. We have addressed this directly with our team to make sure every guide understands and respects this.
We also apologize that the sandbank stop was missed. Depending on the tides and sea conditions on the day, the sandbank is sometimes not accessible - but your guide should have clearly explained this to you on the spot, and we''re sorry that didn''t happen. 
Thank you again for your honest feedback. It genuinely helps us improve. We hope to welcome you back to Zanzibar one day for an experience that is wonderful from start to finish.
Warm regards,
The Rafiki Tours Team

content:
My boyfriend and I went on an excursion today. We were supposed to go snorkeling, have lunch and relax on a sandbar, and visit the mangroves.
We took the boat, but the sea was very rough! In the end, we just went to the sandbar where we stayed for three hours. It was so windy, the sand stung our skin. Like many other tourists, we wanted to head back right after lunch because the situation is very unpleasant. The sea was incredibly rough again, and we spent an hour on the boat with water splashing in our faces, praying we''d get back safe.
This agency seems only interested in money and not in the safety of its tourists. When it came time to pay the bill, the man said he was sorry.
The only positive points were the meal and the captain, who was relatively nice.
response_content:
Dear Laurine, 
thank you for taking the time to share your experience with us. We are truly sorry that your excursion was affected by very rough sea conditions and that the day turned out to be so unpleasant for you. 
Unfortunately, the ocean around Zanzibar can change very suddenly, and weather and sea conditions are something we cannot influence or fully predict in advance. While we always aim to choose the safest and best possible timings for our tours, unexpected weather changes remain one of the biggest challenges for all boat operators on the island. 
That said, your safety and comfort should always be our top priority and we are very sorry that you felt unsafe during the trip. We take your feedback seriously and will discuss this internally with the team. 
We are glad to hear that you enjoyed the lunch and liked the captain.

content:
We booked a private trip. The driver was punctual, guides were friendly and helpful and tried to be accommodating. Other than that, it was a bad experience. The snorkeling equipment was terrible and most of it didn’t fit or was poor quality. We felt very unsafe because the snorkeling areas were so crowded with boats, we had to worry about being crushed between boats or run over. There were so many other people, we kept swimming into others and getting kicked. The reef is mostly dead, and the only reason we saw a lot of colorful fish was because the guides were feeding them, which I consider to be really unethical. People were stepping on the reef, partly because the water was too shallow. We told the guide we weren’t interested in trying to find dolphins as we weren’t interested in chasing them.
I think our experience would have been the same with any tour company. If you care at all about the natural environment, I’d advise saving your time and money and not doing any snorkeling trips to this area. I know that local people are just trying to make a living, but it’s so unfortunate that the government of Tanzania doesn’t care enough to regulate tourism so that the reef will be protected for the future.
response_content:
Dear Karen,
Thank you for taking the time to share your feedback. We’re truly sorry to hear that your experience didn’t meet your expectations, especially regarding the equipment and the situation in the water.
We appreciate your kind words about our team’s friendliness and punctuality, and we’re disappointed that the rest of the tour didn’t reflect the standards we strive to uphold. Your comments regarding overcrowding and reef conditions highlight real challenges in popular snorkeling areas, and we fully agree that more regulation and environmental protection are urgently needed.
We never want our guests to feel unsafe or uncomfortable, and we’ll be looking into your comments internally to make sure improvements are made. Thank you again for your honest review — we value it as an opportunity to do better.
Wishing you all the best on your future travels,
The Rafiki Tours Team

content:
Wir haben mit Rafiki Tours den Ausflug nach Pengume Island gemacht und das Schwimmen mit Delfinen.
Wir haben über Instagram gebucht und per PayPal gezahlt, sehr angenehm und vertrauenswürdig!
Wir wurden pünktlich zur vereinbarten Zeit abgeholt und sind als erstes zu den nicht weit entfernten Delfinen gefahren.
Vor Ort waren etwa 10 Boote mit Touristen, dabei hat man sich schon eher wie ein Jäger gefühlt. Wir hatten ein privates Boot für uns was sehr angenehm war.
Taucherbrille, Schnorchel und Flossen waren mit dabei, auch wenn ich eher empfehlen würde eigenes Equipment mitzubringen.
Da die Delfine sehr schnell sind war das Schwimmen mit ihnen eher hektisch: Boot fährt in die Nähe, man springt samt Ausrüstung ins Meer, sieht für etwa 30 Sekunden die Delfine an einem vorbei schwimmen und muss anschließend wieder auf Boot klettern (relativ anstrengend auch für junge Leute). Das Prozedere wir dann wiederholt bis man sagt, dass man aufhören möchte.
Es ist noch zu erwähnen dass keine Schwimmweste zur Verfügung wurde, was bei anderen Anbietern aber der Fall war.
Danach sind wir wieder zurück zum Ufer gefahren und haben Tische, Stühle und Proviant eingeladen. Anschließend sind wir zu den Mangroven bei Pengume Island gefahren und haben dort sogar zwei Äffchen gesehen. Danach ging es zu einem Schorchelspot: Hier waren jedoch alle Korallen schon tot und nur ein paar Fische waren zu sehen. Dieser Spot wurde aber von mehreren Booten angefahren, d.h von anderen Anbietern.
Anschließend sind wir noch zu einer Stelle gefahren wo wir Seesterne sehen konnten. Danach ging es zu einer Sandbank, wo traumhaft schönes blaues Wasser war und wir mit vorzüglichen gegrillten Meeresfrüchten und anderen Leckereien verköstigt wurden.
Danach wurden wir mit dem Boot an unserem Hotel rausgelassen, da gerade Ebbe war. Alles in Allem ein toller Ausflug und durch die direkte Buchung mit 80€ pro Person ca. 30€ günstiger als an der Hotelrezeption.
Zudem waren die beiden Kapitäne sehr freundlich und zuvorkommend. 100% Empfehlenswert.
translated_content:
We booked the trip to Pengume Island and the dolphin swim with Rafiki Tours.
We booked through Instagram and paid via PayPal, which was very convenient and trustworthy!
We were picked up promptly at the agreed time and headed straight to the dolphins, which weren't far away.
There were about 10 boats with tourists there, which made us feel a bit like hunters. We had a private boat to ourselves, which was very nice.
Snorkeling mask, mask, and fins were provided, although I would recommend bringing your own equipment.
Since the dolphins are very fast, swimming with them was rather hectic: the boat comes close, you jump into the sea with your gear, watch the dolphins swim past you for about 30 seconds, and then have to climb back onto the boat (relatively tiring, even for young people). This process is repeated until you say you want to stop.
It's also worth mentioning that no life jackets were provided, which was the case with other tour operators.
After that, we went back to the shore and loaded tables, chairs, and provisions. Then we went to the mangroves near Pengume Island and even saw two monkeys. Next, we went to a snorkeling spot: however, all the coral was dead, and only a few fish were visible. This spot was frequented by several boats, meaning it was operated by other companies.
Afterward, we went to a place where we could see starfish. Then we went to a sandbar with stunningly beautiful blue water, where we were treated to delicious grilled seafood and other treats.
Afterward, we were dropped off by boat at our hotel, as it was low tide. All in all, a fantastic excursion, and booking directly was about €30 cheaper at €80 per person than booking through the hotel reception.
Furthermore, the two captains were very friendly and accommodating. 100% recommended.

content:
I want to warn other travelers about this experience.
We specifically chose this tour because we were told that snorkeling would be the main activity. We also made it clear that we did not want to see dolphins, as we strongly disagree with the way dolphins are chased by tourist boats in Zanzibar.
Despite this, our guide took us straight to the dolphins. What we witnessed was shocking: around 40 boats surrounding and chasing the dolphins. Tourists were instructed to jump into the water between moving boats in an attempt to get close to them. It felt dangerous for both the tourists and the dolphins. The animals were clearly being harassed and stressed. This should not be promoted as a tourist attraction.
After this disappointing experience, we finally went snorkeling. Unfortunately, the snorkeling spot was completely unsuitable. The current was extremely strong, making it difficult and exhausting to swim. There were also huge numbers of jellyfish, and we were stung repeatedly. To make matters worse, we could constantly smell fuel and engine exhaust from the many boat motors around us while snorkeling, which completely ruined the experience and raised concerns about the environmental impact on the marine life. Even worse, our guide disappeared and was nowhere to be seen while we were struggling in the water. It felt genuinely unsafe.
At that point, we were already upset and told the guide that we wanted to return to the hotel immediately. This seemed to cause panic among the guides, as they clearly did not expect tourists to complain or refuse to continue. We had a serious argument before they finally agreed to take us back.
Please be aware of what you are supporting when booking these tours. Chasing dolphins with dozens of boats is not wildlife tourism—it is animal harassment. The noise, fuel fumes, and constant disturbance are harmful to both the animals and the overall experience. If you care about animal welfare, responsible tourism, and safety, I would strongly recommend avoiding this activity.

translated_content:
Mbemba was the first stop on our wonderful stay in Zanzibar, and believe me, the most spectacular along with the Blue Lagoon Safari, which I'll tell you about later.
When we arrived on this wonderful little island, we were immediately captivated by the spectacular white strip of sand that cuts into the ocean for a few hundred meters.
Turquoise water, a coral reef with countless varieties of tropical fish, and, as if by magic, we saw a colony of dolphins happily dancing in the distance, undeterred by the thought of us seeing them.
Perhaps they're accustomed, but they're also docile and less afraid of human presence than other cetaceans.
We immediately set off on the boat to get up close and take some photos. The tour guides also invited us to dive in and swim with them, which initially left me perplexed, but we were reassured; the dolphins here are accustomed, so my children and I jumped in immediately with immense joy.
It was a pure spectacle, magnificent to be so close. and watch their pirouettes underwater.
We stayed in this stretch of water for a good half hour, then the dolphins disappeared.
We returned to the Mbemba sandbar, relaxed and sunbathed on the beach. Afterwards, the program included snorkeling in the coral reef, which is truly extraordinary for its rich coral and fish of every kind and color.
After snorkeling, the excursion concluded with lunch on the island, which was entirely seafood-based. We've never eaten so many lobsters and sea squirts as in Zanzibar, as I believe in many other tropical countries.
Everything was truly top-notch.

posted_on:
I don't understand the negative reviews; it was one of my best experiences in Zanzibar.
I should point out that if you're looking for convenience, comfort, and shopping, you won't find anything of interest here.
But if you enjoy history, meaningful encounters, nature, and have even a modicum of intellectual curiosity, you'll definitely find something to satisfy you. The GPS clearly indicates the access point, a track that runs through a village. Parking is easy. For a few shillings, a local will kindly act as your guide (stop whining about your shillings; they're only a few euros, and in France, you also pay to visit most places, and much more).
The main entrance is a staircase leading inside. The guidebook doesn't recommend the left side, as it's slippery and the air is thin; it's best avoided. I wanted to take a quick look around; it's impressive to feel your breath become short and to see the bats. I didn't stay long, but I imagined the poor slaves crammed into that space—it was terrible.
The right side has a small freshwater basin, still used for certain religious rituals.
As we went back up the tunnel, the guide made us turn off our lamps (which he had provided) and imagine, in total darkness, the despair of the men imprisoned there, even though slavery had been abolished but the illegal human trade continued.
It was striking and moving (though you need a bit of empathy, of course).
He then showed us the tunnel that the slaves had discovered to escape, which led their captors to build the slave quarters a little further on, when they realized the escapes were happening.
You can climb back up this narrow passage, holding onto the rocks and roots, which is what we did (otherwise, you can turn back and take the stairs).
So yes, for someone with walking difficulties, it's best avoided, but you don't need to be a super-fit athlete either. We're in our fifties, have no athletic training, and are rather sedentary, and we did it.
Afterwards, our guide answered all our questions (I'm very curious), showed us around his village, pointed out the crops, the fields, the trees... and we even ate with him and his family.
For me, that's the beauty of encounters. He didn't ask anything of us; we could see he was happy to share his life and his surroundings with us. We made sure to leave a small gift; it's the least we could do (coming from France, we're not the type to arrive empty-handed when we're invited somewhere).
We spent a large part of the day there, pure bliss, and a true immersion in the villagers' reality.
For that kind of human experience alone, it was fabulous.

A farm worker climbed to the very top of a coconut tree (over 30 meters tall) using his bare hands and a traditional method to pick a coconut, all while singing beautifully 😊

It's not a sanctuary or anything like that. The animals come from the sea and are perfectly healthy; they're caught to be displayed here.

The price was $10 cash per person.
Perfectly acceptable.
There is a shower, changing room, and toilet.

content:
I visited Fumba on my last evening in Zanzibar and it''s quite a great place for family outing with lots of kid''s entertainment. The location is awesome with nice evening breeze Zanzibar has to offer. It is open to public on the weekends but despite the amazing facilities on offer the management has failed terribly in putting in place any simple waste management methods. Vendors of all kinds are allowed to sell their merchandise on site, majority being snacks sellers but the sad fact is with no proper waste management in place all the snack wraps are lazily dropped on the ground by the clueless revellers and swept away by wind into the ocean. Some even throw their waste directly into the ocean. The estimated number of people during my visit was over 500 of which I was made to understand sometimes goes higher.
The management must do something about this, but all in all it''s a great family getaway!

I can recommend Serenity Funerals with full confidence they will come through.

content:
Africa House Garden is a beautiful place with an amazing view and a very relaxing atmosphere. The coffee aroma alone draws you in, and the free WiFi is a great bonus if you want to sit and work or unwind. I ordered a café latte, and it was excellent, very creamy and delicious. The shawarma was okay, not bad, but not particularly memorable.
Unfortunately, the service really took away from the experience. When I first asked for a minute to decide on food, the waiter left the menu and completely forgot about me. I later asked another waiter to call him so I could place my order; he said he would, but he also forgot. After about 40 minutes, I saw the original waiter again and had to remind him myself before my order was finally taken.
The same issue happened when it was time to pay. It was too hot outside, so I moved indoors and asked several waiters sitting near the counter to bring me the bill. All of them forgot and continued chatting. Eventually, when I was about to leave, I asked if it was okay to go without paying, only then did they laugh and finally bring the bill.
The location, view, and coffee are truly lovely, but the service needs serious improvement to match the quality of the setting.

content:
Bin schockiert wie viele Leute hier in den Rezensionen hervorheben wie toll es ist dort mal mit Schildkröten schwimmen zu können.
Fand es super schlimm dort.
To be fair wir hatten uns vorher nicht wirklich informiert weil wir zwei Mädchen getroffen haben die uns spontan eingeladen haben mit zu kommen.
Vorort haben wir dann den Eintritt bezahlt ( 15 dollar für 30 min ) und sind rein.
Wir haben sofort bemerkt, das dort erstaunlich viele Schildkröten auf einem Fleck sind ( kommt in freier Wildbahn so eigentlich nicht vor ) und haben dann gefragt ob die Tiere dort wirklich selbst rein und raus schwimmen können.
Uns wurde gesagt, dass das eigentlich so gut wie unmöglich ist und da haben wir dann endlich gecheckt, dass es sich hier nicht um frei lebende Tiere handelt sondern um eingefangene Schildkröten die dort hin gebracht werden um Touristen zu bespaßen.
Sobald man die ethische Seite des ganzem kritisch hinterfragt wird einem natürlich sofort gesagt, dass es sich hier um eine „Auffangstation“ handeln würde - was einfach straight up gelogen ist.
Die Tiere haben sichtlich keine Wunden oder andere von außen erkennbare Probleme, auch krank können sie nicht sein, da kranke Tiere in freier Wildbahn so gut wie immer von Parasiten befallen werden.
Richtige Auffangstationen haben deshalb auch verschiedene und sterile Becken in denen wirklich auf die Probleme der Tiere eigegangen werden kann.
Außerdem leben in Auffangstationen WILDtiere!!!! Das heißt es ist aus offensichtlichen Gründen nicht erlaubt als random Tourist zu diesen Tieren ins Wasser zu gehen. Bzw. sind die Tiere dann ja auch krank oder verletzt, weshalb man nicht zu ihnen ins Wasser sollte. ( Generell ein guter Richtwert eine ethische Auffangstation zu erkennen. In richtigen Stationen darf man als Besucher keinen direkten Kontakt zu den Tieren aufbauen. )
Dann wird einem erklärt, dass die Tiere ja auch immer wieder frei gelassen werden - nachdem wir mehrmals nachgefragt haben und uns kritisch gezeigt haben wurden uns ein paar mehr Fakten dargelegt.
Die Schildkröten die dort in diesen „Caves“ landen sind Beifang. ( Also Tiere die beim Fischen mit großen Netzen leider auch ins Netzt geraten wie Delphine/ Heie/ Tintenfischen/ Waale und eben auch Schildkröten. )
Also in Endeffekt eigentlich komplett gesunde Tiere die unter unserem massiven Fischkonsum leiden.
Diese dienen dann für eine Zeit als Touristen Attraktion bis sie unter einem großen Act von vorgespielten „Tierschutz“ wieder in ihr eigentliches zuhause entlassen werden.
Fazit: wir sind nach wenigen Minuten diskutieren direkt wieder raus und haben nach einem Refund gefragt ( 15 dollar sind als Backpacker gut und gerne mal ein ganzes Tagesbudget ) den wir natürlich nicht bekommen haben.
Bitte, im Namen des Tierwohls, unterstützt solche Einrichtungen nicht!!!!!
In freier Wildbahn kann man mit ethischen Bootstouren Schildkröten ganz einfach in ihrem natürlichen zu Hause sehen ohne das sie dabei leiden müssen.
translated_content:
I'm shocked by how many people in these reviews rave about the amazing experience of swimming with turtles.
I found it absolutely awful.
To be fair, we hadn't really done our research beforehand because we met two girls who spontaneously invited us along.
We paid the entrance fee ($15 for 30 minutes) and went in.
We immediately noticed the astonishing number of turtles gathered in one spot (something you don't usually see in the wild) and asked if the animals could actually swim in and out on their own.
We were told that was practically impossible, and that's when we finally realized that these weren't wild turtles, but rather captured turtles brought there to entertain tourists.
As soon as you start questioning the ethical aspects of the whole thing, you're immediately told that it's a "rescue center"—which is simply a blatant lie.
We were told that this was practically impossible. The animals clearly have no wounds or other externally visible problems; they can't be sick either, since sick animals in the wild are almost always infested with parasites.
Proper rescue centers therefore have various sterile pools where the animals' problems can truly be addressed.
Furthermore, rescue centers house WILD animals! This means that, for obvious reasons, it's not allowed for random tourists to enter the water with these animals. Besides, the animals would be sick or injured, which is why you shouldn't go in the water with them. (Generally, this is a good indicator of an ethical rescue center. In proper centers, visitors are not allowed to have direct contact with the animals.)
Then we were told that the animals are released again and again – after we asked several times and expressed our concerns, we were given a few more facts.
The turtles that end up in these "caves" are bycatch. (This includes animals that unfortunately get caught in large fishing nets, such as dolphins, sea urchins, squid, whales, and turtles.)
So, in the end, these are perfectly healthy animals that suffer because of our massive fish consumption.
They then serve as tourist attractions for a while until, under a grand guise of "animal welfare," they are released back into their natural habitat.
In short: after a few minutes of discussion, we left immediately and asked for a refund (15 dollars is easily a full day's budget for backpackers), which, of course, we didn't receive.
Please, in the name of animal welfare, do not support such facilities! In the wild, you can easily see turtles in their natural habitat on ethical boat tours without them having to suffer.
full_address: Salaam Cave Tours, Kizimkazi Dimbani, Tanzania

content:
If feeding turtles is on your Zanzibar itinerary, Salaam Cave is definitely worth considering.
The experience costs $12, and it was a lot more hands-on than I expected. Getting to the rock in the middle isn’t as easy as the videos make it look because the rocks under the water are uneven in some places. Once I got there though, I relaxed and really enjoyed being that close to the turtles.
A few things I’d tell anyone visiting: go early if you want fewer people around, take your own towel because you will pay extra if you need one there, and make use of the changing room after your swim. If you are traveling solo, you are allowed to use a tripod, which makes taking your own photos and videos much easier.
One thing I only found out afterwards was that green clothing can attract the turtles because it looks similar to the seaweed they are fed. I can’t say for certain that was why they kept coming towards me, but after hearing that, it made my experience make a lot more sense.

Für unsere Kinder war das Schwimmen mit den Riesenschildkröten ein besonderes Erlebnis. Insgesamt hat uns der Besuch jedoch nur mittelmässig gefallen.
Der Ort wirkt stark auf Fotos, Social Media und Influencer ausgerichtet. Die eigentliche Umgebung fanden wir nicht besonders schön. Während unseres Besuchs fanden zudem Bauarbeiten statt, was den Gesamteindruck vermutlich zusätzlich beeinträchtigt hat.

content:
One of the most unique experiences we had in Zanzibar.
When we first arrived, it was honestly difficult to imagine that such a beautiful cave was hidden there. The area was undergoing some improvements and construction work, so at first glance it does not immediately reveal what is waiting below.
Before entering the water, visitors are asked to shower thoroughly to remove sunscreen, body lotions and other products. We really appreciated this, as it shows how seriously they take the protection of the turtles and their environment.
Once inside, the experience is incredible. The water is crystal clear, the cave itself is beautiful, and we were even able to spot bats hanging from the ceiling. It feels like entering a hidden world.
The turtles are the main attraction and getting so close to them is something truly special. Visitors are given seaweed to feed them, and the turtles quickly swim over looking for a snack. Being able to observe them from such a short distance was unforgettable.
We paid for the one-hour experience, although for many visitors the 30-minute option would probably be enough. Either way, it was well worth it.
One funny piece of advice: avoid wearing green swimwear! My wife was wearing a green swimsuit, and one of the turtles apparently mistook it for seaweed and gave her a little bite on the back. Later, I had a small piece of seaweed attached to my arm and ended up getting a bite as well. Nothing serious at all, but it definitely gave us a good laugh and became one of the funniest memories of the experience.
The facilities are still being improved, and customer service could perhaps be a little more polished in some areas, but it was clear that the team is investing in the site and working to make the experience even better.
Overall, this was an immersive and memorable experience that allowed us to get closer to these amazing animals than we ever expected. The conservation aspect of the project was also very interesting, and learning that the turtles are cared for before eventually being released made the visit even more meaningful.
If you are visiting Zanzibar and enjoy nature and wildlife, Salaam Cave Aquarium is definitely worth adding to your itinerary.
Highly recommended.

content:
Wir haben die Salaam Cave besucht, weil die Beschreibung den Eindruck vermittelt, dass es sich um eine Art Schutz- oder Rückzugsort für Schildkröten handelt, an dem man auch etwas über die Tiere und ihren Lebensraum lernen kann. Mit dieser Erwartung sind wir dorthin gegangen.
Vor Ort hat sich das für uns allerdings anders angefühlt. Es waren viele Menschen gleichzeitig im Wasser mit den Schildkröten, und die Tiere wurden gefüttert, damit Besucher mit ihnen interagieren können. Dadurch wirkte es auf uns eher wie eine touristische Attraktion als wie ein ruhiger Ort, an dem der Schutz der Tiere im Mittelpunkt steht.
Informationen über die Schildkröten oder über mögliche Schutz- und Aufklärungsarbeit haben wir leider kaum bekommen, obwohl wir uns genau das erhofft hatten. Auch der Umgang mit den Tieren hat bei uns einige Fragen hinterlassen.
Etwas unangenehm fanden wir außerdem, dass dort ein Affe an einer Leine gehalten wurde. Das hat für uns nicht wirklich zu dem Bild eines Ortes gepasst, der sich dem Tierwohl widmet.
Diese Rezension soll niemanden schlecht machen, sondern einfach unsere persönliche Erfahrung wiedergeben. Wer überlegt, die Salaam Cave zu besuchen, sollte sich vielleicht vorher gut informieren und für sich entscheiden, ob diese Art von Tierbegegnung das ist, was man unterstützen möchte.
translated_content:
We visited Salaam Cave because the description gave the impression that it was a kind of sanctuary or refuge for turtles, where you could also learn about the animals and their habitat. That was our expectation.
However, our experience there was quite different. There were many people in the water with the turtles at the same time, and the animals were being fed so that visitors could interact with them. This made it feel more like a tourist attraction than a peaceful place where animal welfare is the priority.
Unfortunately, we received very little information about the turtles or about any conservation or educational work being done, even though that's exactly what we had hoped for. The way the animals were treated also left us with some questions.
We also found it somewhat disturbing that a monkey was being kept on a leash. This didn't really fit with our image of a place dedicated to animal welfare.
This review isn't meant to criticize anyone, but simply to share our personal experience. Anyone considering visiting Salaam Cave should perhaps do some research beforehand and decide for themselves whether this type of animal encounter is something they want to support.

content:
Visiting Salaam Cave to feed my favorite animals—the turtles—was truly a wonderful and unforgettable experience. From the moment you arrive, everything is well organized and focused on both safety and respect for the animals. Before entering the cave, you’re required to shower off, and a staff member walks you through a set of simple rules to follow. You’re also given a small container of seaweed to feed the turtles.
The water is cold at first, which can be a bit of a shock, but once you’re in, it becomes comfortable. One of the best tips is to stay calm and move gently. Feeding the turtles small pieces of seaweed helps make the experience last longer and keeps them engaged.
I truly believe the turtles can sense energy and tension. By remaining calm, gentle, and not anxious, the turtles were very peaceful with me. Some tourists who were in the water at the same time seemed scared and tense, and they ended up getting bitten. I, however, did not get bitten at all, even after I ran out of seaweed.
Overall, it was a beautiful, peaceful experience. If you respect the rules, stay calm and treat the turtles gently, visiting Salaam Cave is an incredible experience I would highly recommend—especially for anyone who loves marine life as much as I do. We did not go with a tour guy- went on our own which is a lot better option. $12 per person for 30minutes

⭐ SOS ⭐ Disturbing Treatment of a poor Monkey Baby 🐒
I visited Saalam Cave in November witnessed something extremely upsetting. A young monkey was kept on a short chain next to a “donations” box, apparently for paid photos with tourists. The animal showed clear signs of severe stress — it jumped at visitors and even bit someone. Its only “toy” was an electrical cable, which is dangerously unsafe.
After speaking with animal welfare groups, I learned that situations like this often involve young monkeys being taken from the wild, sometimes violently.
Supporting such practices — even unintentionally — contributes to more animals being captured and mistreated.
⚠️Please try to convince the handler to give you the monkey freely — and importantly, do not make any payment.
If you are able to take the monkey into your care, please contact the animal welfare organizations in Zanzibar immediately.
If you need a contact, feel free to message me on Instagram: @atzimieze ⚠️
I strongly urge all visitors:
• Please do not pay for photos or donate money when animals are being exploited.
• If you witness this monkey or others in distress, speak up and report it.
• Please also report this location directly on Google Maps (“Report this place”) so authorities and platforms are alerted. The more reports they receive, the faster something can change.
• Share this information with other travelers — your voice matters.
This experience was heartbreaking, and I sincerely hope that this monkey receives help as soon as possible. Tourism should never come at the expense of animal welfare. Let’s make sure practices like this have no place here.

content:
I am deeply shocked and disappointed by what I saw at Salaam Cave in Paje. What is promoted as a natural and peaceful turtle experience is, in reality, an overcrowded and exploitative situation where wild animals are mistreated for profit, with no concern from those who manage the site.
Inside a small, fenced-off cave, dozens of tourists (more than 30 at a time) were crammed in, pushing, tugging, and forcing turtles underwater, grabbing and holding them tightly just to take selfies. These turtles were fed nonstop throughout the day, teaching them to associate humans with food, leaving them completely vulnerable when they are eventually released into the wild. The animals were clearly stressed, but no one from management seemed to care.
When a concerned tourist dared to speak up—after witnessing turtles being grabbed, pulled, and brutally treated—rather than receive support, she was aggressively confronted by the manager and security staff, who told her this kind of abuse is necessary for the place to function. Their words, and I quote: "This is a tourist place, and for it to function, things like this have to happen."
It didn't end there.
They then tried to forcefully push the girl and her friends away, grabbing one of them by the arm and telling her that if she took another photo, they would destroy her phone. They added with a superior air that no one would stop them because they are "locals," implying that they are untouchable and above any consequences.
I was in complete shock and left immediately.
This is not conservation. This is not ecotourism. This is abuse—both of the animals and the visitors. The people in charge are profiting from the suffering of beautiful, sentient creatures, while intimidating anyone who tries to intervene.
It breaks my heart for turtles. They deserve protection—not to be imprisoned and abused for entertainment.

content:
Was einem als „Schildkrötenhöhle“ verkauft wird, handelt sich in Wahrheit um absolute Tierquälerei!
Wir haben den Ausflug in unserem Hotel bei unserem zuständigen Reiseleiter gebucht, der meinte, wir könnten mit Schildkröten schwimmen gehen.
Vor Ort angekommen handelte es sich um eine künstlich angelegte Höhle, in der circa 25 Schildkröten eingesperrt sind. Sie haben keine Fluchtmöglichkeit und der Zufluss der Touristen wird durch die Betreiber nicht geregelt. Das heißt, dass während wir dort waren, circa 40-50 Touristen in der kleinen Grotte waren und sich teilweise rücksichtslos verhalten haben (z. B. schreien, Herumschubsen der Schildkröten …). Auf Nachfrage dient diese Höhle dem Schutz der Schildkröten, was natürlich absoluter Schwachsinn ist.
Ich bin echt fassungslos! Absolute Tierquälerei 🥺 Wir bereuen, diesen Ausflug gebucht zu haben! Sehr traurig auch, dass viele andere Touristen die Salaam Cave nicht wirklich reflektieren.
translated_content:
What's being sold as a "turtle cave" is actually absolute animal cruelty!
We booked the excursion through our hotel's tour guide, who told us we could swim with turtles.
Upon arrival, we discovered it was an artificial cave containing approximately 25 turtles. They have no way to escape, and the flow of tourists isn't regulated by the operators. This means that while we were there, there were about 40-50 tourists in the small grotto, some of whom behaved inconsiderately (e.g., shouting, pushing the turtles around). When we asked, they claimed the cave was there to protect the turtles, which is, of course, complete nonsense.
I'm truly speechless! Absolute animal cruelty 🥺 We regret booking this excursion! It's also very sad that many other tourists don't seem to have any real insight into the Salaam Cave.
full_address: Salaam Cave Tours, Kizimkazi Dimbani, Tanzania

Het is een verschrikkelijke ervaring en doet geen eer aan de zogenaamde bescherming van het ecosysteem en de schildpadden.
Een absolute tourist trap en dus een afrader!

The Turtle Cave is a very dubious place to visit. The turtles are trapped in a small cave and have nowhere to go.

Turtles are lifted out of the water contrary to the guidelines, and people enter the water without showering, wearing sunscreen, perfume, and makeup. It is extremely crowded, and to make matters worse, there was a small monkey tied by its tail as an attraction. Tourists could touch the monkey. The animal reacted completely overstimulated to all the people and snapped and bit at the hands that were held out. Very sad to see.
It is a terrible experience and does not do justice to the so-called protection of the ecosystem and the turtles.
An absolute tourist trap and therefore not recommended!

content:
Absolut nicht zu empfehlen – Tierleid für Massentourismus
Ich bin schockiert, wie hier mit den Schildkröten umgegangen wird. Es handelt sich um reinen Massentourismus – viel zu viele Menschen werden gleichzeitig durchgeschleust, es ist laut, chaotisch und vollkommen respektlos gegenüber den Tieren.
Die Schildkröten befinden sich in einem künstlichen Wasserbecken, das als “Höhle” verkauft wird – aber es gibt keinen erkennbaren Ausgang oder natürlichen Rückzugsort für die Tiere. Sie werden offensichtlich angefüttert, damit sie nah an die Besucher kommen. Einige Touristen fassen die Tiere an, schieben sie sogar weg oder kreischen laut herum. Es herrscht keinerlei Rücksichtnahme – und auch keine echte Kontrolle durch das Personal.
Aus meiner Sicht wirken die Schildkröten völlig gestresst, manche schnappen regelrecht um sich. Das Ganze hat mit einem respektvollen Umgang mit Natur oder Tierschutz absolut nichts zu tun. Für 12 Dollar bekommt man 30 Minuten in einem überfüllten, lauten Setting, das nur dem Zweck dient, Touristen schnell durchzuschleusen.
Für mich war das eine verstörende Erfahrung. Ich kann nur jedem davon abraten – bitte unterstützt so etwas nicht.
translated_content:
Absolutely not recommended – animal suffering for mass tourism
I am shocked by the way the turtles are treated here. It's pure mass tourism – far too many people are herded through at once, it's loud, chaotic, and completely disrespectful to the animals.
The turtles are kept in an artificial pool marketed as a "cave" – but there's no discernible exit or natural retreat for them. They are clearly being fed to get close to visitors. Some tourists touch the animals, even push them away or scream loudly. There's absolutely no consideration for the animals – and no real control by the staff.
From my perspective, the turtles seem completely stressed; some are even snapping at each other. This whole thing has absolutely nothing to do with respecting nature or animal welfare. For $12, you get 30 minutes in an overcrowded, noisy setting designed solely to rush tourists through.
For me, this was a disturbing experience. I can only advise everyone against it – please don't support such things.

content:
Salaam Cave Aquarium offers a unique opportunity to interact with turtles in a natural cave pool setting, but sadly, the overall experience falls short in many critical areas. The only standout feature was the excellent videography service provided by one of the staff members—though even this requires haggling to get a reasonable price.
Visitor management is lacking, with far too many people allowed into the pool at once, raising concerns about the turtles’ well-being. There’s no visible system to refresh or filter the water regularly, which is alarming considering the pollution caused by constant human activity. For an attraction that charges a premium fee, the showers and restrooms are subpar and in need of serious improvement.
There are also safety issues. The turkeys on site, likely stressed by captivity, can be aggressive and are prone to biting. Visitors should also tread carefully inside the cave—the uneven rock floor is quite slippery and could lead to injury if one isn’t cautious.
Most disappointing is the lack of education or orientation. A brief welcome speech explaining the cave’s significance and the conservation efforts for the turtles, including their eventual release, would go a long way in improving the experience.
Overall, an average and somewhat underwhelming visit.

content:
Luogo davvero carino dove puoi stare a contatto con le tartarughe marine. All’ingresso ti danno una ciotolina con alghe per dare da mangiare alle tartarughe. Consiglio di usare le ciabattine da scoglio perché il fondo é irregolare.
Le tartarughe sono molte, di vario colore e forma.
Unica pecca la maleducazione delle persone, che chi parla a voce troppo alta, i bambini che gridano e saltano quando é espressamente scritto cosa non fare. Le tartarughe ti passano vicino e ti toccano con le pinne o il carapace ma attenzione qualcuna può mordicchiare, quindi invece che saltare e gridare basta 1.guardarsi intorno e vedere se ci sono tartarughe intorno a noi, 2 se troppo vicine basta spostarle gentilmente con le mani dando una curvatura alla loro rotta…non credo ci voglia molto ma alcune persone non hanno molto rispetto per queste meravigliose creature..
Per il resto staff gentile che ha cercato di placare anche una ragazza con un attacco di panico..
translated_content:
A really nice place where you can interact with sea turtles. At the entrance, they give you a small bowl of seaweed to feed them. I recommend wearing flip-flops because the bottom is uneven.
There are many turtles, of various colors and shapes.
The only downside is the rudeness of the people, from those who talk too loudly to children who scream and jump even when it's specifically written what not to do. The turtles pass by and touch you with their fins or shells, but be careful—some might nip you. So instead of jumping and screaming, just 1. look around and see if there are any turtles around you; 2. if they're too close, just gently move them with your hands, curving their path... I don't think it takes much, but some people don't have much respect for these wonderful creatures.
Otherwise, the staff was friendly and even tried to calm a girl having a panic attack.

content: Okropne miejsce. Jeśli ktoś ma choć trochę współczucia i empatii do zwierząt to absolutnie nie polecam. Ja poszłam za grupą i nie sprawdziłam gdzie jedziemy, za co pluje sobie w brodę. Liczyłam na jaskinię gdzie świat morski łączy się ze światem ludzi, że jakimś cudem żółwie przypływają tam za pożywieniem jako wolne istoty, a trafiłam do dziury na środku parkingu w której nie ma kompletnie żadnego przepływu wody. Wsadzone jest do niej kilkanaście, jak nie kilkadziesiąt przepięknych żółwi których naturą jest przemierzać tysiące kilometrów w samotności. Woda jest tak tłusta od olejków i kremów z filtrem, że ledwo widać dno. Breja w turkusowym kolorze. Żółwie karmione są jedynie jakimiś glonami sprzedawanymi przez chłopów za dolca. Przed jaskinią znajdują się prysznice, ale oczywiście nikt z nich nie korzysta (widziałam nawet kobietę która do jaskini smarowała się kremem tuż przed 🤦🏻‍♀️), co przekłada się na jakość wody w której żyją te zwierzęta. A w naturze żyją nawet do 100 lat! Jednym słowem - to miejsce to koszmar uwięzionych dla uciechy ludzkiej majestatycznych zwierząt. Jeśli chociaż jedna osoba odpuści sobie tą wycieczkę po moim opisie, to będę bardzo szczęśliwa.
translated_content: A terrible place. If anyone has even a shred of compassion or empathy for animals, I absolutely do not recommend it. I followed the group and didn't check where we were going, which is a shame. I was hoping for a cave where the marine world connects with the human world, where turtles somehow swim there for food as free beings, but instead I ended up in a hole in the middle of the parking lot with absolutely no water flow. A dozen or so beautiful turtles are trapped there, their natural instincts being to travel thousands of kilometers alone. The water is so greasy with oils and sunscreen that you can barely see the bottom. It's a turquoise slush. The turtles are fed only some kind of algae sold by farmers for a dollar. There are showers in front of the cave, but of course, no one uses them (I even saw a woman applying sunscreen just before entering the cave 🤦🏻‍♀️), which affects the quality of the water in which these animals live. And in the wild, they can live up to 100 years! In short, this place is a nightmare of majestic animals trapped for human enjoyment. If even one person skips this trip after reading my description, I'll be very happy.
full_address: Salaam Cave Tours, Kizimkazi Dimbani, Tanzania

posted_on:
A fun attraction to discover despite the price and the risk of crowds.
The cave is located in the center of a property managed by a national conservation institute. Don't expect to be able to "walk around" and access it for free; you have to go through the gate and pay to see the cave and go down into it.
The entrance fee is $11 per person for 30 minutes, $22 for 1 hour. (They accept credit cards (+5%) or dollars and give change.)
In my opinion, 30 minutes is plenty of time to enjoy the turtles.
They offer small baskets of seaweed for an extra $1 per person, which isn't necessary to get great photos with the turtles around you, in my opinion.
The cave is small and can only hold a limited number of people. We went early and it was pleasant. We recommend arriving before 9:45 am!
It's important to know that the cave is a closed environment for the turtles; only a small opening to the sea allows for water renewal (tides). The turtles are therefore "prisoners" for 20 years before being released into the open sea.

content:
OMG, this place is amazing, I would give 10* if it was possible!!
It''s a small cave where injured turtles are cared for and rehabilitated before being released back into the sea.
You pay a small fee at the gate for 1/2 hour or 1 hour and have a guide to explain the process.  We brought some seaweed, and as we already had our swimmers on, we went down the ladder into the cave. They do have changing rooms you can use for free.
Once in the cave, we left our bags on the platform, I gave our guide my phone, and we went down another ladder into the water.  The water is fresh at first and comes to waist height if you are 5ft 9, the floor of the cave was very rocky.
As soon as we were in the water, the turtles swam over to us, and we fed them some seaweed. Just watch your fingers as one turtle was quite greedy and nipped my thumb!
They don''t mind you being there and swimming around you. They are very gentle, and you can pet them when they swim past. There are yellow birds that have made their nests above you in the cave.
We got out after half an hour, and our guide gave me my phone back with lots of amazing pictures and videos of me in the water with the turtles. It was a truly lovely time and not too busy when we visited, about 2pm.

V západní části Zanzibaru najdete jednu z přírodních lagun plných mořských želv. V přírodním  akváriu s názvem Saalam Cave na vás vykukují želvy roztomilé želvičky se kterými se můžete vyloženě pomazlit. Využijte jedinečnou příležitost zaplavat si s mořskými želvami.
Nad hlavami vám hnízdí nádherní barevní ptáci. Díky nim zde slyšíte ptačí koncert😁
Během návštěvy můžete také krmit želvy mořskými řasami nebo jen tak trávit čas ve vodě. Měli jsme to štěstí, že jsme tu že začátku byli úplně sami.
translated_content:
Beautiful place
In the western part of Zanzibar you will find one of the natural lagoons full of sea turtles. In the natural aquarium called Saalam Cave, cute turtles will peek out at you, which you can really cuddle with. Take advantage of the unique opportunity to swim with sea turtles.
Beautiful colorful birds nest above your heads. Thanks to them, you can hear a bird concert here😁
During your visit, you can also feed the turtles with seaweed or just spend time in the water. We were lucky enough to be completely alone here at first.

+ tolle Höhle mit Meerwasser
+ sehr klares Wasser
+ man bekommt Algen, um die Schildkröten zu füttern
+ viele Schildkröten

+ sehr viele Fledermäuse an der Decke
- da es so neu ist gibt es noch kaum Regeln. Viele Touristen verhalten sich unmöglich und heben die Schildkröten hoch oder versuchen sie umzudrehen. Ein Kind hat sich sogar beim tauchen an sie drangehängt damit die Schildkröte es zieht
> ich war sehr überrascht, dass die Mitarbeiter hier nichts sagten
- das Betreten der Höhle sollte auf eine bestimmte Personenanzahl begrenzt sein. Wir kamen 5 Minuten vor einer 12er Gruppe welche total laut und rücksichtslos waren. Wir wurden dann nach 30 Minuten rausgeschickt als wir sowieso selbst raus wollten, als es uns zu voll wurde
- als es leerer war durften wir nur „ausnahmsweise“ nochmal für ein kurzes Foto rein
An sich tolle Höhle und ich finde der Preis ist gerechtfertigt für so ein Erlebnis. Wer schreckhaft ist und im Wasser sich ruckartig bewegt sollte aus Rücksicht der Tiere (die auch am Boden liegen und die Gefahr ist darauf zu treten) von den Steinen aus zuschauen und nicht ins Wasser. Außerdem sollte man auf Sonnencreme für die 30 Minuten verzichten, um das Wasser und die Höhle nicht zu verunreinigen.
An sich ein tolles Erlebnis!
translated_content:
+ Amazing cave with seawater
+ Very clear water
+ You get algae to feed the turtles
+ Lots of turtles
+ Friendly staff
+ Lots of bats on the ceiling
- Since it's so new, there are hardly any rules. Many tourists behave terribly, picking up the turtles or trying to turn them over. One child even hung onto a turtle while diving, hoping it would pull them.
> I was very surprised that the staff didn't say anything.
- Entry to the cave should be limited to a certain number of people. We arrived 5 minutes before a group of 12 who were incredibly loud and inconsiderate. We were then asked to leave after 30 minutes, even though we wanted to leave ourselves anyway because it was getting too crowded.
- When it was less crowded, we were only allowed back in "as an exception" for a quick photo.
Overall, it's a great cave, and I think the price is justified for such an experience. Those who are easily startled and move suddenly in the water should, out of consideration for the animals (which also lie on the bottom and are at risk of being stepped on), watch from the rocks and not go into the water. Furthermore, sunscreen should be avoided for the 30 minutes to prevent polluting the water and the cave.
All in all, a fantastic experience!
full_address: Salaam Cave Tours, Kizimkazi Dimbani, Tanzania

Dangerous for shipping, but ideal for sea picnics.
The "disappearing island", as the Zanzibari call it, can give a lot of positive things.
The main thing here is to know the time of high and low tides in order to:
1 - be able to swim to it at low water, when the island is at its largest size, and it is more convenient to dive to the corals,
2 - give time to specially trained guys to prepare dishes of traditional Zanzibari cuisine, that is, assorted fruits and grilled inhabitants of the sea depths, and
3 - have time to get into the boat before high water covers the island from human eyes for a while.

He goes to schools and makes sure the children aren't afraid of them. There's a lot of superstition surrounding them in the local population. We were impressed by Belo's work and highly recommend a visit.

content:
Hier kann man schöne Chamäleons sehen und auf die Hand nehmen. Der Gastgeber Belo hat uns interessante Dinge über Chamäleons und sein Projekt erzählt.
Sein Ziel ist es, Chamäleons zu schützen durch Aufklärung der Bevölkerung, die Chamäleons mit dem Bösen assoziieren und im Absuchen von Stellen, an denen Brandrodungen geplant sind.
Ein Besuch ist eine gute Unterstützung dieses Projektes.
translated_content:
Here you can see beautiful chameleons and even hold them. Our host, Belo, told us interesting things about chameleons and his project.
His goal is to protect chameleons by educating people who associate chameleons with evil and by monitoring areas where slash-and-burn agriculture is planned.
A visit is a great way to support this project.

content:
Sono stata insieme al mio ragazzo in questo luogo gestito da ragazzi locali che hanno come progetto la salvaguardia dei camaleonti.
Prima di vedere gli animali, abbiamo fatto un giro nelle grotte insieme alla guida che ci ha spiegato molto bene tutta la formazione dei cristalli all’interno e ci ha fatto vivere un momento unico all’interno della grotta (non adatto a chi ha paura del buio.) Dopo la visita nelle grotte, siamo andati all’interno dell’area dedicata alla salvaguardia dei camaleonti, potendone vedere di diversi e con la possibilità di tenerli in mano e darli da mangiare. La visita è stata molto interessante e ci ha fornito molte informazioni riguardo questa specie e alla loro tutela.
Ne vale davvero la pena, una delle esperienze più belle sull’isola!
Il costo del biglietto di ingresso è di 15 euro (accettano anche scellini Tanzani ovviamente e dollari, probabilmente la conversione potrebbe essere più economica, errore nostro avere solo euro).
translated_content:
My boyfriend and I visited this place, run by locals who have a chameleon conservation project.
Before seeing the animals, we toured the caves with a guide, who gave us a detailed explanation of how the crystals form and provided a unique experience inside the cave (not suitable for those afraid of the dark). After visiting the caves, we went into the chameleon conservation area, where we were able to see several and even hold and feed them. The tour was very interesting and provided us with a wealth of information about this species and their conservation.
It's definitely worth it; one of the most beautiful experiences on the island!
The entrance fee is 15 euros (they also accept Tanzanian shillings and dollars, of course; converting could probably be cheaper; it was our mistake to only have euros).

content: Хамелеоны – семейство ящериц, способных менять свою окраску тела в зависимости от ситуации, в основном для защиты от опасности, особенно от таких хищников как змеи и обезьяны. Приспособлены к древесному образу жизни, поэтому здесь в небольшом саду для них обустроены деревья и небольшие кустики , норки для закапывания яиц. Персонал кормит их один раз в день, предоставляя 5-7 насекомых каждому. В данном питомнике в настоящее время находится 18 взрослых хамелеонов. Хамелеоны живут обособленно друг от друга, соединяются в пары только в период спаривания. По информации гида,  хамелеоны - самцы могут драться между собой , отстаивая лидерство. Для человека эти ящерицы совершенно безопасны и очень дружелюбны. У нас возникло впечатление что они воспринимают нас как большие деревья,  по которым интересно полазить и изучить. Хамелеоны используют лапки и хвост для баланса и фиксации. Прикасаясь к поверхности кожи человека они делают это очень аккуратно и нежно. Предоставляемых для питания насекомых они ловят языком с ловчей присоской на конце языка, процесс выбрасывания которого длится всего 1/20-ю секунды, то есть очень быстро , как можно видеть на видео. В целом в сопровождении гида мы провели здесь около получаса, было очень интересно. Гид прекрасно говорит на английском и объясняет все особенности ухода за ящерицами, отлично отвечает на все вопросы. Это место посещения для людей любого возраста. С учётом того, что рядом находится пещеры, которые я бы рекомендовала все же ограничивать к посещению для людей пожилого возраста и детей, посещение маленького питомника хамелеонов оправдает ваш визит в деревню Tazari в полной мере. Стоимость посещения питомника всего пять долларов. Доехать до этой деревни можно на тук-тук ки из нуви за 15 минут. Дорога пролегает в основном по трассе однако потом вы съедете на второстепенную дорогу. Стоимость тук-тук очень варьирует,  мы сторговали за 20 000 шиллингов в обе стороны, заплатив на обратном пути. Это было правильным решением, так как с большой вероятностью водитель увеличил бы цену вдвое, если бы мы заплатили сразу 20 000.
translated_content: Chameleons are a family of lizards that can change their body color depending on the situation, primarily to protect themselves from danger, especially predators such as snakes and monkeys. They are adapted to an arboreal lifestyle, so here in the small garden, trees and small bushes have been created for them, along with burrows for burying eggs. The staff feeds them once a day, providing 5-7 insects each. The breeding center currently houses 18 adult chameleons. The chameleons live solitary lives, pairing up only during mating season. According to the guide, male chameleons may fight among themselves to assert dominance. These lizards are completely harmless to humans and very friendly. We got the impression that they perceive us as large trees, interesting to climb and explore. Chameleons use their paws and tail for balance and stability. When touching human skin, they do so very gently and tenderly. They catch insects offered for food with their tongues, which have a suction cup at the end. The process of ejecting the tongue lasts only 1/20th of a second—very quickly, as you can see in the video. Overall, we spent about half an hour here with a guide, and it was very interesting. The guide speaks excellent English and explains all the details of caring for the lizards, answering all questions very well. This is a place to visit for people of all ages. Considering the nearby caves, which I would recommend limiting to older people and children, a visit to the small chameleon nursery will fully justify your visit to Tazari village. The cost of visiting the nursery is only five dollars. The village is a 15-minute tuk-tuk ride from Nuvi. The road is mostly on the highway, but then you'll turn onto a secondary road. Tuk-tuk fares vary widely, but we settled on 20,000 shillings roundtrip and paid on the way back. This was the right decision, as the driver would likely have doubled the price if we'd paid 20,000 upfront.

content:
A fuir de toute urgence… je suis tellement choqué du non respect animalier sur terre pour divertir des touristes.
Particulièrement à Zanzibar. Entre les diverses salam caves (attraction aux tortues) ; la pêche aux dauphins ; vous trouverez ce genre de mini zoo partout sur l’île, comme celui de Nungwi. Le nombre d’animaux vivant sur un sol de moins d’un hectare est abominable ajouté à cela un nombre de touristes perturbateur de leur vie et rythme naturel.
Tout est devenu un buisiness… pour une petite photo avec un caméléon sur votre main vous n’imaginez pas leur petit cœur et leur petit métabolisme mais c’est très fragile et ce que vous faites est cruel. C’est un crime de leur faire subir cela.
Ne pas allez svp ! Même s’ils disent les relâcher après les avoir  habitué à l’homme et nourrit ; pensez vous qu’ils sauront capable de chasser des insectes et de s’acclimater ensuite à leur vrai environnement? … je me pose énormément de questions.
translated_content:
Avoid at all costs… I am so shocked by the lack of respect shown to animals on Earth for the sake of tourist entertainment.
Especially in Zanzibar. Between the various salam caves (turtle attractions) and dolphin fishing, you'll find these kinds of mini-zoos all over the island, like the one in Nungwi. The number of animals living on less than a hectare of land is appalling, and on top of that, the number of tourists disrupts their lives and natural rhythms.
Everything has become a business… for a quick photo with a chameleon on your hand, you can't imagine their tiny hearts and their tiny metabolisms, but they are very fragile, and what you are doing is cruel. It's a crime to make them suffer like this.
Please don't go! Even if they say they release them after getting them used to humans and feeding them, do you think they will be able to hunt insects and then adapt to their real environment? … I have so many questions.

Nach der netten Begrüßung sind wir zur Höhle gegangen und haben die kleine Geschichte dazu erfahren. Anschließend waren wir bei den Chamäleon. Sie sind toll und wunderschön. Ich finde die Idee, sie alle 3 Wochen auszutauschen sehr gut. So müssen sie nicht ein Leben in Gefangenschaft verbringen und gewöhnen sich auch nicht an die Fütterung.
Die Höhlen haben meine Erwartungen bei Weitem übertroffen. Ein großer Stalaktit und viele kleinere, wunderschöne Gebilde. Glitzernde Zahnreihen und Halbkugeln und auch 3 verschiedene Farben. Unbedingt gute Schuhe anziehen!
Diese Lokation ist wirklich einen Besuch wert!!!
translated_content:
After a warm welcome, we went to the cave and learned its little story. Then we visited the chameleons. They are amazing and beautiful. I think the idea of ​​rotating them every three weeks is excellent. This way, they don't have to live in captivity and don't get used to the feeding schedule.
The caves far exceeded my expectations. A large stalactite and many smaller, beautiful formations. Glittering rows of teeth and hemispheres, and three different colors: green, presumably containing copper; yellow, presumably containing sulfur; and pink. It was truly astonishing. We also saw the whip spider, which looks eerie but is completely harmless.
Be sure to wear good shoes!
This place is definitely worth a visit!!!

content:
Wir sind spontan vom Hotel dorthin gelaufen, nachdem ich in Google Maps nach einem Kochkurs in Matemwe gesucht habe. Auf Anfrage hat Amina kurz überlegt und dann waren wir uns einig. Amina hat per Telefon Gemüse bestellt, das nach ein paar Minuten eingetroffen ist. Dann ging es los.
Es ist ein sehr authentisches Kocherlebnis. Auf dem Boden, kein fließendes Wasser, auf dem Feuer. Für empfindliche würde ich es nicht empfehlen.
Die Frauen sind sehr freundlich. Ich glaube, auf manche wirken wir genauso exotisch, wie umgekehrt.
Das Essen war sehr lecker. Man isst aber nicht dort, sondern nimmt es in Gläsern mit, die akribisch und pole pole mit der Hand beschriftet werden.
Insgesamt ein Highlight für uns. Alina spricht englisch. Aber man sollte nicht davon ausgehen, daß immer eine Frau dort ist, die englisch spricht.
Google Translator kann aber auch Suahili :-)
translated_content:
We spontaneously walked there from the hotel after I searched for a cooking class in Matemwe on Google Maps. Amina thought about it briefly when I inquired, and then we agreed. Amina ordered vegetables by phone, which arrived a few minutes later. Then we got started.
It's a very authentic cooking experience. Cooking on the floor, no running water, over an open fire. I wouldn't recommend it for those with sensitive stomachs.
The women are very friendly. I think we seem just as exotic to some of them as they do to us.
The food was delicious. You don't eat there, but take it home in jars that are meticulously labeled by hand.
Overall, a highlight for us. Alina speaks English. But don't assume that there will always be someone there who speaks English.
Google Translate can also do Swahili :-)
full_address: 489Q+C4X Dada Zanzibar Production and Cooking Site, Mwangaseni, Tanzania

content:
We did the Kisongoni Village tour with Bilal as our guide. I''m glad we chose this over a spice farm tour as visiting a village gave insights into the local way of life.
Bilal took us on a two hour walk explaining about the fruits and spices growing in his village and how they are used in medicine and cooking. Bilal is a great conversationalist, asking us questions while informing us about village life, giving the morning a friendly, relaxed vibe.
At just 19, it was inspiring to hear Bilal explain that he set his mind from a young age to study English and history to start a business that would benefit his village.
The tour ended with a fruit tasting and fresh coconut drink. There was an opportunity to buy spices at the end, which we did without haggling as happy to support the village. We booked the day before, and they helpfully arrange a transfer to and from our hotel.
An excellent option if you are staying near Kiwengwa beach and want to meet some local Zanzibaris and learn about their way of life.

content:
感谢导游adil 的耐心讲解，很专业，会问我想要怎样的导览，我说想知道多一些香料而不需要太深度的讲解，我一路上品尝到也闻到了香料，而且也有香料制作的颜料，会给我演示它的用法，让我印象深刻。这对我来说是一个全新的体验，嗅觉味觉触觉都体验到了。导游很博学，他知道中国的害羞草还专门给我看。工作人员也一路给我编织草帽和开椰子水给我喝。我觉得很享受。很开心。
工作人员跟热心，由于我回石头城没有车，所以帮我叫他有摩托车的朋友过来搭我，而摩托车的朋友不认识我要去的地方，也不会英语，所以老板决定搭我回去。老板很健谈，会问我对香料园的感觉和对桑给巴尔的感觉，也会问我会多少种语言之类的问题，而我也很喜欢谈论这些。谢谢老板的搭乘。
总之，推荐大家来这个香料园。我获得了很棒的体验。
translated_content:
Thank you to our guide, Adil, for his patient and professional explanations. He asked what kind of tour I wanted, and I said I wanted to learn more about spices without going into too much detail. I tasted and smelled spices throughout the tour, and he even showed me spice-based dyes and demonstrated their uses, which left a deep impression on me. This was a completely new experience for me, engaging all my senses—smell, taste, and touch. The guide was very knowledgeable; he even showed me the Chinese mimosa plant. The staff also wove straw hats for me and opened coconuts for me to drink. I thoroughly enjoyed it and was very happy.
The staff were also very helpful. Since I didn't have a ride back to Stone City, he called a friend of his who had a motorcycle to give me a ride. However, the friend didn't know where I was going and didn't speak English, so the owner decided to give me a ride. The owner was very talkative, asking about my impressions of the spice garden and Zanzibar, as well as how many languages ​​I spoke, which I enjoyed discussing. Thank you for the ride.
In short, I highly recommend this spice garden. I had a wonderful experience.

content:
Wir waren heute mit unserem 9jährigen Sohn nach StoneTown (kurze Tour, 1,5h) und Prison Island auf dieser schönen Spice Farm. Abdul von der Spicefarm hat uns wirklich unterhaltsam über die Farm geführt. Es wurde sehr viel erklärt und man konnte viele Gewürze und Pflanzen riechen, schmecken und über alles lernen, ohne das es einem zu viel oder langweilig wurde. Selbst unser Sohn fand dass dies die beste Station aus zansibar ist. Uns wurden noch wunderschöne Erinnerungen aus Blättern geflochten und es gab ausreichend Zeit für Fragen und zum Fotografieren. Natürlich möchte man auf der Farm auch etwas verkaufen, das werden sie auf jedem Olivenhain in Italien erleben wie auch in jedem Weinberg am Rhein. Wir haben gern ein paar Dinge auch als Mitbringsel für Freunde gekauft und möchten diese Tour gern jedem empfehlen der die Zeit dazu findet. Abdul möchten wir nochmal ausdrücklich danken, er spricht super deutsch und musste nur 2 mal kurz in sein noch besseres englisch ausweichen.
Nach vielen schlechten Berichten über spice Farms wollten wir das erst garnicht machen und sind aber froh das uns diese Tour empfohlen wurde, scheinbar scheint es von Farm zu Farm sehr verschieden zu sein.. diese hier ist ein MustSee von Sansibar.
translated_content:
Today we took our 9-year-old son to Stone Town (a short tour, 1.5 hours) and Prison Island to visit this lovely spice farm. Abdul from the spice farm gave us a truly entertaining tour. He explained a great deal, and we were able to smell and taste many spices and plants and learn about everything without it being overwhelming or boring. Even our son thought it was the best stop on our trip to Zanzibar. We were even given beautiful souvenirs woven from leaves, and there was plenty of time for questions and photos. Of course, they also want to sell things on the farm, as you'll see in every olive grove in Italy and every vineyard along the Rhine. We happily bought a few things as souvenirs for friends and would highly recommend this tour to anyone who has the time. We would like to give Abdul a special thank you; he speaks excellent German and only had to switch to his even better English twice.
After reading many negative reports about spice farms, we initially didn't want to do it, but we're glad this tour was recommended to us; apparently, it varies greatly from farm to farm. This one is a must-see in Zanzibar.

content:
El Mercado de Especias de Zanzíbar es una experiencia fascinante que, sin duda, despierta los sentidos con sus aromas embriagadores y sus vibrantes colores. Es increíble ver la gran variedad de especias locales, desde la vainilla y el clavo hasta la nuez moscada y la canela, y aprender sobre sus usos tradicionales. La oportunidad de ver la cantidad de especias que pueden llegar a existir es un plus inolvidable que añade un toque auténtico a la visita.
Sin embargo, debo admitir que la realidad no cumplió del todo con mis expectativas. Si bien la riqueza cultural y la belleza natural son innegables, la experiencia se ve ensombrecida por una persistente sensación de ser 'explotado'" como turista. Los precios de los productos están notoriamente inflados para los visitantes extranjeros

responded_on:
The Zanzibar Spice Market is a fascinating experience that undoubtedly awakens the senses with its intoxicating aromas and vibrant colors. It's incredible to see the vast array of local spices, from vanilla and cloves to nutmeg and cinnamon, and to learn about their traditional uses. The opportunity to witness the sheer number of spices available is an unforgettable bonus that adds an authentic touch to the visit.
However, I must admit that reality didn't quite live up to my expectations. While the cultural richness and natural beauty are undeniable, the experience is overshadowed by a persistent feeling of being exploited as a tourist. The prices of the products are noticeably inflated for foreign visitors, far exceeding what locals would pay. Furthermore, the vendors' constant pushiness and pressure can be overwhelming and unpleasant, detracting from what would otherwise be a genuine cultural immersion. It's a shame that the beauty of the place is overshadowed by these commercial practices.

content:
Wir hatten einen richtig spannenden Ausflug auf den Markt und in die Umgebung. Wenn man mit einem Local (Guide) unterwegs ist gibt''s keine größeren Schwierigkeiten. Man wird dennoch an jeder Ecke angequatscht, dass man doch was kaufen soll.
Die Preise auf dem Spice Markt sind deutlich höher als in den umliegenden Geschäften. Natürlich muss man handeln, das gestaltet sich doch oft als sehr zäh.
Auch bei den Guides ist Vorsicht geboten. Man hat schneller eine Tour die man eigentlich gar nicht wollte als man nein sagen kann.
Ein gutes Argument gegen aufdringliche inoffizielle Tourguides ist, dass man sagt, dass man die Tour bereits hatte. Dann sind sie ganz schnell weg.
translated_content:
We had a really exciting trip to the market and the surrounding area. If you're with a local guide, there aren't any major problems. However, you'll still be approached at every turn trying to sell you something.
Prices at the Spice Market are significantly higher than in the surrounding shops. Of course, you have to haggle, but that can often be quite a chore.
You also need to be careful with the guides. You can find yourself on a tour you didn't want before you know it.
A good way to deal with pushy unofficial tour guides is to say that you've already had their tour. Then they'll disappear very quickly.
