Dadurch kommen sie nur an schlechtere bzw alte Gewürze , da einheimische dieses Zeug nicht kaufen sondern nur in bestimmten Läden und sie zahlen viel mehr .
Besser außerhalb der Stadt verkaufen und den Leuten etwas Gutes tun , die sich nicht verarschen und sich über das Geld oder auch ein Trinkgeld freuen .
Ansonsten gibt es Parkplätze die 1000TSN/h oder 3000/day kosten .
Oft wird man auch angesprochen ob man  Geld spendet - wie überall auf Sansibar :)
Bei den Kindern fängt es leider schon an mit einem netten hello und danach direkt ein Money Money ...sehr schade um das eigentlich angenehme Inselchen
translated_content:
It's interesting to stroll around since there's a lot of choice.
Unfortunately, as a tourist, you pay many times more than usual. :)
For example, a bottle of sugarcane juice normally costs 1000 TSN.
Here, they charge between 5,000 and 10,000 TSN, or even 1000 TSN for snacks instead of 200.
No matter how interesting it is, I definitely wouldn't shop here, because people can see that you're white and a tourist.
As a result, you only get inferior or old spices, since locals don't buy this stuff; they only buy it in certain shops, and they pay much more.
It's better to sell outside the city and do something nice for people who aren't being ripped off and are happy to receive money or even a tip.
Alternatively, there are parking lots that cost 1000 TSN per hour or 3000 TSN per day.
You're often asked if you'd like to donate money – just like everywhere else in Zanzibar :) Unfortunately, with the children it starts with a friendly hello, followed immediately by "Money, money"... a real shame for what is otherwise a lovely little island.

translated_content: The local market is a place where you can find all kinds of spices, fruits, vegetables, and small ornaments. First of all, let me say upfront that it's not a very clean area. As for spices, black pepper, ginger, and cloves are really high quality. You can also buy vanilla twigs (orchid flower twigs) that grow in Zanzibar and are quite high quality. You can also buy liquid vanilla, banana, and mango extracts in small bottles; they are both reasonably priced and of good quality. Besides vanilla, Zanzibar is also famous for its cashew nuts. You can find both salted and unsalted nuts at very reasonable prices. They usually sell them in 100, 450, and 900-gram bags. Finally, they sell dried octopus and juvenile fish that they collect from the beach during low tide and salt. The juvenile fish are sold as fish chips; they're not hygienic, but they're worth trying.

content:
I was wandering the alleys, when I bumped into this market, even though I knew that I had to visit it, I had no idea I was going on that direction, as I walk closer and closer, a veeeery distinctive smell was coming out of the fish section, lot of loud voices too. I walk straight in, spectacular experience!! I could witness the auctions, Hammer heads, other sharks, Big Marleys, giant Manta rays and heaps of other species of fish, the men negotiating the prices, chaos, very dirty, just like you see in documentaries, I went for lunch after and returned to it once again.
IT WAS AN AMAZING EXPERIENCE!! loved it so much!! they seem to be doing the same process for centuries.
That market is extraordinary to wander around. I recommend to do it alone and then maybe do it with a guide for better context.
I met a local guide nearby by accident, he gave me the tour then, he took me to the old slave market museum, then back to the market, where we went behind the scenes, sooo many hidden alley ways, I could see, where they butcher the chickens, where all market workers eat in what it seems to be communal kitchens, etc

content:
We heard about Zanzibar local (food and fish) market, now it was the time to see how it is, me and my friend, Colbet from South Africa decided to hv a look. We passed through narrow streets from stone town, and finally we reached to this place.
The Darajani market.
The Darajani Market is famous or known as Darajani Fish market or Darajani Food Market or even Darajani Local Market.
These are the names given by different people from different places according to their perspective and the way they categorize it as.
The Market is Open from around 07:30 Am to 10:30 pm and sometimes more depends on the customers.
The Darajani Market tour is one of things to do and you should never miss once you are in this Island, It became one of the most popular and most visited by tourist from around the world and local people, so its a tourist attraction.
Since it have More of the Variety of the Local food, and More Experience in Local trading and marketing experience, Small trade activities.
This is a cash only place, No Cards Services here.
This is One of the famous local food market in Zanzibar.
it''s a place where you can find and have almost everything you need in the food section, (Fresh and at a very low / reasonable price.)
The market is very famous due to its unique style, arrangement (Specified Portions) and Running style.
The market has Beef Butches section, Fresh fish Section, Spice section , Fresh Fruits and mixed / different variety Section. so if you fail to find what you are looking for, just go to mixed / different variety Section, there you will get what you want.
so the Sellers have arranged them self in that way to make more life easy to their customers and quest visiting the market. Though the market is very populated especial during the afternoon since different people from part of Zanzibar going there for shopping but still you will find path ways to move around the market.
So if you need some fresh fruits, Vegetables, Fish and meat, Spices and further more even to experience Zanzibarian local life style this is the right place to visit.
I like the way people are so humble, everyone has his or her own internal motivation, Not only youth but even, Women and Older people they all seat together as a community with the aim of one goal to sell as the best they can,
once you are at the market it''s a normal thing to see everyone is welcome you at his or her business. content:
Le marché en lui même vaut carrément le détour, il reste très typique et la zone viande et poisson est un vrai bon dans le temps.
Par contre attention aux arnaques pour les touristes les pris sont largement sur évalués. Je prends l''exemple d''un sachet de 250g de poivre noir. Dans les échoppes du marché, on m''en propose 25000 shillings. En négociant, je tombe a 15000. Puis en cherchant dans les ruelles a l''arrière, là où les locaux semblent plus aller se servir, le prix est de 8000. Je fais ici 2 ou 3 emplettes, mais le marchand n''a pas tout les épices que je souhaite. Il m''amène chez un fournisseur mieux achalandé et dans cette échoppes, le prix du même poivre est a 4000. Voilà un prix divisé par ... 6. J''ai donc fait le plein d''épices et reviens avec plus de 3 kilos.
C''est pareil pour les tissus, une fois au marché, traversez la grand rue et allez vous perdre dans les ruelles de l''autre côté. Vous avez ici les échoppes dans lesquelles les locaux font leurs courses. Les prix sont beaucoup plus bas et quasiment sans marge de négociation.
translated_content:
The market itself is definitely worth a visit; it remains very authentic, and the meat and fish section is a real step back in time.
However, beware of tourist scams; prices are significantly inflated. For example, a 250g bag of black pepper was quoted at 25,000 shillings in the market stalls. After some haggling, I got it down to 15,000. Then, looking in the back alleys, where locals seem to shop, the price was 8,000. I bought two or three things there, but the vendor didn't have all the spices I wanted. He took me to a better-stocked supplier, and in that stall, the same pepper was 4,000 shillings. That's a price divided by... six! So I stocked up on spices and came back with over 3 kilos.
It's the same with fabrics; once you're at the market, cross the main street and wander through the alleyways on the other side. Here you'll find the stalls where the locals do their shopping. The prices are much lower and there's practically no room for negotiation.

content: Giro di Stone Town e visita del mercato. La città, nelle parte storica è decadente. Il mercato è un classico mercato africano, con la parte di verdure e spezie (niente di che, le classiche bustine che si trovano ormai ovunque), e la classica parte di carne e pesce freschi, adatta, come ogni mercato del genere, ne ho visti molti, solo a persone con stomaco forte, visto l''odore. Alcuni vicoletti nei dintorni, con cucine a cielo aperto (bracieri con pentoloni), con tavolate locali. Niente di che.
translated_content: Tour of Stone Town and visit to the market. The historic part of the city is in a state of disrepair. The market is a classic African one, with a section selling vegetables and spices (nothing fancy, just the usual sachets you find everywhere these days), and the usual section selling fresh meat and fish. Like any market of this kind—I've seen many—it's only suitable for those with a strong stomach, given the smell. A few alleyways nearby have open-air kitchens (braziers with large pots) and locals sitting at tables. Nothing special.

translated_content: A cultural immersion filled with smells and colors. However, I don't understand the comments saying you can find everything there, because I found it was mostly spices (all the stalls look alike), a few shops selling toiletries, small supermarkets, butchers, and vegetable stalls. Opposite these are the fabric stalls. It's worth seeing, but I expected more choice since each stall is similar, and apart from the spices, there's nothing interesting for tourists to buy; it's more the place where locals do their shopping. But it's very exotic and culturally interesting!

content: Darajani Market is the perfect place to witness an authentic Zanzibari experience on the island.  The market is usually boisterous from morning until late in the night, and the stalls are crowded with buyers looking to purchase a variety of items on display. With scents of spices filling the air, the market is a hive of activity and features an array of items for purchase including fabrics, fresh fruits, meats, spices, live chicken, DVDs and mobile phones. The best time to visit Darajani Market is in the morning when the perishable goods are fresh. However, you can visit Darajani Market in the afternoon when it’s less chaotic. If you have never been to an African market, this is the place to try out your haggling skills. The market is called the Estella Market and Marikiti Kuu.

Local ground coffee is strong, and also of good quality.

content:
Quella di Bilal non è stata solo una classica escursione ad una piantagione di spezie, ma un vero viaggio in una comunità di Zanzibar che vive ancora per la quasi totalità in case tradizionali,  fatte di legno e fango. Abbiamo visto la piantagione e assaggiato tutte le spezie colte dall''albero, mangiato frutta appena raccolta insieme a Duly, simpaticissima ed esperta guida che sta imparando l''italiano. Abbiamo visitato il villaggio con Bilal che ci ha parlato della sua comunità, delle incontrando bambini sorridenti e festosi (portatevi un sacchetto di caramelle,  li farete tutti felici!). C''è anche la possibilità, se si vuole, di dare un piccolo contributo acquistando riso o altro nel piccolo emporio del villaggio. L''intera visita ci ha assorbito
per più di tre ore, spendendo circa 20 euro a testa, la metà se si vuole solo visitare la piantagione di spezie.
Grazie Bilal e Duly per questa impagabile esperienza!
translated_content:
Bilal's wasn't just a typical excursion to a spice plantation, but a true journey into a Zanzibar community that still lives almost entirely in traditional houses made of wood and mud. We visited the plantation and tasted all the spices picked from the trees, ate freshly picked fruit with Duly, a very friendly and expert guide who is learning Italian. We toured the village with Bilal, who told us about his community, meeting smiling and cheerful children (bring a bag of sweets; you'll make them all happy!). There's also the option, if you'd like, to make a small contribution by purchasing rice or other items at the village's small store. The entire visit took us
over three hours, spending about 20 euros each, half that if you just wanted to visit the spice plantation.
Thank you, Bilal and Duly, for this priceless experience!

content:
Visiting Bilal’s place for the spice and village tour was, without a doubt, one of the most meaningful, eye-opening, and unforgettable experiences I have ever had in Zanzibar.
As a European, being welcomed into the local community and having the opportunity to experience their culture, traditions, daily life, kindness, and incredible humility was something truly special. It gives you a completely different perspective and reminds you how much we can learn from people who live differently from us.
This is so much more than a tour. It is a genuine human experience, one that touches you deeply and stays with you long after you leave.
The village tour is an absolute MUST. Meeting the local people, seeing their everyday life, interacting with the children and families, and realizing how even a small donation can help provide food for the village makes the experience incredibly meaningful. What may feel like a small gesture to us can genuinely make a difference here.
You are not simply visiting Zanzibar. You are connecting with the real people who make this island so extraordinary.
I truly, truly recommend visiting Bilal and taking the time to discover this side of Zanzibar. And please, help spread the word. Tell your friends, recommend this experience to your hotel, and encourage other travelers to visit. The more people know about places like this, the more we can support local communities directly while experiencing something authentic and unforgettable in return.
Zanzibar is famous for its paradise beaches, but there is so much more behind them. If you come here, give yourself the chance to meet these wonderful people, listen to their stories, understand their way of life, and experience the true heart and soul of the island.
You may arrive thinking you are simply going on a spice and village tour, but you might leave with something much more valuable: a different perspective on life.
Please visit. Please support them. And most importantly, please speak about them.
Some experiences deserve more than five stars. ❤️
Highly, highly recommended.

What we loved: it was authentic and supports the local village directly.
Budget extra beyond the quoted price for water/rice contributions. It''s of course voluntary, but the whole village queues up for the rice after you commit to buying. I choose $20 and 20 eur (there were two shops). Bilal told us 20 euros is not enough for a bag of rice and I didn''t understand how much was enough (probably because I already felt stressed about people queuing up). To be honest it was the only dent in an otherwise authentic and good experience. Having this information upfront would make it much better.
Also, prepare to be assertive when being offered to buy soap or oils, but that applies all around.
The village tour made us feel a bit uncomfortable because we were walking into peoples houses. Bilal explained villagers are grateful for the benefits it brings, but I wonder how sustainable that is. I would probably opt in for going into one home and actually sitting down to get to know the family (even if only a little).
We had an elderly person with us, so didn''t go for the cooking class, but if we were to choose again I would probably go spice+cooking and pre agree for village contribution (eg. two bags of rice for $XX).

content:
Absolut empfehlenswert!
Wir haben die Spice Tour, die Tour durchs Dorf und den Kochkurs gemacht. Alle Beteiligten waren sehr freundlich, gut informiert und immer hilfreich.
Die Spice Tour bietet viele neue Eindrücke und Informationen über alltägliche Gewürze. Super interessant, die Pflanzen und rohen Früchte so zu sehen.
Die Tour durch das Dorf ist interessant. Freundliche Gastgeber in einem für die Gegend normalen Dorf. Die Lebensumstände sind nicht einfach. Man bekommt traditionelle und aktuelle Wohnverhältnisse sowie Bauweisen gezeigt. Anschließend kann man die Bewohner durch Einkäufe im örtlichen Shop unterstützen. Hier gibt es klassische Souvenirs oder auch Süßigkeiten und Haushaltsgegenstände. Letztere beiden sind zur Unterstützung des Dorfes bzw. am Wochenende für die Kinder.
Der Kochkurs findet im Anschluss statt. Hierfür lohnt es sich, mit leerem Magen zu kommen, es gibt sehr leckeres Essen! Die Köchin kocht auf 5–6 Kohlen gleichzeitig und lässt das auch noch einfach aussehen. Die Gewürze der Farm landen reichlich in allen Gerichten, von Fisch über Pilau bis hin zum Bananen-Nachtisch.
Alles in allem kann ich es nur jedem empfehlen!
P.S. für meine Almans: Die Tour wird auf Englisch durchgeführt
translated_content:
Highly recommended!
We did the Spice Tour, the Village Tour, and the Cooking Class. Everyone involved was very friendly, knowledgeable, and always helpful.
The Spice Tour offers many new impressions and insights into everyday spices. It's incredibly interesting to see the plants and raw fruits in person.
The Village Tour is fascinating. Friendly hosts in a typical village for the region. Living conditions aren't easy. You get to see traditional and modern housing and building styles. Afterward, you can support the residents by shopping at the local store. They sell classic souvenirs, sweets, and household items. The latter two support the village and are available for the children on weekends.
The Cooking Class follows. It's worth coming hungry for this, as the food is delicious! The cook cooks over five or six coals at once and makes it look effortless. The farm's spices are used liberally in all the dishes, from fish and pilau to banana dessert.
All in all, I highly recommend it!
You'll find classic souvenirs as well as sweets and household items. P.S. for my fellow Germans: The tour will be conducted in English.

content:
Eine unglaublich beeindruckende Tour durch ein Village und die Pflanzenwelt von Zanzibar. Bilal, der Gründer der Company leistet unglaubliches auf eine sehr freundliche Art. Die Führung durch das ursprüngliche Dorf war zutiefst beeindruckend und erdet ungemein. Die Einwohner leben sehr einfach und versuchen durch den Verkauf ihrer geflochtenen Dachabdeckungen, Gewürze und Früchte zu überleben. Sie bauen auch Reis an, allerdings zu wenig. Leider kommen sie damit nur mäßig aus, daher haben sie zwei kleine Shops wo Grundnahrungsmittel (Reis, Bohnen, Seife, Windeln und ein paar Süßigkeiten, nein, nichts von Ferrero) verkauft werden. Wer helfen will, kann sie kaufen und direkt spenden. Bilal macht sehr feinfühlig und ohne Druck darauf aufmerksam. Und wenn man dann die glücklichen Gesichter der Bewohner, insbesondere der Kinder mit ihren Lutschern sieht, weis man was 20€ vor Ort bewirken können. Ich hatte definitiv Tränen in den Augen. So freundliche und gut gelaunte Menschen, trotz der sehr einfachen Lebensumstände. Nach dem Besuch des Dorfes hat uns Ibrahim die Pflanzenwelt der Gewürze und deren Nutzung auf eine tolle Weise näher gebracht, und ich gehe mal davon aus, ohne jemals einen spitzfindigen Kommunikationskurs gemacht zu haben. Ich habe Fakten mitgenommen, die ich hier nicht verraten werde - brauche ich noch zum angeben😊. Die angebauten Früchte (Mangos, Melonen, Ananas und Kokosnuss, Guaven und BaoBao Zeit ist gerade nicht) durften wir dann selbstverständlich auch reichlich genießen.
Die Buchung zur Tour ist über die Seite völlig unkompliziert. Bilal antwortet über Whatsapp „in no time“. Er hat auch den Transport von Nungwi und zurück perfekt und zu einem sehr guten Preis organisiert. Es war alles perfekt - danke Bilal😍.
Es war ein unglaublicher Tag und ich bin super glücklich, dass ich über die Seite gestolpert bin, mich dafür entschieden habe, und nicht für eine „null acht fünfzehn Touristentour“
translated_content:
An incredibly impressive tour through a village and the flora of Zanzibar. Bilal, the company's founder, does amazing work in a very friendly way. The guided tour through the traditional village was deeply moving and incredibly grounding. The inhabitants live very simply and try to survive by selling their woven roofing materials, spices, and fruits. They also grow rice, but not enough. Unfortunately, it's not enough to get by, so they have two small shops selling basic foodstuffs (rice, beans, soap, diapers, and a few sweets—no, nothing from Ferrero). Anyone who wants to help can buy these items and donate them directly. Bilal raises awareness very sensitively and without pressure. And when you see the happy faces of the residents, especially the children with their lollipops, you know what €20 can do locally. I definitely had tears in my eyes. Such friendly and cheerful people, despite their very simple living conditions. After visiting the village, Ibrahim gave us a fantastic introduction to the world of spices and their uses, and I'm guessing he did it without ever having taken a sophisticated communication course. I learned some facts that I won't reveal here – I need them to show off! 😊 Of course, we also got to enjoy plenty of the local fruits (mangoes, melons, pineapples, coconuts, guavas, and bao bao, though they're not in season right now).
Booking the tour through the website is incredibly easy. Bilal responds to WhatsApp messages in no time. He also perfectly organized the transportation to and from Nungwi at a very good price. Everything was perfect – thank you, Bilal! 😍
It was an incredible day, and I'm so glad I stumbled across the website and chose this tour instead of a run-of-the-mill tourist trip.

content:
Я зашел в Peace Memorial Museum в Стоун Тауне без особых ожиданий. С улицы здание выглядит так, будто оно пережило не одно поколение.
Белая круглая ротонда, старые стены, тени от пальм. Его построили в начале двадцатого века, когда Занзибар еще был под британским протекторатом.
Архитектором был Джон Синклер, тот же, что проектировал Занзибарский дом чудес. В архитектуре намешано много всего: арабские линии, немного колониального стиля, местная штукатурка и ощущение жаркого восточного побережья.
Внутри музей простой, немного хаотичный, но в этом есть своя честность. Старые фотографии султанов, оружие, морские карты, документы о торговле, вещи из домов местных жителей.
Экспозиция местами выглядит уставшей, но предметы сами по себе сильные. История острова тяжелая, особенно если вспомнить, что Занзибар долгое время был крупным центром работорговли и морской торговли между Аравией, Индией и Восточной Африкой.
Я провел там около часа. Ходил медленно, читал таблички, слушал шаги в пустых залах. Ощущение, что попал в место, которое помнит больше, чем рассказывает. Как будто музей стоит на стыке эпох, где колониальный мир, арабская культура и африканская жизнь смешались и до сих пор не разошлись.
Если любишь историю и хочешь увидеть Занзибар не только со стороны пляжей, а через его корни, туда стоит зайти. Место тихое, немного потрепанное, но живое.
translated_content:
I walked into the Peace Memorial Museum in Stone Town without much expectation. From the street, the building looks as if it's been around for generations.
A white, round rotunda, old walls, shaded by palm trees. It was built in the early twentieth century, when Zanzibar was still a British protectorate.
The architect was John Sinclair, the same one who designed the Zanzibar House of Wonders. The architecture is a mixture of many elements: Arabic lines, a touch of colonial style, local plaster, and a feeling of the hot east coast.
Inside, the museum is simple, a bit chaotic, but there's a certain honesty to it. Old photographs of sultans, weapons, nautical charts, trade documents, and items from local homes are on display.
The exhibits look tired in places, but the objects themselves are powerful. The island's history is difficult, especially considering that Zanzibar was long a major center for the slave trade and maritime trade between Arabia, India, and East Africa.
I spent about an hour there. I walked slowly, reading the signs, listening to footsteps in the empty halls. I felt like I'd entered a place that remembers more than it tells. It's as if the museum stands at the junction of eras, where the colonial world, Arab culture, and African life have mingled and still remain connected.
If you love history and want to see Zanzibar not just from the beaches but through its roots, it's worth a visit. It's a quiet place, a little worn, but vibrant.

content:
Внутри живут воробьи и мошки! Мошки кусаются.
Здание изначально было построено как мемориал в память о занзибарцах - участниках Первой мировой войны. Об этом есть 3 таблички - снаружи и внутри. Никакого информационного стенда нет, сотрудница музея не знает, сколько жителей Занзибара участвовало, сколько погибло. Подробностей военных действий не разглашает, пришлось мне самой Википедию читать.
Экспозиция представляет искусства и ремесла Занзибара. Аннотации на английском и суахили. Витрины старые, нормальной подсветки нет. Музей выглядит очень неухоженным, заброшенным. Портрет первого президента стоит прямо на полу.
Стенд, посвященный Фредди Меркьюри - за гранью добра и зла.
Очень грустно, что музей в таком состоянии. В нем действительно есть интересные экспонаты. Надеюсь, финансирование увеличат, сделают ремонт и у музея наступят лучшие времена.
translated_content:
Sparrows and midges live inside! The midges bite.
The building was originally built as a memorial to Zanzibaris who fought in World War I. There are three plaques about this – one outside and one inside. There's no information board, and the museum staff doesn't know how many Zanzibaris fought or died. She doesn't disclose any details of the war, so I had to look it up on Wikipedia.
The exhibit showcases Zanzibari arts and crafts. The information is in English and Swahili. The display cases are old, and there's no proper lighting. The museum looks unkempt and neglected. A portrait of the first president sits right on the floor.
The Freddie Mercury display is beyond good and evil.
It's very sad that the museum is in such a state. It does have some interesting exhibits. I hope funding will be increased, renovations will be done, and better times will come for the museum.

content:
This is at the southern end of stone town, near the junction of creek road and kaunda road in the area called Mnazi Moja. It is also known by its local title: Beit El Amani (House of Peace). With its distinctive dome, arabesque windows and whitewashed walls, the building looks like a mosque or basilica church. It was designed by the British architect J H Sinclair, who also designed the high court, the British residency and several other public buildings around Zanzibar town.
''Museum'' is a misnomer nowadays, as virtually all its viewable exhibits have been shifted to the rapidly developing museum in the House of Wonders and the place now serves as a library. Its well-known giant tortoises have been transferred to Prison Island.

They force you to hire a guide "so you don't get lost," and of course, to pay them a tip. At first, they tried to trick us into paying the guide from the start.

Then they took us out of the national park in our own vehicle and drove us across the road to a public path where all the monkeys and a lagoon were. Basically, they make you pay to go to a public place where you can go by yourself in your car or on your motorbike. It's a disgrace. content:
Disappointing and Disturbing Experience at Jozani Forest
I visited Jozani Forest hoping to witness the rare and critically endangered red colobus monkeys in their natural habitat. Unfortunately, what I saw was far from respectful or responsible wildlife tourism.
Despite clear rules to keep a 3-meter distance from the monkeys, many tourists completely ignored them—getting far too close, even standing on or over the animals to get their photos. The monkeys appeared visibly stressed, and it was heartbreaking to watch.
Even more concerning was the behavior of the guides. Rather than ensuring the safety and well-being of the animals, they seemed more focused on collecting tips and pleasing the tourists. I saw no efforts made to correct or guide inappropriate behavior. It felt chaotic and disrespectful.
We left early, unable to continue watching such blatant disregard for the welfare of these beautiful, vulnerable animals. I hope real conservation efforts are implemented soon—before it''s too late for the red colobus monkeys.

content:
Cette excursion ne vaut pas le détour !
L’entrée du parc est facturée 12 USD par personne avec guide inclus (sans compter les pourboires à laisser au guide, qui n’a pas manqué de nous le rappeler à plusieurs reprises lors de la visite).
Nous sommes tombés sur un guide qui s''est limité à nous faire un tour de deux fois 15 minutes, sans nous donner d’explication sur la forêt, les singes ou même la mangrove.
Le premier etait soit disant consacré à la découverte de la forêt de Jozani, mais nous sommes restés une bonne vingtaine de minutes sous un arbre en bord de route a observer des singes (très jolis au demeurant) pendant que le guide hurlait dans son téléphone. Puis nous sommes entrés dans la forêt, où nous avons marché 200 mètres puis retour au point de départ …
Le deuxième consistait à la visite de la mangrove située a 1.5 kilomètres de la foret où nous avons marché 200 mètres sur une passerelle en bois construite dans la mangrove puis retour à la case départ.
Attention si vous n’avez pas de voiture,  ôtez guide nous a conduit mais voulait nous faire payer le trajet !!!
Un petit conseil, passez votre chemin !
translated_content:
This excursion is not worth it!
The park entrance fee is $12 USD per person, including a guide (not including tips, which the guide reminded us of several times during the visit).
We ended up with a guide who only gave us two 15-minute tours, without providing any explanation about the forest, the monkeys, or even the mangroves.
The first tour was supposedly about exploring the Jozani Forest, but we spent a good 20 minutes under a tree by the roadside watching monkeys (very cute, by the way) while the guide shouted into his phone. Then we entered the forest, walked 200 meters, and then returned to the starting point…
The second tour was a visit to the mangroves located 1.5 kilometers from the forest, where we walked 200 meters on a wooden boardwalk built in the mangroves before returning to the starting point. Beware if you don't have a car! The guide drove us but wanted to charge us for the ride!
A word of advice: avoid this place!

-Prices are good. 40cents to 80cents depending on the ride.
-They offer a waterpark, not as huge but I think it is $2 or so. I would def recommend you go there as early as possible in a day and get out as soon as it starts getting crowded unless it is not a public holidays.
-On special days here in Zanzibar, don''t even think of visiting this place, children might get lost, the queues are gonna be too long so u might as well visit just on a random normal weekend day.
-Id think they operate on work days.
-For me as a Zanzibari, i qould dwf recommend the Mtoni Marine Waterpark next to Hotel Verde more. And ride-wise, i would recommend the Legends in Kisakasaka, ofc not special days. content:
The House of Wonders or Palace of Wonders (Arabic: Beit-al-Ajaib, بيت العجايب) is an iconic building in Stone Town, Zanzibar, Tanzania.
It is the largest and tallest building in Stone Town, located between the Old Fort and the former Sultan's Palace.
It is one of six palaces built by Barghash bin Said, the second Sultan of Zanzibar, and is said to stand on the site of the palace of Queen Fatuma, who lived in the 17th century.
The House of Wonders currently houses the Museum of History and Culture of Zanzibar and the Swahili Coast.
The palace was built in 1883 for Barghash bin Said, the second Sultan of Zanzibar.
It was conceived as a ceremonial palace and official reception hall, celebrating modernity. That's why it was named "House of Wonders," because it was the first building in Zanzibar with electricity, and also the first building in East Africa to have an elevator.
In front of the building, there once stood a lighthouse that was destroyed during the Anglo-Zanzibarian War of August 27, 1896. This brief war also destroyed the Beit al-Hukum Palace and severely damaged the Beit al-Sahel Palace.
The House of Wonders suffered only minor damage. During reconstruction in 1897, a new clock tower was integrated into the building's facade. Beit al-Hukum was not rebuilt, and its site was transformed into a garden.
Mteppe inside the House of Wonders
The House of Wonders was only fully occupied by the Sultan and his harem after the bombardment.
In 1911, it was converted into government offices and served as the main secretariat for the British government authorities.
After the 1964 Zanzibar Revolution, it was converted into a school and museum for the Afro-Shirazi party with North Korean support. Development of the museum began between 1992 and 1994. Today, it serves as a museum and is one of Stone Town's main tourist attractions.
The House of Wonders Museum, opened in the early 2000s, features permanent exhibits on aspects of Swahili and Zanzibar culture, as well as the East African environment.
The inner courtyard is entirely occupied by a mtepe (a traditional Swahili boat).
Around this courtyard, which unfolds over three floors, are several rooms with other exhibits on a variety of topics, including Swahili fishing tools and traditional boats, ceremonial kangas, portraits of sultans and other notable people (including a famous portrait of the notorious slave trader Tippu Tip), furniture from the sultans' palaces, and information on the biomes of East Africa.
One of the rooms on the ground floor houses an old car that belonged to President Abeid Karume.[4]
At the entrance to the palace are two old Portuguese bronze cannons from the 16th century.
They were captured by the Persians in 1622 and later given to the sultans of Oman, who brought them to Zanzibar.
The larger cannon bears the emblem of King John III of Portugal. The House of Wonders is now closed due to its poor condition.
The museum has been relocated.

*House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib)*
History
- Built in 1883 by Sultan Bargash bin Said
- Served as a palace and a repository for Zanzibar''s treasures
- Damaged by British warship HMS Philomel in 1896
- Restored in 2010-2012
Attractions for Tourists
1. *Exhibition halls*: Showcasing Zanzibar''s history, culture, and natural environment
2. *Historic artifacts*: Including furniture, jewelry, and other relics from the palace
3. *Zanzibar''s oldest elevator*: Built in 1883, it''s one of the oldest in Africa
4. *Panoramic views*: Of Stone Town and the harbor from the top floor
Food and Beverages
1. *Traditional Zanzibari cuisine*: Including dishes like urojo (a spicy soup), mandazi (fried doughnuts), and chapati (flatbread)
2. *Seafood*: Fresh catches from the Indian Ocean, often served grilled or in curries
3. *Local fruits*: Like mangoes, coconuts, and pineapples
4. *Coffee and tea*: Served in traditional cafes and restaurants
Tips for Visitors
1. *Dress modestly*: Respect local customs and traditions
2. *Remove shoes*: When entering the palace or mosques
3. *Respect local rules*: No photography in certain areas, and no touching of artifacts
4. *Haggle politely*: When shopping in local markets
The House of Wonders is a must-visit attraction in Stone Town, Zanzibar. Its rich history, cultural significance, and stunning architecture make it an unforgettable experience.

Es war mal das größte und beeindruckendste Haus in Stone Town. Heute leider geschlossen ( November 2022), da Einsturzgefahr.
1883 erbaute ein britischer Marineoffizier im Auftrag des Sultans Bargash das Haus. Es war das erste Haus, vielleicht sogar in Afrika das über technische Errungenschaften der westlichen Welt verfügte. Elektrisches Licht, fließendes Wasser, Toilette mit Spülung und einen Fahrstuhl. So sein Name Haus of Wonders. Das Haus vereint arabische und viktorianische Baustile. Ob es wieder öffnet und wann können wir nicht sagen. Aber Bauaktivitäten waren nicht wahrzunehmen. 🤔
translated_content:
It was once the largest and most impressive house in Stone Town. Unfortunately, it's now closed (November 2022) due to the risk of collapse.
In 1883, a British naval officer built the house on behalf of Sultan Bargash. It was the first house, perhaps even in Africa, to feature Western technology: electric light, running water, a flushing toilet, and an elevator. Hence its name, the House of Wonders. The house combines Arabic and Victorian architectural styles. We don't know if or when it will reopen, but no construction activity was visible. 🤔

content: Wonderful landmark building in Stone Town, Zanzibar. Largest tallest building in Stone Town,  facing the Forodhani Gardens on the old town''s seafront, in Mizingani Road. First building to have electricity in Zanzibar and an elevator in East Africa. Light house which stood in front the building got destroyed in the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 causing minor damage to Beit Al Ajaib. Renovation in1897 brought in Clock Tower into the façade of the building. It was a government office, a school and later a museum. After renovation it will shine fully with bygone glory. It is and will be one of Stone Town''s major tourist attractions. Good luck.

content:
|The House of Wonders was once the most modern building in East Africa—it was the first building to have electricity and an elevator—and it mixes elements of European style and Zanzibari tradition by including cast iron columns, elaborate door carvings, coral rag, open central courtyards, and mangrove ceilings that together form a truly unique architectural achievement. Just next to it is the Palace Museum, built by the second sultan of Zanzibar in 1883, which is an opulent palace comprised of beautiful marble flooring, coral stone walls, and silver decorations. The palace was built in the Omani style as an extravagant Arab mansion, and holds many relics that offer a rare glimpse of a past era. The House of Wonders and Palace Museum have been converted into popular cultural destinations; the House of Wonders presents exhibitions dedicated to Swahili culture and the Palace Museum highlights its ties to Zanzibar''s Omani history. |

content:
Nungwi Beach es realmente preciosa. La arena blanca, el color del agua y el paisaje son espectaculares.
Lamentablemente, nuestra experiencia se vio bastante afectada por la cantidad de vendedores y personas ofreciendo servicios constantemente.
Mientras caminas por la playa te abordan una y otra vez para ofrecerte excursiones, souvenirs, masajes y todo tipo de servicios. No tendría ningún problema con que alguien se acercara una vez a ofrecer algo; entiendo perfectamente que están intentando ganarse la vida. El problema es la frecuencia y, sobre todo, la insistencia.
Muchas veces decir educadamente “no, gracias” no es suficiente.
Algunos continúan caminando a tu lado, haciendo preguntas o intentando mantener una conversación después de que ya has dejado claro que no estás interesado. Cuando esto ocurre cada pocos minutos, algo tan sencillo como caminar tranquilamente por la playa termina siendo agotador en lugar de relajante.
Mi pareja también se sintió especialmente incómoda por la cantidad de atención que recibía, lo que hizo que pudiéramos disfrutar todavía menos de la playa.
Ojalá en el futuro puedan gestionar mejor esta situación para que los visitantes puedan disfrutar de un lugar tan espectacular sin sentirse constantemente abordados.
translated_content:
Nungwi Beach is truly beautiful. The white sand, the color of the water, and the scenery are spectacular.
Unfortunately, our experience was significantly marred by the sheer number of vendors and people constantly offering services.
While walking along the beach, you're approached repeatedly with offers of excursions, souvenirs, massages, and all sorts of other services. I wouldn't mind someone approaching you once to offer something; I completely understand they're trying to make a living. The problem is the frequency and, above all, the persistence. Often, politely saying "no, thank you" isn't enough.
Some people continue walking beside you, asking questions or trying to maintain a conversation even after you've made it clear you're not interested. When this happens every few minutes, something as simple as a peaceful walk on the beach becomes exhausting instead of relaxing.
My partner also felt particularly uncomfortable with the amount of attention she received, which made it even harder for us to enjoy the beach.
Hopefully, in the future they can manage this situation better so that visitors can enjoy such a spectacular place without feeling constantly harassed.

content: Zanzibar''s beaches boast dazzling white sand and turquoise waters. Choosing the perfect beach depends on your preferences, so here are a few tips: For year-round swimming (no tides): Nungwi and Kendwa, located in the north of the island. These areas allow you to swim all day and offer magnificent sunsets. For kitesurfing and a local atmosphere: Paje, on the east coast, is a world-renowned spot for watersports enthusiasts, lined with lively cafes. For tranquility and authenticity: Jambiani and Matemwe offer wild and unspoiled stretches of coastline, ideal for long walks and snorkeling. You can explore these different locations and organize excursions through specialized platforms or simply ask the locals; they are very kind and help tourists with a big heart and without any sarcasm.

We spent the day at Nungwi beach (northern part of the island) to jet ski and take a sunset cruise. It is a very busy and touristy part of the island (we stayed on the south east coast). The water is absolutely amazing and good vibes all round but the roads and parts of the beach are very busy.
Sunset Cruise on a Dhow: the entire experience lasted from about 4pm to 7pm. There is music on board, traditional songs and instruments. They also served fresh tropical fruit and drinks (drinks cost extra). At one point they stopped and allowed to jump off into the water, which my husband enjoyed! All in all a lovely experience!
Jet skis: we took a shorter ride option and it was safe and lots of fun! We negotiated the price down.
Be prepared with umbrella/chairs, else you pay to have shade and a lounger.
You will be approached by lots of locals trying to sell their services for jet skis and cruises, be prepared.  We had our own guide with us so it was easy enough to avoid long talks etc. Understand that this is their way of earning a living, and they must make the most of the busy season as the island basically shuts down in the rainy months.

content:
Nungwi je přesně ten typ pláže, kde si člověk uvědomí, proč se létá tisíce kilometrů za „obyčejným“ pískem a mořem. Jemný bílý písek, tyrkysová voda a palmy jak z katalogu, ale bez sterilního pocitu umělého ráje. Tady to žije.
Velké plus: minimální odliv. Na rozdíl od jiných částí Zanzibaru se dá koupat prakticky celý den, což zní banálně, dokud to nezažiješ jinde. Moře je klidné, teplé a ideální jak na plavání, tak na jen takové to „stát ve vodě a koukat do prázdna“.
Atmosféra je mix místního života a pohodového turismu. Rybářské lodě, Masajové, beach boys, restaurace přímo na písku, západy slunce, které si fakt nezaslouží filtr. Nungwi není tiché útočiště pro poustevníky – je to živá pláž, ale ne otravná.
Jídlo? Čerstvé ryby, krevety, chobotnice, jednoduché beach bary i lepší restaurace. Ceny jsou férové, když víš, kdy se usmát a kdy slušně říct ne.
Minusy? Více lidí, hlavně v sezóně, a občas až příliš aktivní prodejci. Ale upřímně – to je daň za místo, které funguje.
Verdikt:
Nungwi Beach je jedna z nejlepších pláží na Zanzibaru. Nejen hezká na fotky, ale skutečně skvělá na pobyt. Pokud chceš pláž, kde se dá žít, koupat, jíst, pít a večer koukat na západ slunce bez přemýšlení o čase – Nungwi je správná volba.
translated_content:
Nungwi is exactly the type of beach where you realize why you travel thousands of kilometers for “ordinary” sand and sea. Fine white sand, turquoise water and palm trees like from a catalog, but without the sterile feeling of an artificial paradise. This is where it lives.
A big plus: minimal low tide. Unlike other parts of Zanzibar, you can swim practically all day, which sounds banal until you experience it elsewhere. The sea is calm, warm and ideal for swimming or just “standing in the water and staring into space”.
The atmosphere is a mix of local life and relaxed tourism. Fishing boats, Masai, beach boys, restaurants right on the sand, sunsets that really don’t deserve a filter. Nungwi is not a quiet haven for hermits – it’s a lively beach, but not annoying.
Food? Fresh fish, shrimp, octopus, simple beach bars and better restaurants. Prices are fair, if you know when to smile and when to say no politely.
Cons? More people, especially in high season, and sometimes overly active vendors. But honestly – that’s the price of a place that works.
Verdict:
Nungwi Beach is one of the best beaches in Zanzibar. Not only pretty for photos, but really great to stay. If you want a beach where you can live, swim, eat, drink and watch the sunset in the evening without thinking about the time – Nungwi is the right choice.

I also spotted three sea snakes with striking black-and-white bands, beautiful but venomous, so awareness is essential. As well as the cone snails to make sure you are aware of those and to avoid them. Lionfish, a lone jellyfish, and an abundance of sea urchins make appearances too, so reef shoes and a snorkelling mask are highly recommended.
That said, relaxing on the beach can be a challenge. You are frequently approached by vendors selling everything imaginable. While it’s easy to understand the economic reality behind this, the constant interruptions can be exhausting. The people are however quite respectful of a no thank you. The people on the beach too offering dolphin yoirs is something to research, they are often not licensed, uneducated about marine conservation and often do more harm to the natural life and harass the dolphins. I would recommend doing dolphin tours through the aquariums who actually add to marine conservation and do good.
All of this aside, the beach truly is beautiful. I would recommend staying somewhere with security or choosing a quieter, less crowded stretch of sand usualy at the end of the beach, and keeping your wits about you at all times. With the right precautions, it’s a place well worth experiencing

Nasz przewodnik zabrał nas do Nungwi, bo jest to tradycyjna wioska rybacka, a nie tylko piękna plaża. To miejsce zrobiło na nas ogromne wrażenie. translated_content:
Our guide took us to Nungwi, a traditional fishing village, not just a beautiful beach. This place made a huge impression on us. We saw carpenters hand-building a mahogany boat – an incredible process, without machinery, just craftsmanship and the strength of their hands. We also walked along the local houses. We could see women and children sitting at the entrances; there were so many children… The houses are very dark, and their condition reflects the early days of settlement.
We also visited the fish market, where fresh fish were being processed straight from the catch. We even stumbled upon an auction, vibrant, loud, and authentic, as if from another world.
The beach around the village is gorgeous! The white sand and the views are breathtaking. The contrast between the beauty of nature and the harsh everyday life of a fishing village is thought-provoking. It's a place that makes you stop for a moment and appreciate what WE have... 🥹
An incredible, valuable experience... not just for tourism, but for life.

content: Пляж Nungwi расположен на берегу одноимённой деревни, на севере острова Унгуджу. Этот остров самый крупный в агломерации Занзибар, и поэтому его часто называют собственно Занзибар. Деревня Нунгви одна из самых густонаселённых на острове , не считая ,конечно,  столицы. Это прежде всего рыбацкая деревня соответствующими атрибутами. Индийский океан на этом пляже тёплый и чистый, в основном неглубокий в прибрежной зоне. Так как эта рыбацкая гавань то здесь можно увидеть сотни парусных рыбацких традиционных лодок в океане. Здесь очень много морских звёзд которые просматриваются при прогулке на мелководье в момент отлива. При этом почти нет ежей. Ежи в большом количестве присутствуют ближе к маяку. Отливы здесь максимально 500 м, что совсем немного. Поэтому отлив здесь - это как развлечение, чтобы пройти по дну океана за уходящей водой. Ширина песчаной линии до 50 м даже в полной прилив. Пляж гораздо шире в части, которая ближе к деревне Кендва. Однако, и в Нунгви пляж широкий достаточно. Даже для игры в футбол. Песок белый и мелкий,  как мука. translated_content: Nungwi Beach is located on the shores of the village of the same name, in the north of Unguja Island. This island is the largest in the Zanzibar metropolitan area, and therefore is often referred to as "Zanzibar." Nungwi is one of the most densely populated villages on the island, not counting the capital, of course. It is primarily a fishing village, with its corresponding attributes. The Indian Ocean at this beach is warm and clear, mostly shallow in the coastal zone. As this is a fishing harbor, hundreds of traditional sailing fishing boats can be seen in the ocean. There are numerous starfish here, visible when walking in the shallow water at low tide. Sea urchins are almost absent, though they are abundant closer to the lighthouse. Low tides here reach a maximum of 500 meters, which is quite a bit. Therefore, low tide here is a fun way to walk along the ocean floor behind the receding water. The sand line is up to 50 meters wide, even at high tide. The beach is much wider in the section closer to the village of Kendwa. However, in Nungwi, the beach is also wide enough, even for playing soccer. The sand is white and fine as flour. The beach is very well-developed in terms of infrastructure. There are numerous restaurants, decent shops, souvenir stalls, and wonderful locals, who are a unique experience.

content: Du kommst an – und plötzlich hält die Zeit den Atem an. Der Sand liegt vor dir wie gesiebter Puderzucker, grellweiß, weich wie Schlaf, durchwirkt von winzigen hellblauen Steinen, die aussehen wie geschliffene Tropfen des Himmels. Es heißt, sie gäbe es nur hier – Noni-Steine, halb Mythos, halb Erinnerung. Das Meer? Weiß. Klar. Makellos. So rein, dass es wie Selterswasser wirken würde – wenn es nicht so salzig wär. 26 bis 28 Grad warm, flüssiges Licht auf der Haut. Kein Wasser. Eine Verlockung. Zwischen Wellen leuchten rote und blaue Seesterne, so klar, als hätte jemand vergessen, sie auszuschalten. Die Sonne? Keine. Ein Brennglas. Wer ohne Sonnencreme oder Schatten einfach fünfzehn Minuten am Strand entlangläuft – obwohl nur 30 °C auf dem Thermometer stehen – verbrennt sich die Haut wie in einer Mikrowelle. Dritte Stufe. Gratis. Die Ozonschicht scheint hier nur noch als Erinnerung zu existieren. Schatten gibt es nur unter den Palmen, und selbst die schauen streng. Sonnencreme? SPF 50 ist der höfliche Anfang. Wer sie vergisst, wird Teil der Geologie – rot wie Korallen, still wie Felsen. Und doch: Man bleibt. Weil dieser Strand – Nungwi, ganz im Norden Sansibars – nicht nur blendet, sondern verwandelt. Es gibt Gästehäuser, die wirken wie verlorene Gedichte, zwei Läden mit allem und nichts, und den besten Fisch servieren sie dir barfuß, direkt am Grill, während das Meer sich nicht zurückzieht. Ebbe gibt es auch hier – aber sie kommt leise. Kein großes Zurückweichen, nur ein Flüstern, ein kurzes Aufdecken der Unterwelt, bevor das Meer wieder Besitz ergreift. Wie ein Atemzug, nicht wie ein Rückzug. Und dann: ein Thunfisch, gelb-blau wie gemalt, von Fischern eingefangen, später auf dem Grill direkt am Strand serviert. Rauch mischt sich mit Salzluft und der Musik einer Gitarre, die niemand wirklich spielt – sie erklingt durch das Wispern des Windes heraus, im Rauschen der Palmen, die sich in den Winden wiegen. Und sie hören zu. So wie du. Der Ort spricht nicht. Er antwortet. Wer sich von hier aus nach Stone Town aufmacht – etwa zwei Stunden südlich – sollte zwischen 40 und 70 Euro für das Taxi einplanen, je nach Verhandlungsgeschick auch 80. Ich selbst habe vom Flughafen bis zum Hilton in Nungwi 70 gezahlt – fair verhandelt. Und es lohnt sich. In Stone Town duftet es aus engen Gassen nach Rosmarin und Fenchel – eine kleine italienische Pizzeria, geführt von einer Frau aus den Abruzzen, backt dort Pizza wie bei Mamma. Sie lässt sich das Mehl direkt aus Italien liefern, sagt man – und man glaubt es, wenn man in den heißen Straßen plötzlich meint, Neapel zu riechen. Wer den Film gesehen hat, wird auch den Besuch in Freddie Mercurys Geburtshaus lieben – ein kleines Museum, eine Führung, ein paar Minuten, in denen man glaubt, einen Schritt näher an ihn heranzurücken. Und dann ist da noch die Schildkröteninsel – mit einem kleinen Boot erreichbar. Einige der ältesten Tiere der Welt, sagen sie. Hundert Jahre, manche älter. Und kräftig – so kräftig, dass man glaubt, sie könnten einen tragen. Man darf sie füttern, man darf sie streicheln – es ist wie ein Altersheim auf der anderen Seite des Wassers, in dem Zeit langsamer läuft. Und wer genau hinschaut: Die alten Türen in Stone Town – gewaltig, mit Eisen beschlagen – wurden gebaut, um Elefanten draußen zu halten. Früher gingen sie hier durch die Gassen. Heute nur noch Geschichten. Und irgendwo zwischen den Schatten dieser Häuser sitzen Männer, die aus Leder Schuhe machen, gemessen am Fuß, genäht mit der Hand. Ein anderes Tempo, eine andere Welt. Und dann bist du zurück. Dort, wo der Himmel das Meer berührt, der Horizont die Delfine mit Farben verführt, kommt’s Bewusstsein heran wie ein Schlag ins Gesicht – man erkennt sich selbst… und vergisst sein Gedicht. Der Thunfisch wird dort nicht einfach gebraten, nein – erst charmant von den Wellen beraten, er springt auf den Grill mit ’nem Hauch Zitrone – das war ein Mahl. 14.-28. Januar
translated_content: You arrive – and suddenly time stands still. The sand lies before you like sifted powdered sugar, dazzling white, soft as sleep, interspersed with tiny, pale blue stones that look like polished drops of the sky. They say they only exist here – noni stones, half myth, half memory. The sea? White. Clear. Immaculate. So pure it would seem like sparkling water – if it weren't so salty. 26 to 28 degrees Celsius, liquid light on your skin. No water. A temptation. Red and blue starfish glow between the waves, so clear it's as if someone forgot to turn them off. The sun? Non-existent. A magnifying glass. Anyone who walks along the beach for fifteen minutes without sunscreen or shade – even though the thermometer only reads 30°C – will burn their skin like in a microwave. Level three. Free. The ozone layer seems to exist here only as a memory. Shade is only found under the palm trees, and even they look stern. Sunscreen? SPF 50 is the polite start. Forgetting it makes you part of the geology – red like coral, silent like rocks. And yet: you stay. Because this beach – Nungwi, in the far north of Zanzibar – doesn't just dazzle, it transforms. There are guesthouses that seem like lost poems, two shops with everything and nothing, and they serve you the best fish barefoot, right at the grill, while the sea doesn't recede. There's low tide here too – but it comes quietly. No great retreat, just a whisper, a brief unveiling of the underworld before the sea reclaims it. Like a breath, not a withdrawal. And then: a tuna, yellow and blue like a painting, caught by fishermen, later served on the grill right on the beach. Smoke mingles with the salt air and the music of a guitar that no one is really playing – it emerges through the whisper of the wind, in the rustling of the palm trees swaying in the breeze. And they listen. Just like you. The place doesn't speak. It answers. Anyone heading south from here to Stone Town – about two hours – should budget between 40 and 70 euros for a taxi, or even 80 depending on their bargaining skills. I myself paid 70 euros from the airport to the Hilton in Nungwi – a fair deal. And it's worth it. In Stone Town, the narrow streets are fragrant with rosemary and fennel – a small Italian pizzeria, run by a woman from Abruzzo, bakes pizzas just like Mamma used to. They say she has the flour delivered directly from Italy – and you believe it when, in the hot streets, you suddenly think you can smell Naples. Anyone who's seen the film will also love visiting Freddie Mercury's birthplace – a small museum, a guided tour, a few minutes in which you feel like you're taking a step closer to him. And then there's Turtle Island – accessible by small boat. Some of the oldest animals in the world, they say. A hundred years old, some even older. And strong – so strong you'd think they could carry you. You can feed them, you can pet them – it's like a retirement home on the other side of the water, where time moves more slowly. And if you look closely: the old doors in Stone Town – massive, clad in iron – were built to keep elephants out. They used to roam these alleys. Now they're just stories. And somewhere among the shadows of these houses sit men making leather shoes, measured by foot, sewn by hand. A different pace, a different world. And then you're back. There, where the sky touches the sea, where the horizon seduces the dolphins with colors, consciousness hits you like a slap in the face – you recognize yourself… and forget your poem. The tuna isn't simply fried there, no – first charmingly advised by the waves, it leaps onto the grill with a hint of lemon – that was a meal. January 14-28

content:
Decepcionado es la palabra. Mi visita a Zanzíbar ha sido una profunda decepción, muy lejos de la idílica imagen que se suele proyectar. La experiencia ha estado marcada por una serie de puntos negativos que me han dejado con una constante sensación de frustración y, en ocasiones, de estafa.
En primer lugar, los costes iniciales son sorprendentemente altos. No solo el transporte para llegar a la isla resulta caro, sino que se exige el pago de un seguro de entrada a la isla, a pesar de ya contar con un seguro de viaje contratado desde mi país de origen. Esta duplicidad de gastos es, cuanto menos, injustificable y te hace sentir que te están sacando dinero desde el primer momento.
La higiene es otro de los puntos más críticos y desoladores. La isla está sumamente sucia, con una omnipresencia de plásticos y basura por doquier. Las playas, que deberían ser el principal atractivo, están lamentablemente contaminadas, afeando el paisaje y haciendo que la experiencia de disfrutarlas sea desagradable. Es realmente impactante ver tal nivel de descuido ambiental en un lugar que vive del turismo.
Además, la sensación de ser constantemente estafado es palpable. Los precios para los turistas son descaradamente más altos que para los locales, lo que te hace sentir explotado en cada transacción, desde la compra de un simple souvenir hasta el regateo por un servicio o coger el autobus. Para ir de Stone Town a Nungwi a la ida me cobran 10000tzh cuando a los nativos les cuesta 2500 y a la vuelta me cobran 5000. Un sin sentido. Si bien la comida en los restaurantes puede ser asequible, comer en la calle es una lotería y, con frecuencia, se traduce tambien en un engaño económico.
Lo único rescatable de mi estancia ha sido la amabilidad de sus gentes. Sin embargo, incluso esta cualidad se ve empañada por su constante insistencia en venderte algo, lo que, aunque comprensible en un contexto turístico, puede llegar a ser agotador. Comparado con mi experiencia en la parte continental de Tanzania, donde me sentí mucho más cómodo y a gusto, Zanzíbar no me ha transmitido esa sensación de hogar ni de autenticidad. Definitivamente, me siento defraudado y yo por lo menos no volveré.
translated_content:
Disappointed is the word. My visit to Zanzibar has been a profound disappointment, far removed from the idyllic image it usually projects. The experience has been marked by a series of negative points that have left me with a constant feeling of frustration and, at times, of being ripped off.
First of all, the initial costs are surprisingly high. Not only is transportation to the island expensive, but they also require payment for entry insurance, despite already having travel insurance purchased in my home country. This duplication of expenses is, to say the least, unjustifiable and makes you feel like you're being taken advantage of from the very beginning.
Hygiene is another of the most critical and disheartening aspects. The island is extremely dirty, with plastic and trash everywhere. The beaches, which should be the main attraction, are sadly polluted, marring the landscape and making the experience of enjoying them unpleasant. It's truly shocking to see such a level of environmental neglect in a place that depends on tourism.
Furthermore, the feeling of being constantly ripped off is palpable. Prices for tourists are blatantly higher than for locals, making you feel exploited in every transaction, from buying a simple souvenir to haggling over a service or taking the bus. To get from Stone Town to Nungwi, I was charged 10,000 tzh one way, while it costs locals 2,500, and then 5,000 tzh the return trip. It makes no sense. While food in restaurants can be affordable, eating on the street is a gamble and often results in being financially ripped off.
The only redeeming quality of my stay was the friendliness of the people. However, even this is overshadowed by their constant push to sell you something, which, while understandable in a tourist context, can become exhausting. Compared to my experience on the Tanzanian mainland, where I felt much more comfortable and at ease, Zanzibar didn't give me that sense of home or authenticity. I definitely feel let down and I, for one, will not be returning.

content:
Zanzibar is actually really disappointing for me, online you see a paradise with beautiful beaches, people snorkelling and swimming with turtles but in reality it’s not at all glamorous, there is rubbish all over the ground everywhere you go, people are living in super run down houses right next to massive fancy hotels, low tide is during the middle of the day so all of the beaches you want to swim at are just sand and reef until high tide at night time and it’s EXPENSIVE. There are much nicer places with lovely beaches that you can travel to for much cheaper and are easier to get around! (Thailand and the Philippines especially)
As a young person travelling Africa with a currency that’s not USD, Euro or Pound (we’re travelling on the Australian dollar -Aud) it’s been pretty reasonable with the conversion but in Zanzibar specifically it’s been crazy expensive, they try to charge everything in USD so trying to hire a moped or scooter for three days they wanted not only $60 USD for the hire ($97 Aud) but also $15 USD ($25 Aud) for a “government driving permit” even when we both have an international license or an IDP (international driving permit) that’s the second “government” fee we’ve come across because you now have to get mandatory Zanzibar insurance when entering at the airport which was $45 USD ($73 Aud) aswell as the Visa I needed for entrance to Tanzania which was $50 USD ($80 Aud) what is the government doing with all this money they’re extorting from tourists if it’s not to try clean up atleast some of the rubbish that’s everywhere, making nice roads or helping with peoples housing.
All of the restaurant menus are in USD and obviously not what the local price is because what local is paying $7 USD ($12 Aud) for a stew, no one. It’s just frustrating because they do obviously make their livings off of tourists (especially the middle age demographic of Americans) which is what you would expect from a popular destination like this but it’s pushing the price of everything up for everyone else. It’s disappointing as someone who loves to travel because of course things cost money but this has got to a point of actually just being ridiculous.
We’re staying where we heard most people stay in Jambiani which was an hour from the airport (it cost us 90,000 TZS/ $35 USD which is $56 Aud) because they only do taxi there’s no ride share app in Zanzibar so trying to get to and from the airport is crazy expensive.
So because we’re staying in Jambiani if we wanted to go and do a snorkelling tour, the turtle sanctuary cave or anything like that it’s all up on the top of the island (roughly a 2 hour drive) in Matemwe which would already be hard on a rented scooter but because the scooter hire is expensive we’d have to try get either a tuk tuk, taxi or on the back of a motorbike all the way there and back for the day it would be not only hard to find someone who would do it but also costly as well, so if you’re planning on doing those things while in Zanzibar (snorkelling tour, swimming with dolphins, turtle sanctuary cave, anything like that) it’s most likely up near Matemwe so definitely spend the extra money on accommodation up there to save the hassle of trying to get there.
Zanzibar is a tourist scam. End of story.

content:
A great large beach at the northernmost tip of Zanzibar.
There’s plenty of space to walk along the shore or swim along the coast. White sand, calm warm water. The tides can be quite noticeable, especially in the area where women collect seaweed. But that’s part of the charm — watching them work and walking through the shallow water yourself.
You can swim, snorkel, ride horses, get a massage, or buy souvenirs, which are offered in abundance here. Nungwi has many restaurants, so you won’t go hungry. The best beachfront restaurants in Zanzibar are found here. You can enjoy a wide variety of cuisines, including a rarity for Tanzania — delicious desserts.
The vendors and dressed-up Maasai can be a bit annoying, but it’s the most touristy place apart from Stone Town. The beach is suitable for families, couples, groups, and solo travelers. The weather is always nice, and the water of the Indian Ocean is warm.

aber so etwas habe ich noch NIE gesehen.
Es gibt so viele schöne Strände auf der Welt
wie in Indonesien, Mexiko, Australien, Malediven ....
Das Sansibar ist nicht, dass das Ihr in Instagram kennt
Ich kann euch nur warnen, geht lieber wo anders hin.

translated_content:
Pushy and disrespectful people (Marsais)
Unfortunately, we couldn't relax on the beach because every five minutes a vendor would approach us trying to sell us something. It's not inherently bad, but everyone wants to talk to you for four to six minutes before selling you anything, and if you don't want to, they become disrespectful.
My wife and mother were harassed, and when I said enough was enough and to move along, I was told that this was my country and that I should go back to Europe.
I've been to many countries, including some with pushy people, like Turkey, Morocco, and Egypt,
but I've NEVER seen anything like this.
There are so many beautiful beaches in the world, like in Indonesia, Mexico, Australia, and the Maldives.
This isn't the Zanzibar you see on Instagram.
I can only warn you: go somewhere else.
If you've already booked, go to a gated resort.

The road to Nungwi immediately gives you a sense of what a trip to this corner of Africa is like. Palm trees everywhere, people between cars, local shops that I have no idea what they were selling, lights nowhere, potholes that forced car owners to change their tires every 2 months, scattered houses with tin roofs, honking good mornings and smiles. The hotels are lined up on the beach, which is closed to locals and who can only access it from the village side. We visited 1 of the 3 schools in the village and after talking for a while with the teachers we gave stationery and toys to the children and took pictures with them after asking first of course. In Nungwi there is the phenomenon of tides and beach boys (whom we deal with with patience and kindness because they can be a little persistent but are generally polite and relaxed. If we say a polite and decisive no they will walk away saying hakuna matata, answer the same..)
All hotels have restaurants with traditional food pizzas fries pasta soups burgers seafood and alcohol. In the village there are bars and restaurants which we did not visit, but we did shop for local products and souvenirs (necklaces bracelets, fabrics, landscapes on banana leaves, paintings, wood carvings, drums and more). Support the locals!!. Except for those who sell shells and starfish (it is illegal). Among all of us are the young Maasai, a tribe that lives in the Serengeti desert from northern Tanzania, who have their own style and different way of approaching things (I should say that a little Maasai who followed us every day on our walk on the beach at low tide gave us a necklace as a gift..he was a very sweet and shy child). From Nungwi you can go to Mnemba for snorkeling, walk in Stone Town, to Nakupenda, visit Prison Island for its history and to see the huge turtles and take a sunset cruise.. we did all of that and it was all perfect ✨(all via beach boy Ricky). In Nungwi almost everyone speaks English because it is the second official language of the country. I think the important thing is to give these people a chance to talk to you, to get to know a little about their culture and their way of life, and they are all willing to tell you everything, about their family and the bond they feel, the political indifference and corruption, about the schools and the tuition they are forced to pay, while those who don't have them simply don't get an education, about their difficult living but everyone in the end smiles at you and says hakuna matata..no problem..!!!!!
I love you guys ❤️❤️❤️
ps: they don't care about the starfish that stay behind the low tide...a few seconds are enough for a single photo... out of water they die!!! We saw other tourists having these unfortunate beautiful animals out of the water for 3-4 and 5 minutes to take photos and selfies in all possible poses. Stop this..
Also be aware that at the airport, starfish shells raise an alarm and are confiscated..this does not offer anything to the animal, but it is a way to prevent theft from the sea or illegal trade..

content:
Superbe plages, en trois parties distinctes, l''est vers kwenda avec ces hôtels restaurants sur pilotis ces club de plongée et le port de bâteaux pour touristes, zone pas toujours très bon marché.
Puis le cap avec le marché au poisson avec port de pêche, un fabuleux restaurant sur la plage entre l''école coranique et le marché au poisson.
Enfin l''ouest après le phare de Nungwi avec une grande plage continue accessible à marée basse et lors de marée de faibles coefficient et une ribambelle d''hôtels plus ou moins acceuillants.
Beaucoup de rabatteurs pour excursion et de masaïs près à délester le touriste avec sourire et gentillesse mais pas toujours au meilleurs prix.
Éviter la plage seul(e) la nuit pour pas finir, sans même un slip ou une culotte (mésaventure vécue par un anglais de l''hôtel)...
Attention toute fois, une surexploitation incontrôlée de la plage (pêche des poulpes, poisson, crustacés et crevettes et ceuillette des coquillages, ) et des récifs est en train de  stériliser la zone...
translated_content:
Superb beaches, divided into three distinct sections: the eastern section towards Kwenda, with its hotels and restaurants on stilts, diving clubs, and the tourist boat port—an area that isn't always very affordable.
Then there's the cape with its fish market and fishing port, and a fabulous beach restaurant between the Koranic school and the fish market.
Finally, the western section, past the Nungwi lighthouse, boasts a long, continuous beach accessible at low tide and during spring tides, and a string of hotels of varying quality. There are many touts offering excursions and Maasai people ready to take advantage of tourists with smiles and friendliness, but not always at the best prices. Avoid going to the beach alone at night to avoid ending up without even underwear (a misadventure experienced by an Englishman staying at the hotel)...
However, be aware that uncontrolled overexploitation of the beach (fishing for octopus, fish, crustaceans and shrimp, and harvesting of shellfish) and the reefs is sterilizing the area...

Em van dir que aquesta és una de les millors platges de Zanzíbar, però després de visitar-la he de dir que no estic d''acord amb aquesta opinió general.
He de dir que la vaig visitar en un dia ennuvolat, cosa que potser m''ha fet veure-la d''una altra manera, però vaig caminar per tota la platja i el que vaig veure va ser una platja bruta, plena d''algues i plena de barques de pesca, força lluny. d''una platja idíl·lica.
També hi havia molts edificis (restaurants, hotels) construïts sobre la platja, sobre pilars de fusta, que ocupaven la platja i que quan puja la marea la sorra desapareix i és difícil caminar-hi.
D''altra banda,  molt positiu, és una platja plena de vida local, ja que hi ha molts pescadors locals treballant a les seves barques, i els nens i les dones estan contínuament a la sorra, jugant o esperant els homes amb les seves captures ... o fins i tot ramats de vaques prenent el sol a la platja.
Hauria de visitar-la en un dia assolellat i potser la meva percepció seria diferent... però tot i això, el passeig fou molt agradable
translated_content:
I was told that this is one of the best beaches in Zanzibar, but after visiting it I have to say that I do not agree with this general opinion.
I have to say that I visited it on a cloudy day, which may have made me see it differently, but I walked along the entire beach and what I saw was a dirty beach, full of seaweed and full of fishing boats, quite far from an idyllic beach.
There were also many buildings (restaurants, hotels) built on the beach, on wooden pillars, which occupied the beach and that when the tide rises the sand disappears and it is difficult to walk on it.
On the other hand, very positive, it is a beach full of local life, since there are many local fishermen working on their boats, and children and women are continuously on the sand, playing or waiting for the men with their catches ... or even herds of cows sunbathing on the beach.
I should visit it on a sunny day and maybe my perception would be different... but even so, the walk was very pleasant.

content:
Очень красивый пляж. Во время прилива - бирюзовая чистейшая вода, замечательное время для купания. Во время отливов  - купаться почти не реально. Зато очень интересно ходить по морскому дну и рассматривать разную живность.
Немного отвлекает местная детвора и масаи. Они предлагают что угодно за деньги. Даже звездочки показывают. Но всей этой живность итак много, если самой ходить.
Людей многовато, но друг на друге никто не сидит.
По пляжу происходит постоянная миграция людей/туристов/масаев.
Иногда можно понаблюдать, как рыбаки ловят рыбы.
Очень много чисто африканских картин из жизни местных жителей: в основном связанных с рыбалкой.
Ежи есть вдалеке. Их видно только при отливе. Во время прилива можно спокойно купаться даже без специальной обуви. Ближайшие метров 20 от края берега - чистый песок.
translated_content:
A very beautiful beach. At high tide, the water is crystal clear and turquoise, a wonderful time for swimming. At low tide, swimming is almost impossible. However, it's very interesting to walk along the seabed and observe the various creatures.
The local children and Maasai are a bit distracting. They offer anything for money. They even show you stars. But there's plenty of this wildlife, if you walk around on your own.
There are a lot of people, but no one is sitting on top of each other.
There's a constant migration of people/tourists/Maasai along the beach.
Sometimes you can watch fishermen catching fish.
There are many purely African scenes from the lives of the locals, mostly related to fishing.
There are sea urchins in the distance. They are only visible at low tide. At high tide, you can safely swim even without special shoes. The nearest 20 meters from the edge of the shore is clean sand.

content: Пляж Nungwi великолепен, хотя достаточно маленький по сравнению с соседним Kendwa. Белоснежный песок , невозможно ходить без солнцезащитных очков. Море -лазурное , в солнечные дни особенно красивое . Присутствуют отливы и приливы. На закате , в 18-00  океан начинает уходить  метров на 100-150, а примерно  с 13-00 начинает прибывать , в 16-00 можно  уже купаться. Днем в пешей доступности 15 мин можно купаться на пляже Kendwa, там отливов практически нет или они  не более 25-50 метров. В оливах есть свои плюсы- можно любоваться  , гуляя по дну океана, морскими звездами и прочими обитателями океана. Для прогулок приготовьте коралловые тапочки . На пляже есть несколько ресторанчиков и баров, также два алкогольных магазина. Цены вполне приемлемые. Между ресторанами Coco Cabana и Gelato Italiano на маленьком участке пляжа очень много надоедливых Beach-boy,s , каждые 5 минут предлагают какие-то экскурсии , и не только ... Если с ними не любезничать, и не заводить беседы, они уходят. Но к закату это все порядком надоедает, это большой минус . Между этими ресторанами есть прямо на берегу отличный бар с холодными напитками . Можно сидеть под зонтиком и наблюдать закат. В 5 мин от пляжа имеется мини-маркет , аптека, в деревне недорогие фрукты и сувениры. Торгуйтесь, торгуйтесь и еще раз торгуйтесь.
translated_content: Nungwi Beach is magnificent, although quite small compared to neighboring Kendwa. The sand is so white it's practically impossible to walk around without sunglasses. The sea is azure, especially beautiful on sunny days. The water has both high and low tides. At sunset, around 6:00 PM, the ocean begins to recede by 100-150 meters, and around 1:00 PM, it begins to rise, and by 4:00 PM, you can swim. During the day, Kendwa Beach is a 15-minute walk away; the low tide there is virtually nonexistent, or no more than 25-50 meters. The olive grove has its advantages – you can admire starfish and other ocean inhabitants while walking along the ocean floor. Bring coral slippers for walking. There are several restaurants and bars on the beach, as well as two liquor stores. Prices are quite reasonable. Between the Coco Cabana and Gelato Italiano restaurants, the small stretch of beach is filled with annoying beach boys, offering excursions and other things every five minutes. If you don't be friendly and start a conversation, they'll leave. But by sunset, this can get pretty annoying, which is a big minus. Between these restaurants, there's an excellent bar right on the shore with cold drinks. You can sit under an umbrella and watch the sunset. Five minutes from the beach, there's a minimarket, a pharmacy, and inexpensive fruit and souvenirs in the village. Bargain, bargain, and bargain some more.
