While it's true there's a big difference between low and high tide, and seaweed appears when it's very low, you can also enjoy seeing the shells left on the beach and the small white crabs that appear at night, as well as a starfish if you're lucky—it's simply wonderful! The water is very calm, at least when we were there, and you can snorkel since the visibility is excellent. During the middle of the day, there aren't as many boats, as they're busy with other activities, and at dawn and dusk, they provide a spectacular backdrop for your photos. content:
A fascinating and well managed addition to Zanzibar''s tourist attractions.
It''s a welcome short break from the beach, and shows you a completely different side to the island.
Good for couples, groups and families, and easily accessible with a short drive from any hotels on the north-east coast.
This cave system is in a vast & beautiful protected forest.
There''s a professional reception area with good washrooms.
You take a guided walk through the forest and descend down some steps into the caves. You get to walk quite a distance comfortably, past wonderful natural rock sculpures, stalegmites & stalegtites, and tiny bats clinging to the roof of the cave. Look out for the beautiful sparkling crystal rock, and then you get to the ''Kiwengwa Challenge'' area, where the cave tightens and gets very low, and you have to crawl a few metres on the ground till you emerge into a bright little grotto, open to the sky and surrounded by forest creepers. You don''t have to do this, but it''s good fun & worth it for the end view. Be prepared to get very dirty! You need good walking shoes - and don''t wear your best clothes..
The attention to safety & conservation is impressive. You are guided to stay on the forest tracks to avoid the sink holes into the cave below, given safety helmets & torches, and advised not to touch the rock formations or shine light onto the bats.
The management is committed to protesting the forest flora & fauna.
There are several lovely forest trails you can also take.
The temperature is cooler, the birdlife is interesting, there are butterflies, and there are red colobus and blue monkeys.
You can spend just an hour, or more there, and it''s definitely worth the trip!
response_content: Thanks for your wonderful review. We are so happy you enjoyed the Kiwengwa Challenge and got to enjoy the surrounding forest. We are so much more than a cave visit. We are a conservation project, hiking trails and want to educate people on the importance of the caves and forest. See you next time on a hike through the forest with a ranger.

content: Wir sind als Familie hingefahren und haben 3 Dollar pro Person gezahlt.  Wir haben Helme und Taschenlampen erhalten. content:
In het Kiwengwa-Pongwe Forest Reserve liggen de Kiwengwa-grotten. Deze kalksteengrotten strekken zich uit over meer dan 150 meter en bieden een fascinerend ondergronds ecosysteem.
De grotten zijn rijk aan stalactieten en stalagmieten, gevormd door het oplossen van calciumcarbonaat uit koraalsteen. Binnen de grotten leven verschillende vleermuissoorten, insecten en vogels. Bezoekers kunnen ook indrukwekkende boomwortels en schors zien die door de grotten groeien. Historisch gezien bezochten lokale bewoners de grotten om hun voorouders te vereren en brachten ze offers bij heilige stenen.
Erg leuke grotten voor een normale prijs. Kassim was een leuke gids die ons van alles vertelde. Ik ga niet alles verklappen. Kortom een aanrader.
Ps ik weet een goede gids met een busje voor een goede prijs die u over het eiland kan rijden. U boekt hem voor een hele dag. Hij weet leuke plekken en denkt met u mee. Pb mij voor meer info hierover.
translated_content:
The Kiwengwa Caves are located in the Kiwengwa-Pongwe Forest Reserve. These limestone caves extend over more than 150 meters and offer a fascinating underground ecosystem.
The caves are rich in stalactites and stalagmites, formed by the dissolution of calcium carbonate from coral rock. Various bat species, insects, and birds live inside the caves. Visitors can also see impressive tree roots and bark growing through the caves. Historically, local residents visited the caves to venerate their ancestors and made offerings at sacred stones.
Very nice caves for a reasonable price. Kassim was a nice guide who told us all sorts of things. I won't give everything away. In short, highly recommended.
PS I know a good guide with a van for a good price who can drive you around the island. You book him for a whole day. He knows nice spots and is very helpful. PM me for more info about this.

Villaggio rurale nella zona di Upenja, sulla strada per Kiwengwa (che con la sua bella spiaggia ed i suoi grandi resorts è forse la località turistica più famosa di Unguja), immerso nella folta vegetazione di palme, alberi ed arbusti che in Europa si possono  trovare solo in orti o giardini botanici.
Le abitazioni sono spesso costruite con legno e fango oltre che in mattoni, quasi tutte comunque, presentano il tradizionale tetto in makuti. Gli abitanti sono sempre sorridenti e ben disposti verso i turisti.

The houses are often built of wood and mud as well as brick, although almost all feature the traditional makuti roof. The residents are always smiling and welcoming to tourists.

content:
Super entreprise, super propriétaire. Nous logions près de cette plage et, depuis notre hébergement, on nous avait proposé une excursion pour observer les dauphins à 100 USD pour deux personnes. Nous avons donc décidé de comparer les prix. Le propriétaire nous a fait la meilleure offre directement, sans marchandage, ce qui nous a fait gagner du temps. Nous avons aussi testé l''excursion à Nungwi, moins chère (environ 50 USD pour deux), mais c''était une excursion partagée avec huit autres personnes, et nous ne voulions pas faire 50 minutes de route pour ça. Nous avons donc pris contact avec le propriétaire la veille. Il nous avait préparé une grande quantité de fruits, bien plus que nécessaire pour deux. Son service client était excellent : il nous a demandé notre avis et s''est assuré que les skippers ne nous forçaient pas à revenir. Nous avons vu des dauphins et avons pu nager avec eux trois fois sur quatre. Nous avons ensuite fait du snorkeling à un ou deux endroits avant de nous détendre sur le banc de sable. Le banc de sable était magnifique, l''une des plus belles plages que j''aie jamais vues. Nous aurions pu y refaire du snorkeling, mais l''eau commençait à être un peu froide, alors nous avons préféré y renoncer.  Certaines personnes ont trouvé des étoiles de mer ici.
Le service était très professionnel. Nous avions un guide local nommé Cappuccino et le capitaine s''appelait Mobi. Cappuccino nous guidait dans l''eau et avait également une bouée avec lui pour notre sécurité pendant toute la durée de notre sortie snorkeling.
Le trajet de cette plage jusqu''au site d''observation des dauphins a été plus long que prévu. En raison de la marée basse et du faible tirant d''eau, le bateau avançait très lentement tout le long. Il a donc fallu près d''une heure aller-retour. Prévoyez-en dans votre temps total. Nous avons choisi de partir à 7h30 (nous sommes partis vers 7h40) et sommes rentrés juste après 12h10.
Pour éviter la foule, je suggère de partir à 6h30 comme le suggérait le propriétaire, mais c''était trop tôt, nous avons donc demandé à partir de 7h30. Il y avait déjà beaucoup de bateaux. Si vous souhaitez prendre des photos des dauphins, assurez-vous de le faire avant de partir pour le snorkeling, car vous ne pourrez plus faire demi-tour pour les revoir une fois partis.
translated_content:
Great company, great owner. We were staying near this beach, and from our accommodation, we were offered a dolphin-watching excursion for $100 USD for two people. So we decided to compare prices. The owner gave us the best offer directly, without any haggling, which saved us time. We also tried the excursion to Nungwi, which was cheaper (around $50 USD for two), but it was a shared tour with eight other people, and we didn't want to drive 50 minutes for that. So we contacted the owner the day before. He had prepared a large quantity of fruit for us, much more than we needed for two. His customer service was excellent: he asked for our feedback and made sure the skippers didn't pressure us to come back. We saw dolphins and were able to swim with them three out of four times. We then went snorkeling in one or two spots before relaxing on the sandbar. The sandbar was magnificent, one of the most beautiful beaches I've ever seen. We could have gone snorkeling again, but the water was starting to get a bit cold, so we decided against it. Some people have found starfish here.
The service was very professional. We had a local guide named Cappuccino, and the captain's name was Mobi. Cappuccino guided us in the water and also had a buoy with him for our safety throughout our snorkeling trip.
The journey from this beach to the dolphin watching site took longer than expected. Due to the low tide and shallow draft, the boat moved very slowly the whole way. It took almost an hour round trip. Factor this into your total time. We chose to leave at 7:30 a.m. (we left around 7:40 a.m.) and returned just after 12:10 p.m.
To avoid the crowds, I suggested leaving at 6:30 am as the owner had suggested, but that was too early, so we asked for 7:30 am. There were already a lot of boats. content:
Wunderbarer Ort um die Wartezeit auf das Essen im angeschlossen Bashasha Restaurant zu überbrücken.
Die Tour beginnt mit einer Einführung zu den Lebensstadien eines Schmetterlings mit schön viel Anschauungsmaterial. Bevor es dann weiter geht, würde gefragt, ob wir ein domestiziertes Bushbaby sehen wollen. Natürlich wollten die Kinder das. Der Guide hat es dann aus seiner Schlafbox geholt und gehalten. Wir konnten Fotos machen und die Kinder konnten es vorsichtig streicheln. Im Gegensatz zu anderen Rezensionen hat er es aber zu keiner Zeit aus der Hand gegeben, uns eher noch darauf hingewiesen, dass das nicht erlaubt sei. Nach der Fotosession hat er es alleine wieder in seine Schlafbox laufen lassen.
Dann ging es in einen kleinen Chamäleon Garten. Zur Zeit waren nur zwei Tiere da. Der Guide erzählte ein bisschen zum Lebensraum der Tiere und der Bedrohung durch die lokale Bevölkerung.
Zum Schluss ging es in das Schmetterlingsgehege. Die flatterten munter vor sich hin und konnten mit Blüten, die der Guide den Kindern in die Hand gedrückt hat, angelockt werden.
Wir konnten so lange wir wollten in den Gehegen bleiben. Bei den Chamäleons hat der Guide Heuschrecken zum Füttern gesucht, bei den Schmetterlingen Blumen. Immer war er sehr darauf bedacht, dass wir viel sehen, aber dabei sehr behutsam mit den Tieren umgehen.
Im Großen und Ganzen ein schöner kleiner Park.
translated_content:
A wonderful place to pass the time while waiting for food at the attached Bashasha Restaurant.
The tour begins with an introduction to the life stages of a butterfly, complete with plenty of visual aids. Before continuing, we were asked if we wanted to see a domesticated bushbaby. Of course, the children did. The guide then took it out of its sleeping box and held it. We were able to take photos, and the children could gently pet it. Contrary to other reviews, he never let go of it; in fact, he pointed out that this wasn't allowed. After the photo session, he let it run back into its sleeping box on its own.
Then we went to a small chameleon garden. At the time, there were only two animals. The guide told us a bit about the animals' habitat and the threats they face from the local population.
Finally, we went to the butterfly enclosure. They fluttered merrily about and could be attracted with flowers that the guide gave to the children.
We were able to stay in the enclosures as long as we liked. The guide found grasshoppers to feed the chameleons and flowers to feed the butterflies. He was always very careful to ensure we saw a lot while handling the animals gently.
All in all, a lovely little park.

content:
🇬🇧 Terrible experience, a place to absolutely avoid out of respect for the animals that are mistreated inside.
I visited the facility this morning with friends to see the butterflies and, between a chrysalis and a caterpillar, the guide brought out some galagos (bush babies) for us to take pictures with. The animals appeared stressed and terrified—one of them was even forcibly placed on my friend’s hand and ended up biting him!
The guide didn’t know what to do, so instead suggested we continue the cruel tour by holding other animals (chameleons).
We had to rush to the hospital to start rabies treatment, while the staff at the butterfly centre made jokes about what happened, downplaying our reaction and repeatedly saying “hakuna matata, mzungu” (literally “white people, don’t worry” in a dismissive tone), without offering a single apology.
It was a disrespectful and dangerous attitude towards tourists, but most of all, it was cruel to the poor animals kept in captivity.
We regret not having read the reviews beforehand, as this was a last-minute activity.
Please don’t support facilities that exploit animals in this way.

content:
If you think animal welfare is important, DO NOT VISIT THIS PLACE. IT IS NOT THE ZANZIBAR BUTTERFLY CENTRE. There was a bushbaby kept in a tiny cage without any enrichment! Awful to see. The guide also touched the animal, which was understandably very afraid and stressed out. He wanted to take it out to let us hold it, but we were not okay with that. It’s never okay to directly interact with wild animals to ‘please’ visitors. Also, bushbaby’s are nocturnal animals, so putting them on display in a tiny cage during the day, touching them, holding them,… is just pure animal cruelty. Keep them in their natural habitat, not in cages. We really didn’t expect to witness something like that and it made us very upset. There were also elephant shrews in an enclosure. The guide ‘chased’ them so they would move and we could take a ‘good picture’. We told him many times to stop, cause it scared them and we only wanted to see them in peace. He also grabbed a chameleon and put it on my partner’s hand. We put it immediatly back on the leaves, for the same reason as mentioned above. Don’t touch them, don’t stress them out, don’t keep them in cages. Let the animals be in peace. We visited because we thought it was the Zanzibar butterfly centre where they help them reproduce and then set them free in the wild, but it is not.
If we knew there were other animals there locked up and being handeld by humans, we would’ve never been there. I hope from the bottom of my heart that they release the shrews, squirrels, bushbaby’s, chameleons, lizzards, … back into the wild. And if that’s not possible because they wouldn’t survive cause they have been locked up too long, PLEASE make them a gigantic enclosure that resembles their natural habitat and don’t ever let visitors into their enclosure or touch them. Please leave them in peace…

content:
Schöne kleine Anlage, man erfährt von einem Guide viel Interessantes über die heimischen Schmetterlinge, mit dem Eintrittsgeld unterstützt man zudem die lokale Dorfgemeinschaft, die zugunsten des Nationalparks die Bewirtschaftung des Waldes aufgegeben hat und sich nun hauptsächlich durch den Tourismus finanziert. Neben einer kleinen Schmetterlingsvoliere kann man auch Chamäleons hautnah erleben und sich Bush-Babies und Schildkröten in einer Auffang-/Auswilderungsstation anschauen. Für unsere Kinder war es ein sehr schönes Erlebnis, die Tiere auch mal aus der Nähe betrachten zu können.
Zu betonen ist hier noch, dass der Guide während unseres Besuchs mit jedem einzelnen Tier, Ei, Puppe, Kokon etc. äußerst behutsam sowie respekt- und rücksichtsvoll umging und das Tierwohl absolut im Vordergrund stand. Dieser Grundsatz ist meines Erachtens auch für jeden einzelnen Besucher verpflichtend. Ich hatte zu keinem Zeitpunkt das Gefühl, dass die Tiere vordergründig präsentiert werden, um die Sensationsgier zahlungswilliger Touristen zu befriedigen. Von daher kann ich einen Abstecher sehr empfehlen, allein schon, um die lokale Dorfgemeinschaft und damit den Fortbestand des Nationalparks zu unterstützen.
translated_content:
A lovely little facility where a guide shares fascinating information about native butterflies. The entrance fee also supports the local village community, which gave up managing the forest in favor of the national park and now relies primarily on tourism for its livelihood. Besides a small butterfly aviary, you can also experience chameleons up close and see bush babies and tortoises in a rescue/rehabilitation station. It was a wonderful experience for our children to be able to observe the animals so closely.
It's worth emphasizing that during our visit, the guide handled every single animal, egg, pupa, cocoon, etc., with the utmost care, respect, and consideration, and the animals' welfare was clearly the top priority. In my opinion, this principle should be binding for every visitor. At no point did I feel that the animals were being presented superficially to satisfy the sensationalism of paying tourists. Therefore, I highly recommend a visit, if only to support the local village community and thus the continued existence of the national park.

content:
Непременно стоит посетить!
Это памятник ЮНЕСКО. Вход платный. В феврале 2021 года - 5000 местных денег (около 150 рублей). В эту сумму включена прекрасная экскурсия на английском языке.
Музейный сотрудник Мубарак рассказал нам о том, каким был дворец до пожара, показал фотографии, остатки лестниц, фрагменты созранившейся отделки итальянским мрамором и другие детали. Рассказал, какой была жизнь дворца: где были пышные приемы, в какой части жили наложницы султана и какой была их жизнь. Как по аквидуку вода приходила в бассейны, баню, туалеты дворца, как была устроена система коммуникаций.
Если любите тренировать воображение, глядя на руины ушедших эпох, обязательно посетите этот музей!
translated_content:
Definitely worth a visit!
This is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Admission is charged. In February 2021, it was 5,000 local currencies (approximately 150 rubles). This price includes a wonderful English-language tour.
Museum employee Mubarak told us about the palace before the fire, showing photographs, remnants of staircases, fragments of surviving Italian marble trim, and other details. He described life in the palace: where lavish receptions were held, where the sultan's concubines lived, and what their lives were like. He also explained how the aquiduct supplied water to the palace's pools, bathhouse, and toilets, and how the utility system was constructed.
If you enjoy exploring the ruins of bygone eras, be sure to visit this museum!

content:
Непременно стоит посетить!
Это памятник ЮНЕСКО. Вход платный. В феврале 2021 года - 5000 местных денег (около 150 рублей). В эту сумму включена прекрасная экскурсия на английском языке.

Рассказал, какой была жизнь дворца: где были пышные приемы, в какой части жили наложницы султана и какой была их жизнь. Как по аквидуку вода приходила в бассейны, баню, туалеты дворца, как была устроена система коммуникаций.
Если любите тренировать воображение, глядя на руины ушедших эпох, обязательно посетите этот музей!
Добраться, наверно, можно на каком-то транспорте. Но мы дошли из Стоун Тауна пешком - тут всего 5 километров.
translated_content:
Definitely worth a visit!
This is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Admission is charged. In February 2021, it was 5,000 local currencies (about 150 rubles). This price includes a wonderful English-language tour.
Museum employee Mubarak told us about the palace before the fire, showing photographs, remnants of staircases, fragments of surviving Italian marble trim, and other details. He described life in the palace: where lavish receptions were held, where the sultan's concubines lived, and what their lives were like. He also described how water was supplied to the palace's pools, bathhouse, and toilets through an aquiduct, and how the utility system was constructed.
If you enjoy exploring the ruins of bygone eras, be sure to visit this museum!
You can probably get there by some form of transport. However, we walked from Stone Town—it's only 5 kilometers.

content:
There are many palaces on the Zanzibar coast over a distance of 5km from Zanjibar towards north towards Bububu. Noteworthy are the Marihubi Palace ruins historical sites and Mtoni Palace ruins.
As you move 4km north of Zanzibar town one reach the Maruhubi Palace located overlooking the coast.  Built between 1880 and 1882 for Sultan Said Barghash for his secondary wives while he lived at the Palace in Zanzibar Town. The palace gets the name from the original owner of the land who sold it to Sultan Barghash. Coral stone and wood were used to build the Marihubi Palace and was one of the most beautiful structure on the island, which later distroyed by a fire and left in ruins. The photo of the palace taken at the end of the 19th century housed at the House of Wonders in Zanzibar Town, depicts its past glory. What now remains is  massive stone pillars, the Persian-style bathhouses,  a low stone basin containing water lilies and undulating lawns.
Come to Zanzibar. Reach Maruhubi Palace ruins Historical Sites and take a stroll through the history of this once magnificent place. The  Maruhubi and Mtoni Palace ruins are a quiet peaceful places for a picnic away from the bustle of Stone Town and a place to wade through the history of Zanzibar. Good luck.

Absoluut geen aanrader!!!!!

Don't go to this spice farm!

At the end of the tour, we were given a coconut. We didn't see any fresh fruit. An extra assistant joined us there too. Then came the announcement about tips. It started with a starting point of 10,000 shillings.
This really rubbed us the wrong way. We wanted to pay for the perfume bottles again, but again, they supposedly didn't have change. When we decided not to buy the perfume bottles, they suddenly did give us change.
The atmosphere also changed somewhat. So, we weren't planning on tipping. Our goal was to get back to the taxi as quickly as possible. They followed us a little bit, but luckily, we got away safely. Absolutely not recommended!!!!!

Locals gather to exchange stories, the scent of cloves mingling with the salty air. Children dart along the shoreline, their laughter a melody that merges with the waves. It is here, at twilight, that Omar, a quiet observer of life, finds his muse. Sitting at the edge of the sand, he watches the ocean meet the dusk, his thoughts weaving between tradition and ambition. This is more than a beach; it is the soul of Zanzibar—a meeting point of history, community, and dreams yet to unfold.

content:
Ciao a chi legge. Siamo una famiglia di 2 adulti e 2 ragazzi e attualmente siamo a Zanzibar.
Ieri abbiamo fatto questa escursione e vi voglio raccontare la nostra esperienza.  Fino ad oggi è stata una delle più belle esperienze, vissute a Zanzibar. La nostra guida Marcello parla benissimo italiano e sa tutto delle piante, che crescono sull''isola e che si usano nella cucina e nella medicina in tutto il mondo.
In questo tour vi faranno assaggiare le spezie e la frutta coltivate da loro. Vorrei precisare, che non si è obligati acquistare le spezie.
A parte le spezie, lo staff del posto vendono anche le saponette naturali oli per i massaggi, essenze profumate.
Per chi si lamenta del prezzo vorrei ricordare che in Italia 1 stecca di vanilla costa attorno i 5 euro, nei sacchetti , che vendono loro sono 6-8 pezzi. Per 2 sacchetti di vanilla abbiamo speso 8 euro.
Per quanto riguarda Stone Town,  è tappa quasi obbligatoria non solo per vedere come vive questo popolo, ma anche per ammirare l''architettura fondata da diverse culture.
Un caro saluto
translated_content:
Hello everyone. We are a family of two adults and two children, and we're currently in Zanzibar.
Yesterday we took this excursion, and I want to tell you about our experience. It was one of the most beautiful experiences we've had in Zanzibar so far. Our guide, Marcello, speaks excellent Italian and knows everything about the plants that grow on the island and are used in cooking and medicine around the world.
On this tour, you'll taste the spices and fruits they grow. I should point out that you're not obligated to buy the spices.
Aside from spices, the staff also sell natural soaps, massage oils, and scented essences.
For those who complain about the price, I'd like to point out that in Italy, a vanilla pod costs around €5, while the bags they sell cost 6-8. For two bags of vanilla, we spent €8.
As for Stone Town, it's an almost mandatory stop, not only to see how these people live, but also to admire the architecture, a legacy of different cultures.
Best regards

content:
Our visit to Old Dispensary was a delightful experience and a visual treat while exploring Stone Town. This building instantly stands out with its unique architecture and beautifully restored façade.
What makes the Old Dispensary so special is its intricate design. The carved wooden balconies, stained glass windows, and detailed decorative elements reflect a blend of Indian, Arab, and European influences. It’s one of those places where you can just stand and admire the craftsmanship for a while.
Originally built in the late 19th century, the structure has an interesting history and today serves as a cultural center. Walking through the building, you get a sense of its past while also appreciating how well it has been preserved and restored.
We enjoyed taking our time here, especially observing the finer details — from the ornate railings to the colorful glasswork. It’s not a place where you spend hours, but it definitely adds depth to your exploration of Stone Town.
Located close to the seafront, it’s easy to include this as a stop while walking around the area. Overall, the Old Dispensary is a great example of heritage preservation and architectural beauty — simple, elegant, and definitely worth a visit.

In the heart of Zanzibar stands the Great Baobab Tree, a living symbol of the island's natural and cultural history. This tree is one of the largest living organisms in Tanzania, with trunks reaching over 10 meters in diameter and estimated to be hundreds of years old, perhaps even exceeding a thousand. What distinguishes the baobab is its ability to store thousands of liters of water within its spongy trunk to withstand drought. For this reason, it is called the "Tree of Life," as it provides food, medicine, and shelter for both humans and animals.
Historically, Zanzibar was a strategic trading post in the Indian Ocean. Omanis and other Arabs were among the most prominent contributors to its development during the 19th century, particularly after Sultan Said bin Sultan made it his capital. Their role extended beyond trade; they established infrastructure including roads, markets, and palaces, and forged strong relationships with local communities. They were among the first to appreciate the importance of Zanzibar's environment and natural heritage, including ancient trees like the baobab, which served as natural road markers or temporary shelters for trade caravans.
Baobab fruit is highly nutritious, rich in vitamin C, iron, and calcium, and is used in juices and health products. Its seeds are dried and used to make oils beneficial for skin and hair, while the bark is used to make ropes and straw baskets and has traditional medicinal uses for treating fever and stomach ailments. Thus, the baobab is not just a tree, but a small ecosystem in itself that sustains rural communities.
Visiting a baobab in Zanzibar offers touristic, cultural, and environmental benefits. It connects visitors to the past, allowing them to see how ancient communities lived in harmony with nature and appreciate how preserving this tree to this day is a form of environmental stewardship. Today, the baobab has become a focal point for researchers, photographers, and tourists, and is often included in tour itineraries that also encompass Jozani Forest and spice plantations.
In short, the baobab tree is not just a huge trunk, but a living record that speaks of Zanzibar’s history, the details of ancient life, and the spirit of sustainability that the people of Omani and Zanzibari origins, the owners of the place, still maintain to this day.

content:
Ein ganz besonderer Ort auf Pemba!
Der Leuchtturm ist definitiv einen Besuch wert. Schon allein die Aussicht von oben ist einfach atemberaubend – man hat einen fantastischen Blick über die Küste und das Meer von Pemba.
Was diesen Ort aber wirklich besonders macht, ist der Leuchtturmwärter. Er kümmert sich bereits seit 30 Jahren um diesen Leuchtturm und erzählt mit unglaublich viel Herzblut von seiner Geschichte. Besonders beeindruckt hat uns, dass er sich die Geschichte und seine Erklärungen in mehreren Sprachen angeeignet hat – unter anderem sogar auf Deutsch!
Man merkt sofort, wie sehr ihm der Leuchtturm am Herzen liegt. Seine Erzählungen und seine herzliche Art machen aus dem Besuch weit mehr als nur einen schönen Aussichtspunkt.
Für uns ein echtes Highlight auf Pemba und absolut empfehlenswert. Wer auf der Insel ist, sollte sich diesen besonderen Ort und die Begegnung mit seinem Leuchtturmwärter nicht entgehen lassen!
translated_content:
A truly special place on Pemba!
The lighthouse is definitely worth a visit. The view from the top alone is simply breathtaking – you have a fantastic panorama of the coast and the sea off Pemba.
But what truly makes this place special is the lighthouse keeper. He has been caring for this lighthouse for 30 years and tells its story with incredible passion. We were particularly impressed that he has learned the story and his explanations in several languages ​​– including German!
You can immediately tell how much the lighthouse means to him. His stories and his warm personality make the visit so much more than just a beautiful viewpoint.
For us, a real highlight on Pemba and highly recommended. Anyone visiting the island shouldn't miss this special place and the chance to meet its lighthouse keeper!

content: Mnemba Island is a single small island located about 3 km off the northeast coast of Unguja, the largest island of the Zanzibar Archipelago, Tanzania, opposite Muyuni Beach. It is roughly triangular in shape, about 500 metres (1,640 ft) in diameter and about 1.5 kilometres (0.9 mi) in circumference. It is surrounded by an oval reef seven by four kilometres in extent. These reefs have been declared a marine conservation area. Mnemba Island and its reef are sometimes called Mnemba Atoll which is incorrect because an atoll is an island that encircles a lagoon, which is not the case for Mnemba Island.

content:
Ich bin mit dem Boot von Stone Town nach Changuu Island gefahren, und schon die Überfahrt hat sich wie ein Übergang in eine andere Welt angefühlt: türkisblaues Wasser, warmes Licht, Palmen am Horizont. Die Insel ist klein, aber sie trägt Geschichte und Natur in einer Intensität, die mich tief berührt hat.
Unser Guide hat uns auf der Tour nicht nur die Schildkröten gezeigt – was für sich schon unglaublich war –, sondern uns konkret und fundiert in die Geschichte eingeführt: Changuu wurde im 19. Jahrhundert zunächst von arabischen Sklavenhändlern als Ort genutzt, an dem unruhige oder widerspenstige versklavte Menschen festgehalten wurden, bevor sie nach Stone Town und weiter verkauft wurden. Später planten die Briten dort ein Gefängnis, das aber nie als solches in Betrieb ging und stattdessen als Quarantänestation für Gelbfieber und andere Krankheiten diente. Heute sind nur noch die Ruinen dieser Anlagen erhalten, und sie wirken wie ein stiller, aber kraftvoller Zeuge dessen, was hier geschah.
Das, was mich besonders beeindruckt hat, war, wie respektvoll unser Guide diese Geschichte vermittelt hat – nicht beschönigend, nicht sensationsheischend, sondern klar, sachlich und menschlich. Wir sind durch die Ruinen gegangen, haben gelauscht, Fragen gestellt und verstanden, dass dieser Ort weit mehr ist als nur ein Fotospot.
Aber Changuu ist gleichzeitig ein wunderbarer Ort der Natur. Die Aldabra-Riesenschildkröten dort lassen einen innehalten: Diese uralten Tiere, einige über hundert Jahre alt, bewegen sich gelassen durch die Schatten der Palmen, nehmen Futter aus der Hand und wirken so friedvoll und würdevoll, dass man sich diesen Moment wirklich merken will.
Der Rundgang ist durchdacht: Informationsschilder erklären sowohl die ökologische Bedeutung als auch den historischen Kontext. Die Guides beantworten jede Frage – und zwar nicht nur oberflächlich, sondern mit Hintergrundwissen, Authentizität und Respekt vor den Menschen und der Natur, die diese Insel geprägt haben.
Was mich außerdem beeindruckt hat: Die Insel ist kein bloßes „Tierpark-Ziel“, sondern ein Ort, an dem Bewahrung, Vermittlung und Besuchererlebnis auf Augenhöhe funktionieren. Man spürt, dass hier nicht nur attraktiv präsentiert, sondern tatsächlich geschützt und erklärt wird – und das macht den Besuch zu einem Erlebnis mit Tiefe.
Die Bootsüberfahrt, die Ruinen, die alten Geschichten, das Zusammentreffen mit den Schildkröten – alles ergibt zusammen ein Bild, das meine Wahrnehmung von Sansibar verändert hat. Wer wirklich wissen will, wie Inseln, Tierwelt und Geschichte zusammenspielen, beginnt hier.
Mein Fazit: Changuu Island ist nicht nur ein lohnenswerter Tagesausflug ab Stone Town. Es ist ein Ort der Begegnung – mit Natur, mit Geschichte, mit Wahrheit. Eine Empfehlung, die bei mir lange nachhallt.
translated_content:
I took a boat from Stone Town to Changuu Island, and even the crossing felt like stepping into another world: turquoise water, warm light, palm trees on the horizon. The island is small, but it carries history and nature with an intensity that deeply moved me.
Our guide not only showed us the turtles on the tour—which was incredible in itself—but also gave us a concrete and well-informed introduction to the island's history: In the 19th century, Changuu was first used by Arab slave traders as a place to hold restless or unruly enslaved people before they were sold on to Stone Town and beyond. Later, the British planned a prison there, but it never functioned as such and instead served as a quarantine station for yellow fever and other diseases. Today, only the ruins of these facilities remain, standing as a silent but powerful witness to what happened here.
What impressed me most was how respectfully our guide conveyed this history – not embellishing it, not sensationalizing it, but clearly, factually, and with empathy. We walked through the ruins, listened, asked questions, and understood that this place is far more than just a photo spot.
But Changuu is also a wonderful place of nature. The Aldabra giant tortoises there make you stop and think: These ancient animals, some over a hundred years old, move serenely through the shade of the palm trees, take food from your hand, and appear so peaceful and dignified that you really want to remember that moment.
The tour is well-planned: Information panels explain both the ecological significance and the historical context. The guides answer every question – not just superficially, but with in-depth knowledge, authenticity, and respect for the people and nature that have shaped this island.
What also impressed me: The island isn't just a "zoo destination," but a place where conservation, education, and visitor experience work together seamlessly. You can sense that it's not just about attractive presentation, but genuine protection and explanation – and that makes the visit a truly profound experience.
The boat trip, the ruins, the ancient stories, the encounter with the tortoises – everything comes together to create a picture that has changed my perception of Zanzibar. Anyone who truly wants to understand how islands, wildlife, and history intertwine should start here.
My conclusion: Changuu Island isn't just a worthwhile day trip from Stone Town. It's a place of encounter – with nature, with history, with truth. A recommendation that will stay with me for a long time.

content:
You have to pay for a boat across from Stone Town (included with our pre-booked guided trip).
Before getting on said boat, you must pay 3usd tax to a government desk on the beach, per person. No idea why. This will increase to 10usd from 1st September 2025.
To board your boat, it''s feet in the filthy water. A choppy 25 minute crossing and you do the same the other end, although at least the water is clean here. There are taps upstairs to wash your feet off before refitting shoes etc.
At this point, you then find out that it''s actually a zoo. The remains of the ''prison'' (actually a quarantine facility) have been converted into a zoo, which they rarely refer to as a tortoise sanctuary but they''re captive, you can''t get away from it. From what I understand as soon as a tortoise appears near the path everyone flocks to it for photos which I imagine would be very stressful for them. The young are taken away from them and put in cages until they''re older.
It costs an additional 12usd per person to enter the zoo when you arrive. After realising what it was we decided not to pay and returned to stone town on our dhow.
All information we found out previously suggested ''Prison Island'' was the site of a long since ruined prison where giant tortoises are free to roam, unhindered. This is absolutely not the case, our guide told us that it used to be like that, but the government realised there was money to be made as a tourist attraction.
Waste of time and money.

content:
Our visit to Slave Market was one of the most powerful and emotionally heavy experiences of our trip. This is not just a place you visit — it’s a place that makes you pause, reflect, and truly understand a difficult part of history.
Walking through the site, especially the underground chambers where enslaved people were once held, gives you a stark sense of the extreme conditions they endured. The spaces are small, dark, and suffocating even today — it’s hard to imagine how many people were confined there under such inhumane circumstances. It’s an experience that stays with you long after you leave.
The memorials and exhibits around the site help provide context and tell the stories of those who suffered here. The displays are informative and thoughtfully put together, helping visitors understand the scale and impact of the slave trade in this region.
The area also includes the Anglican Cathedral, which stands as a symbol of hope and transformation, built on the very grounds of the former market. The contrast between the painful history and the present-day setting is quite striking.
We would definitely recommend taking a guide here, as it helps you better understand the historical significance and the stories behind what you’re seeing. It adds depth and meaning to the visit.
Overall, the Slave Market is not an easy place to visit, but it is an important one. It offers a sobering reminder of the past and leaves you with a deeper appreciation of history and humanity.

content: Informative museum on the East African slave trade. Dark times for humanity. The shame of many prosperous countries in the world. It really gives you a lump in your throat here, looking at the depictions of villages being burned and families split up and shipped away. The East Africans were sent as slaves to mainly Arabia, after being imprisoned and bought here in Stonetown, Zanzibar. I knew a lot about the slave trade to the Caribbean, but not so much here, so it was very educational. Lots of history, pictures and illustrations in the museum, and stories on individuals. I got a good background on how Dr. Livingstone was on the side of the slaves and tried to promote trade  of resources to phase out slavery. There are also some stories on the individual slave traders, if you can stomach their greed and heartlessness. There is also a basement under the church where the slaves were imprisoned, that you can explore. A guide is allocated to you with the price of admission. Our guide was really good.

content:
My visit to the Old Slave Market/Anglican Cathedral in Zanzibar, Tanzania, was a sobering and thought-provoking experience. The site was formerly a slave market, where thousands of enslaved Africans were bought and sold during the 19th century.
The history of the site is presented in a clear and informative way, with displays and exhibits that detail the brutal reality of the slave trade. The guided tour was insightful and provided a greater understanding of the horrific conditions that the enslaved people were subjected to.
The Anglican Cathedral, which now stands on the site of the former slave market, is a beautiful and striking building that provides a fitting tribute to the victims of the slave trade. The architecture is impressive, with high ceilings, stained glass windows, and intricate details.
Overall, my visit to the Old Slave Market/Anglican Cathedral was a powerful and moving experience that left a lasting impression. It is a reminder of the inhumanity and cruelty of the slave trade and serves as a call to action to continue to work towards a more just and equitable society. I highly recommend a visit to this historic site for anyone looking to gain a deeper understanding of the history of Zanzibar and the impact of the slave trade.

content:
Sansibar war im 19. Jahrhundert Dreh- und Angelpunkt des Sklavenhandels in Ostafrika. Auf dem Sklavenmarkt wurden die Menschen begutachtet und je nach Alter und Gesundheitszustand ein Wert festgelegt.
Jetzt befindet sich dort ein einfaches Museum mit der Geschichte und man kann die Kellerräume besichtigen, die als Unterkunft dienten. Dort wurden auf engstem Raum bis zu 80 Sklaven untergebracht, einfach bedrückend.
Waren mit lokalem Guide unterwegs, Eintritt 8 Euro pro Person. Besucht im November 2022.
translated_content:
Zanzibar was a hub of the slave trade in East Africa during the 19th century. At the slave market, people were inspected and their value determined based on their age and health.
Now, a simple museum tells the story, and you can visit the cellars that served as living quarters. Up to 80 slaves were crammed into these tiny spaces—simply oppressive.
We went with a local guide; admission was €8 per person. Visited in November 2022.

No val la p na la visita, l''únic que veuràs es una exposició que de plafons amb informació que pots trobar en internet, una església simple i una obra d''art morbosa que es el reclam turístic a 5$ l''entrada i uns guies que t''assalten a l''entrada i que expliquen coses no certes i venen un passat vergonyos com una atracció.
Història de la catedral:
Es va construir en set anys, posant la primera pedra el dia de Nadal de 1873 fins a l''obertura el Nadal de 1879,  basant-se en una visió d'' Edward Steere , tercer bisbe anglicà de Zanzíbar, que va contribuir activament al disseny. Com la majoria dels edificis de Stone Town, està fet principalment de pedra corall . Té un sostre de formigó únic amb forma d''una inusual volta de canó (això va ser la idea de Steere) i l''estructura general barreja detalls gòtics perpendiculars i islàmics .  La catedral va ser consagrada el 1903 i va rebre el nom de la catedral de Canterbury .
L''església es troba a Mkunazini Road, al centre del nucli antic, i ocupa una gran àrea on antigament hi havia el mercat d''esclaus més gran de Zanzíbar; de fet, la construcció de la catedral estava destinada a celebrar la fi de l''esclavitud.  Es diu que l''altar es troba al lloc exacte on abans hi havia el 'post de fuet'" principal del mercat. A la plaça hi ha un conegut monument als esclaus (unes quantes figures humanes encadenats que surten d''una fossa) així com un museu sobre l''esclavitud.

translated_content:
It's not worth the visit, all you'll see is an exhibition of panels with information you can find on the internet, a simple church and a morbid work of art that is the tourist attraction at $5 per entrance and some guides who assault you at the entrance and who explain things that are not true and sell a shameful past as an attraction.
History of the cathedral:
It was built in seven years, laying the first stone on Christmas Day 1873 until the opening on Christmas Day 1879, based on a vision of Edward Steere, third Anglican Bishop of Zanzibar, who actively contributed to the design. Like most of the buildings in Stone Town, it is made mainly of coral stone. It has a unique concrete roof in the shape of an unusual barrel vault (this was Steere's idea) and the overall structure mixes Perpendicular Gothic and Islamic details. The cathedral was consecrated in 1903 and was named after Canterbury Cathedral.
The church is located on Mkunazini Road, in the centre of the old town, and occupies a large area where the largest slave market in Zanzibar used to be; in fact, the cathedral was built to celebrate the end of slavery. The altar is said to be located on the exact spot where the market's main "whip post" used to be. The square houses a well-known slave monument (a series of chained human figures emerging from a pit) as well as a museum about slavery.
Edward Steere died of a heart attack when the cathedral was almost completed and was buried behind the altar. Inside the church is a cross made from the wood of the tree that grows where David Livingstone's heart was buried, in Chitambo.
Like many other historic coral stone buildings in Stone Town, the cathedral is experiencing decay and structural problems and is in need of restoration.
The cathedral is linked to Ely Cathedral, in the Diocese of Ely, Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom.

translated_content: From a purely architectural perspective, it's a very beautiful place, as is the cathedral. There's a good exhibition about the history of the slave trade, presented on printed canvases—no artifacts or items of historical value are on display. In the basement, there are two cells where people were held in inhumane conditions before being sold. It's quite a difficult place emotionally, as are similar places. The toilet at the entrance is smelly and unsanitary. There's a monument to slaves in the courtyard. The grounds are adjacent to a private school, so if you took candy, you can give it to the children through a teacher at the school.

content:
Apparently there is more than just the exhibit with panels and pictures, and a place underground also. We couldn''t find it, and you might need to pay a guide extra for that (on top of admission to the exhibit).
A few rooms details the history of the market in display panels with photos and renderings and a lot of reading. There is a monument that you can see in the photos. The interior of the cathedral is nice. They have services on Sundays in Swahili. There is a service in English at 8AM in the chapel. The price of admission is high, but you''re not paying for new information, simply just to get past the gates to see the monument and read some panels, and be in the same place where it all happened. The information presented is definitely sobering and good knowledge to have when visiting and touring Stone Town, but if you can read about it online and have no need to be in the same location as where it happened (and could be content with just looking past the gate--or visiting on Sunday for church to get on the grounds), you won''t be missing much.

content: We were really excited for our cave trip, but it turned out to be nothing like what''s advertised, and we were really disappointed. The cave itself is nice, cool clean, deep water and tiny fish which are very cute. However there was something else in the water that looked like little lice, that bit really hard and meant we couldn''t stay swimming for as long as we would have liked to. The advertised facilities (the restaurant, showers, yoga area, seating area, lockers) were all closed or out of order - we were told we couldn''t even buy a bottle of water, and it was a very hot day. We mentioned this to the staff and even to the manager, but we were told there was nothing that could be done. We felt it would have been fair to tell us about the closed facilities before we''d paid 15 dollars entree fee each, or if the price would have been adjusted to reflect the total lack of facilities at the time. As it was, we were really disappointed, especially by the manager''s total lack of care.

content: We were so looking forward to this, after reading the reviews, and so disappointed. The admission fee was quite high, at USD15 each, and the reception staff didn''t warn us that almost all the facilities were unavailable. The cave itself is nice and cool to swim in, with some tiny fish and but also a lot of small stinging creatures. The advertised changing space and lockers didn''t appear to exist. There were 2 toilets, one with a door that didn''t close, no electricity, and a shower that didn''t work. It was a very hot day, and we had planned to have lunch in the advertised restaurant, but it was closed (long-term) and there was nowhere even to get a bottle of water. The gardens are pretty, but the sitting areas were out of action and cushions wet or moldy. We read that there was a second beach, but found no sign of this, nor of the advertised yoga space. The cave is about 20 minutes'' walk along a narrow bumpy track from the main road. We asked politely if we could have a reduction in the price once we realised the advertised facilities weren''t available, but were told this was impossible.
full_address: The Cave, Jambiani, Tanzania

street: Great place! We visited the cave in September 2021. It's definitely less well-known than Kuza Cave, recommended by our local guide. Thanks to the cave's slightly "hidden" location, fewer tourists get there, which was a huge plus for us. Besides the four of us, there were only two groups (one of them also Polish) – one was leaving when we arrived, and the other arrived as we were leaving. Therefore, we were alone in the cave pool. The access to the water was easy, and the water was crystal clear – perfect for cooling off during the heatwave. Homemade papaya moonshine is available for purchase on site. I recommend it to everyone!

content: Eine tolle und noch nicht zu bekannte Höhle. Der Eintritt kostet 10 $ pro Person. Man kann den ganzen Tag dort verbringen. Es gibt viele liebevoll gestaltete Sitzecken und eine kleine Bar. Ins Wasser kann man aus etwa 3 Meter Höhe springen oder an der Seite reingehen. Wer empfindlich ist, sollte Badeschuhe mitnehmen, die Steine sind manchmal etwas spitz. Im Wasser gibt es einige Schwimmreifen und man kann sich herrlich treiben lassen und mit der Schwimmbrille die klare Unterwasserwelt beobachten. Die Inhaber sind sehr freundlich. Wer Fotos machen möchte, sollte vor 9 Uhr dort sein. Dann fällt die Sonne hinein und das Wasser funkelt wunderschön.
translated_content: A fantastic and still relatively unknown cave. Entry costs $10 per person. You can easily spend the whole day there. There are many charmingly designed seating areas and a small bar. You can jump into the water from a height of about 3 meters or enter from the side. If you have sensitive feet, you should bring water shoes, as the rocks can be a bit sharp. There are some inflatable rings in the water, and you can float along and observe the clear underwater world with your goggles. The owners are very friendly. If you want to take photos, you should arrive before 9 a.m. That's when the sun shines in and the water sparkles beautifully.

content:
Superbe lieu, magnifique le matin très tôt car le soleil entre dans la grotte.
Une eau fraîche, superbe si vous avez des coups de soleil 😂
La grotte est profonde, n''oubliez pas votre masque et votre tuba si vous voulez vraiment en profiter.
Ils proposent des cocktails et rafraîchissements et il y a une soirée gratuite le samedi soir.
Le prix pour entrer est de 10$ par personne, c''est assez cher mais nous avons pu y passer la journée. Il n''y a pas de limite de temps.

translated_content:
A stunning spot, especially beautiful early in the morning as the sun streams into the cave.
The water is refreshingly cool, perfect if you have sunburn 😂
The cave is deep, so don't forget your mask and snorkel if you really want to enjoy it.
They offer cocktails and refreshments, and there's a free party on Saturday nights.
The entrance fee is $10 per person, which is quite expensive, but we were able to spend the whole day there. There's no time limit.
And best of all: we were practically alone all morning. It's much less crowded than the other cave in Jambiani.
Note: If you're coming from Paje on foot, don't follow Google Maps! Stay on the main road until you see the sign.

content: Sporo zdjęć jest z jaskini Cuza. Ta w przeciwieństwie do niej jest sucha. Dojście wg Googla. Droga w rzeczywistości prowadzi prosto do jaskini. Po drodze słyszeliśmy, że szły z nami w roślinności zwierzęta, jednak mimo strachu, to gdy zdecydowały się one już przeciąć nam drogę okazywały się być wiewiórkami :p Strach ma wielkie oczy. Przy muzeum nikogo nie było, próbowaliśmy dojść ścieżką za muzeum (ale to nie ta właściwa), a następnie tą sugerowaną przez google. Wejście darmowe. Myślę, że gdyby był właściciel muzeum to jak w poprzednich kometarzach wejście byłoby płatne. Po komentarzach spodziewaliśmy się śmieci w jaskini, jednak w rzeczywistości były 2 legowiska w głębi jaskini i na środku kilka ubrań - to tyle. Później byliśmy też w Cuza, której zdjęcia są tutaj, ale nie zrobiła takiego wrażenia. Kuumbi jest zdecydowanie warta zobaczenia.
translated_content: There are a lot of photos from Cuza Cave. This one, in contrast, is dry. The entrance is according to Google. The path actually leads straight into the cave. The cave itself is large and impressive. Along the way, we heard that animals were following us through the vegetation, but despite our fear, when they finally decided to cross our path, they turned out to be squirrels :p Fear has big eyes. There was no one at the museum; we tried the path behind the museum (but it wasn't the right one), and then the one suggested by Google. Entrance is free. I think if the museum were the owner, as in previous comments, there would be an entrance fee. Based on the comments, we expected trash in the cave, but in reality, there were two beds deep in the cave and a few clothes inside – that's all. Later, we also visited Cuza, which has photos here, but it wasn't as impressive. Kuumbi is definitely worth seeing.

Our first time in Zanzibar and today we visited Jozani forest. We chose the 3 hour/middle tour which was very enjoyable; it was quite hot and humid so for those interested in doing this tour I would definitely advise bringing plenty of drinking water and appropriate shoes (the terrain is not suitable for flip flops!)

Our tour guide Kasi was very knowledgeable and had an excellent eye for pointing out a variety of animals - lizards, millipedes, snakes, elephant shrews, cicadas, crabs (the final part of the tour involves a short visit to the mangrove part of the forest).
It was lovely seeing the Colobus monkeys and they came very close to us on their own accord. As they have no predators on the island they were not shy to get close to us!
I would highly recommend a tour of Jozani forest, especially as a nice change from your typical day of water sports / time on the beach / snorkelling etc

content:
Our nature walk with Kesi in Jozani National Park was nothing short of spectacular. We started our adventure walking through the mangroves spotting small crabs in the mud and learning about the mangrove tree species. Kesi found some mangrove seed pods and we were able to drop them in the mud to plant a new mangrove tree. Then we found ourselves amongst a troop of blue monkeys. These monkeys are difficult to capture on camera due to their quick movements and inability to sit still. Kesi gave us plenty of time to observe their habits, munching on fruit and leaves, swinging through the trees, grooming each other and even engaging in creating the next generation. We continued our hike, Kasi pointed out birds, giant snails, lizards and skinks along the way. Eventually we made our way to a red colobus monkey troop. Picturesque in nature, these monkeys were playful and exhibited the same behaviors as the blue monkeys. This red colobus subspecies endemic to Zanzibar was giving us a show. We saw up to 5 young red colobus playing together, rolling around and nipping and chasing each other around the trees. We saw plenty of baby red colobus breastfeeding from their mothers and eventually settling into the trees for an early afternoon nap. We eventually found another troop of red colobus a little deeper in the forest, these ones seemed a little less keen on humans observing their behaviors and stayed high up in the trees. Kesi spotted a snake and an elephant shrew. It was a great tour but bring something to eat and plenty of water.
Also, Abdul, our driver serenaded to and from the destination with his soulful voice.
full_address: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour, Jozani 0000, Tanzania

content:
I really enjoyed visiting Stone Town and staying for two nights.
It’s the oldest part of Zanzibar City and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The narrow, maze-like streets are full of souvenir shops, and wandering around is part of the fun, even if you get a bit lost.
Darajani Market is a must-see for fresh fruit, fish, spices, and local products, while the Forodhani Gardens night market is perfect in the evening.
Stone Town also has great rooftops with Arabic and African-inspired décor.
The Freddie Mercury House is nice for a quick photo, and some shops selling tanzanite are worth checking out.
I felt completely safe and really enjoyed the experience.
Stone Town is authentic, vibrant, and full of charm — definitely worth spending a night or two here.

The basil you recognized, the coriander leaves swaying gently in the breeze, the dried oregano hanging under shade all these plants are not only culinary delights but also symbols of connection. content:
We booked the original Safari Blue experience, and after doing a few other snorkelling tours around the island, I can confidently say this was the best one.
We didn’t manage to see any dolphins, but the snorkelling spots we visited were absolutely amazing. There weren’t many boats around, and the Safari Blue boats seemed to coordinate with each other really well to make sure that none of the spots became too crowded. We saw plenty of fish and sea stars, and the masks provided were also surprisingly good quality. On all the other snorkelling tours we did, the masks would constantly leak, so this made a big difference!
The lunch was absolutely amazing — probably one of the best meals we had during our holiday. Everything was very fresh, and the seafood was excellent quality. There were also plenty of soft drinks and fresh fruit available throughout the trip.
The staff were really fun and friendly and definitely added to the experience. The only thing missing was a bit of music on the boat — otherwise, it was a fantastic day and I would highly recommend it!

content:
Safari blue est un grand mot à préciser. L''accueil est chalereux et le bateau est typique sur le bleu de l''océan mais le safari se résume à 2 sites de 45 mins au fonds sans réel intérêt sauf si vous êtes  impressionné par des poissons attirés par la nourriture jetée depuis le bateau.
Tous les autres touristes avaient droit à une dégustation de fruits sur l''îlot de sable sauf nous, réduit à se partager le plateau sur le bateau.
La suite et fin sur l''île de Kwale est une hall commerciale en enfilade se terminant par un vieux Baobab touristique sacrifié de tags et de 2 crabes coco grimpant à la photo payante avec en prime la centième chanson fatiguée du jour d''Hakunamatata.
Le repas avec des langoustes à la taille de grosses crevettes clôturera l''excursion.
translated_content: "Safari Blue" is a bit of an exaggeration. The welcome was warm, and the boat was typical of the blue ocean, but the safari itself consisted of two 45-minute dives to uninteresting underwater sites, unless you're impressed by fish attracted by food thrown from the boat. All the other tourists were treated to a fruit tasting on the sandbar, except for us, who were relegated to sharing the platter on the boat. The rest of the trip on Kwale Island was a series of shopping malls ending with an old, touristy baobab tree covered in graffiti and two coconut crabs climbing up for a paid photo, accompanied by the tired, hundredth rendition of "Hakuna Matata." The excursion concluded with a meal of lobsters the size of large shrimp.

content:
Le transfert ainsi que le guide ont été excellents et ont largement contribué à la réussite de l’excursion. Le snorkeling, le banc de sable et la piscine naturelle étaient également très appréciables.
En revanche, le déjeuner est clairement à revoir. J’ai prévenu la veille de l’activité que ma mère souffrait d’allergies sévères à certains aliments, notamment au citron, avec un risque potentiellement fatal. L’organisateur nous a confirmé que l’information avait été transmise aux équipes. Par précaution, nous avons également vérifié auprès du guide le jour même, qui nous a assuré que tout avait bien été pris en compte.
Quelle n’a pas été notre surprise lorsque ma mère a goûté les frites et découvert qu’elles avaient été arrosées de jus de citron. Quant aux fruits de mer, non seulement des morceaux de citron étaient disposés sur le plat, mais l’ensemble de la préparation contenait du citron. Résultat : ma mère a fait une réaction allergique et n’a pu manger pratiquement aucun des plats prévus.
Heureusement qu’elle disposait de ses médicaments et qu’elle a réagi rapidement. Une telle négligence concernant une allergie signalée à plusieurs reprises est inacceptable. Malgré nos messages, nous n’avons reçu que des excuses et aucune réponse concernant notre demande de geste commercial, alors même que ce repas était inclus dans le prix de l’excursion. Le fait d’être une petite entreprise locale ne saurait justifier un tel manque de rigueur sur un sujet aussi grave.
translated_content:
The transfer and the guide were excellent and greatly contributed to the success of the excursion. The snorkeling, the sandbar, and the natural pool were also very enjoyable.
However, lunch definitely needs improvement. I informed them the day before the activity that my mother suffers from severe food allergies, particularly to lemon, which can be life-threatening. The organizer confirmed that this information had been passed on to the team. As a precaution, we also checked with the guide on the day itself, who assured us that everything had been taken care of.
Imagine our surprise when my mother tasted the fries and discovered they had been drizzled with lemon juice. As for the seafood, not only were pieces of lemon arranged on the platter, but the entire dish contained lemon. As a result, my mother had an allergic reaction and was unable to eat almost any of the planned dishes.
Luckily, she had her medication and reacted quickly. Such negligence regarding a repeatedly reported allergy is unacceptable. Despite our messages, we received only apologies and no response to our request for compensation, even though this meal was included in the price of the excursion. Being a small, local business cannot justify such a lack of diligence on such a serious matter.

content:
Tout simplement Magnifique.
Nous avons pris contact par whatsapp pour un devis pour une sortie avec un bateau privatisé pour deux.
Il existe plusieurs formules avec groupe ou privatisation du bateau.
Le lendemain, un chauffeur est venu nous chercher à l’hôtel à l’heure précise du départ (8h00) du matin ( transfert privé pour deux).
Puis débute une balade magnifique en direction d’un banc de sable.
En cours de route, il y a avait des dauphins. On coupe le moteur pour les observer sans les déranger ( certaines compagnies traquent les dauphins pour satisfaire les clients).
La rencontre des dauphins n’est pas garantie car cela reste des animaux sauvages.
Puis on arrive sur un bancs de sable pour faire des photos.
On retourne sur le bateau en direction d’un premier spot de snorkeling.
Le capitaine et son aide restent à bord . Votre guide plonge avec vous. Il a toujours une bouée si vous êtes fatigué et des gilets de sauvetage si vous ne savez pas nager . On vous prête masque et tuba.
Le guide plonge avec vous et vous donne les explications sur les noms des poissons et étoiles de mers . Les coraux sont magnifiques.
On va ensuite sur un autre spot de snorkeling.
Là arrive la faim! Et bien très bien, on arrive sur île oú une table privee sur la sable vous attend avec homard, thon, écrevisses au barbecue. Le vin blanc est frais que demander de plus .
Après cette magnifique pause , direction en bateau la mangrove pour se baigner dans une piscine  naturelle.
Puis retour à la base mais là encore belle surprise, comme nous sommes bateau privé et que le vent est bon le retour est à la voile ( 1h00).
Bref , c’est magique , l’équipage est gentil et pro.
il faut faire cette sortie en groupe ou en privé comme nous .
A noter , avoir des chaussures plastiques c’est mieux car à marrée basse pour aller sur le bateau tôt le matin c’est compliqué, il y a quelques cailloux, ça coupe et ça glisse .

Simply magnificent.
We contacted them via WhatsApp for a quote for a private boat trip for two.
There are several options available, including group bookings and private boat rentals.
The next day, a driver picked us up at the hotel at the precise departure time (8:00 am) (private transfer for two).
Then began a magnificent boat trip towards a sandbar.
Along the way, we saw dolphins. We turned off the engine to observe them without disturbing them (some companies actively seek out dolphins to satisfy their customers).
A dolphin encounter is not guaranteed, as they are still wild animals.
Then we arrived at a sandbar to take photos.
We returned to the boat and headed towards our first snorkeling spot.
The captain and his assistant remained on board. Your guide dives with you. He always has a buoy if you get tired and life jackets if you can't swim. Masks and snorkels are provided. The guide dives with you and explains the names of the fish and starfish. The corals are magnificent.
Then we head to another snorkeling spot. And that's when hunger strikes! We arrive at an island where a private table on the sand awaits us with barbecued lobster, tuna, and crayfish. The white wine is chilled—what more could you ask for?
After this wonderful break, we take a boat to the mangroves to swim in a natural pool.
Then it's back to the base, but here's another pleasant surprise: since we're on a private boat and the wind is good, we sail back (1 hour).
In short, it's magical, the crew is friendly and professional. You should definitely do this trip, either in a group or privately like we did.
Note: it's best to wear plastic shoes because at low tide, getting to the boat early in the morning is tricky; there are some sharp, slippery pebbles.
full_address: The Safari Blue, Zanzibar, Fumba Village, Zanzibar, Tanzania

content:
Lasciate perdere!
Un''ora di pulimino scomodo (dipende da dove si parte) e 2 ore in barca malconcia per non vedere nulla.
Volte una spiaggia bella e spettacolare, di vera sabbia bianchissima? Recatevi a Nungwi. Evitate questa trappola turistica.
25, 25 barche sulla lingua di sabbia color marroncino chiaro e NON BIANCA. Centinai di persone ammassate e barche ovunque.
Non parliamo dello snorkeling! I coralli non esistono e vedrete solo ed esclusivamente dei pesci sargente attirati dal cibo che viene gettato loro. Ora, se non avete mai visto dei pesci saregente tutti assieme si, diventa carino, ma non aspettatevi altro. Infine la piscina nelle mangrovie è una palude. Se decidete di prendere parte a qusta follia e regalare i vostri soldi, portatevi almeno le scarpette da scoglio. Pranzo frettoloso e tutto fritto. Polpo, calamari, patate, gamberi e mezza aragostella di numero a testa. Volete una birra fredda? La pagherete oltre 3 euro (prezzo da discoteca di zanzibar, non da gita in spiaggia). Ovviamente non mancheranno le varie occasioni di vendita promosse dalla guida. Immancabili anche le foto con animali vari tenuti in cattività, matrattati e utilizzati a scopo economico (scimmiette varie e granchi del cocco).
Infine, se decidete in ogni caso di andare a farvi spennare, cercate di trattare! A noi hanno sparato 150$ in due. Alla fine abbiamo chiuso a 80$. Ho sentito di persone che hanno pagato 110/130$ senza battere ciglio. Ripeto, evitate.
translated_content:
Forget it!
An hour on an uncomfortable minibus (depending on where you're departing from) and two hours on a battered boat to see nothing.
Want a beautiful, spectacular beach with real, pure white sand? Go to Nungwi. Avoid this tourist trap.
25, 25 boats on a strip of light brown, NOT WHITE, sand. Hundreds of people crowded together and boats everywhere.
Let's not even talk about snorkeling! There's no coral, and you'll only see sangria fish attracted by the food thrown to them. Now, if you've never seen sangria fish all together, yes, it's cute, but don't expect anything else. Finally, the pool in the mangroves is a swamp. If you decide to take part in this madness and give away your money, at least bring water shoes. Lunch was a quick one, and everything was fried. Octopus, calamari, potatoes, shrimp, and half a lobster each. Want a cold beer? You'll pay over €3 (Zanzibar nightclub price, not beach trip price). Of course, there will be plenty of sales opportunities promoted by the guide. Photos with various animals held in captivity, mistreated, and exploited for profit (various monkeys and coconut crabs) are also a must.
Finally, if you decide to go and get fleeced, try to bargain! They charged us $150 between the two of us. We ended up paying $80. I've heard of people paying $110-$130 without batting an eyelid. Again, avoid.

content:
Il Safari Blue con Zantour è un’escursione ben organizzata, anche se rimane un’esperienza piuttosto turistica e poco “selvaggia” come suggerirebbe il nome. La giornata parte con la classica uscita in dhow e le tappe sono più o meno quelle note: snorkeling, sosta sulla lingua di sabbia e pranzo sull’isoletta.
Lo snorkeling è carino, anche se le zone visitate tendono a essere affollate e la barriera non è tra le più spettacolari della zona. La sosta sulla sandbank è piacevole ma breve, e il mare, per quanto bello, risente un po’ della concentrazione di barche e gruppi.
Il pranzo è abbondante, con pesce e frutta fresca, e il personale Zantour è disponibile e ben coordinato. Il tour però segue uno schema abbastanza rigido, quindi tutto risulta un po’ “di routine”.
In sintesi: una giornata diversa e ben gestita, adatta a chi vuole fare un assaggio delle attività marine di Zanzibar senza complicazioni. Bella, ma non aspettarsi un’esperienza particolarmente esclusiva o fuori dal tracciato turistico.
translated_content:
The Safari Blue with Zantour is a well-organized excursion, although it remains a rather touristy experience and not as "wild" as the name suggests. The day begins with a classic dhow excursion, and the stops are more or less the usual ones: snorkeling, a stop on the sandbank, and lunch on the islet.
The snorkeling is nice, although the areas visited tend to be crowded and the reef isn't among the most spectacular in the area. The stop on the sandbank is pleasant but brief, and the sea, while beautiful, suffers somewhat from the concentration of boats and groups.
The lunch is plentiful, with fresh fish and fruit, and the Zantour staff is helpful and well-coordinated. However, the tour follows a fairly rigid schedule, so everything feels a bit routine.
In summary: a different and well-managed day, suitable for those who want a taste of Zanzibar's marine activities without complications. It's beautiful, but don't expect a particularly exclusive or off-the-beaten-path experience.

content:
We did the full day group snorkel tour which was just okay. From the start there were no clear instructions of what was going on and over 100 people waiting around for direction.
Once split into groups all the boats end up at the same locations and most places are overcrowded. The first of the two snorkel spots was decent, nice coral but nothing spectacular, around 30 minutes spent there.
At the second spot, barely any of our group got in the water for some reason so those of us who did were rushed and maybe had 10 minutes before being put back on the boat.
You then end up spending most of the day at the lunch spot. We ended up going to explore the island as we were given no direction and then came back to our whole group waiting for us on the boat. The guides at least could’ve given us a time to all meet back. We felt horrible.
All in all, an okay tour but it could be executed better with some clearer communication and limit of boats going out. For a snorkel tour we also expected more time actually snorkelling

content:
Plaża Fumba to miejsce gdzie  rozpoczyna się Blue Safari. Stoi tu dużo zacumowanych  tradycyjnych łodzi Dhow. Na brzegu pełno straganów z różnego rodzajami lokalnych  pamiątek, tkanin Kanga i Kitenge, drewnianych  rzeźb Makonde oraz biżuterii z koralików.
Blue Safari jest to rejs tradycyjną  łodzią  Dhow z plaży Fumba po obszarze  chronionym zatoki Menai ze snurkowaniem w Błękitnej Lagunie i przerwą na lunch na wyspie Kwale. Stąd możesz popływać w naturalnym basenie między starymi skałami koralowymi i drzewami namorzynowymi. Z łodzi można obserwować delfiny w Oceanie Indyjskim. Podczas tego rejsu można nurkować z rurką w obszarze chronionym Menai, który jest w dużej mierze dziewiczy i obserwować kolorowe ryby, a czasem żółwie, które zamieszkują ten obszar. Można podziwiać wystające z wody niezwykłe formacje skalne. Sandbank czyli znikająca w czasie przypływu wyspa piaskowa jest miejscem na odpoczynek w trakcie  rejsu  podczas którego serwowane są  przekąski w postaci owoców.
translated_content:
Fumba Beach is the starting point for the Blue Safari. Many traditional dhows are moored here. The shore is full of stalls selling a variety of local souvenirs, Kanga and Kitenge textiles, Makonde wooden carvings, and beaded jewelry.
The Blue Safari is a traditional dhow cruise from Fumba Beach through the Menai Bay Conservation Area, with snorkeling in the Blue Lagoon and a lunch stop on Kwale Island. From here, you can swim in a natural pool among ancient coral reefs and mangroves. From the boat, you can observe dolphins in the Indian Ocean. During this cruise, you can snorkel in the largely untouched Menai Conservation Area, observing the colorful fish and occasional turtles that inhabit the area. You can admire the unusual rock formations jutting out from the water. Sandbank, a sand island that disappears at high tide, is a place to rest during the cruise, where fruit snacks are served.
